How big is Boston and what is it bordered by?

Boston is the capital and largest city in Massachusetts, and it lies in Suffolk County. Its total area is about 89.6 square miles, but only 48.3 square miles of that is land. The other 41.3 square miles is water.

The city is bordered by several communities that matter when you compare sale prices and property tax bills:

  • Winthrop and the Boston Harbor Islands to the east
  • Revere, Chelsea and Everett to the northeast
  • Somerville and Cambridge to the north
  • Watertown to the northwest
  • Newton and Brookline to the west
  • Dedham, with small portions of Needham and Canton, to the southwest
  • Milton and Quincy to the southeast

The Charles River separates Allston-Brighton, Fenway-Kenmore and Back Bay from Cambridge and Watertown. The Neponset River forms the line between southern Boston and Quincy and Milton. The highest point in the city is Bellevue Hill at 330 feet.

What are the neighborhoods of Boston?

The city's Office of Neighborhood Services recognizes 23 neighborhoods, which is why Boston is often called a city of neighborhoods. Your neighborhood affects how a house sells more than the city name does.

AreaNeighborhoods
Downtown coreDowntown or Financial District, Beacon Hill, West End, North End, Chinatown, Bay Village
Central and waterfrontBack Bay, South End, Seaport District, South Boston, East Boston, Charlestown
West and southwestAllston, Brighton, Fenway-Kenmore, Mission Hill, Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, Hyde Park
SouthRoxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan

Boston also has 53 ZIP codes, so check the ZIP and the neighborhood on your assessment record instead of assuming they match.

How did Boston's land and housing take shape?

Boston was settled in 1625, named in 1630 and became a city in 1822. More than two thirds of the modern land area of inner Boston did not exist when the city was founded. It was created by filling tidal areas, using earth from leveling the three original hills and gravel brought by train from Needham to fill Back Bay.

That history shows up in the housing. Back Bay has single family homes along with wooden and brick multi-family row houses. The South End Historic District is the largest surviving contiguous Victorian era neighborhood in the country. Downtown and South Boston have low rise masonry buildings in Federal and Greek Revival styles beside modern towers.

The Central Artery/Tunnel Project, known as the Big Dig, ran from 1991 to 2007 and replaced the elevated highway through downtown with tunnels, new green spaces and open areas. The South End is a designated historic district, so if your house is in an area like it, ask the city whether review rules apply to exterior work.

How dense is Boston, and why does it matter to sellers?

Boston is the most densely populated state capital in the country, and the third most densely populated large US city of more than half a million residents. Its density is about 13,977 people per square mile of land.

The daytime population is larger than the resident count. Around 1.2 million people may be inside city limits during work hours, and as many as 2 million during special events, because suburban residents commute in. For a seller, that means on-street parking, building access and noise are real selling points or objections, and buyers will ask about them when they walk the house.

What employers drive the Boston economy?

Health care and education dominate Boston's employer list. The city ranks among the top 30 most economically powerful in the world And the Greater Boston metro area had a GDP of about $645 billion in 2024.

6Boston Medical Center
7Boston University School of Medicine

The 2018 list of Boston's largest companies by revenue included General Electric, Liberty Mutual, State Street and American Tower.

What does Boston weather mean for a house?

Boston has hot, humid summers and cold, stormy winters, with occasional periods of heavy snow. Under one common classification it is humid subtropical, and under another it is humid continental.

  • July is the warmest month, with a mean temperature of 74.1 degrees F.
  • January is the coldest, with a mean of 29.9 degrees F.
  • The freezing window runs from about November 9 to April 5.
  • The most recent reading below zero was minus 10 degrees F on February 4, 2023, and sub-zero readings usually occur every three to five years.

Winters can bring wide swings, and in winter the immediate coast often sees rain where inland areas see snow.

How do Boston property tax and abatements work for a seller?

Massachusetts assessors value property as of January 1 before the fiscal year, and an owner who thinks the value is too high must first file an abatement application with the city's assessors. That application is due on or before the due date of the first actual tax bill. In towns that bill quarterly, that is generally February 1.

The Appellate Tax Board then hears appeals. It holds hearings at 100 Cambridge Street in Boston at Government Center, and often by video. Most single family hearings run one to two hours, and a case takes about four months to a year to reach a hearing.

Ask the Boston Assessing Department for the current rate, whether your home qualifies for the residential exemption, and your abatement deadline. Your actual bill states the due dates.

What does a Boston closing involve?

Boston is in Suffolk County, so your deed is recorded at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. Massachusetts charges a deed excise tax when a deed is recorded. The neighboring Norfolk County registry lists $2.28 for each $500 of the price or fraction of it, and the same state statute applies in Suffolk County, so ask the Suffolk registry or your attorney for its fee schedule.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. You need a certificate of compliance from the local fire department. Schedule the inspection as soon as you have a closing date, and expect to pay a fee.
  • Attorney involvement. A Massachusetts court has held that lender side closings need an attorney's substantive participation, so most sales involve a real estate attorney.
  • Home inspection. State regulation 760 CMR 74 stops sellers of certain residential properties from conditioning an offer on a waiver of the buyer's inspection.
  • Title systems. Most properties are recorded land, but some Massachusetts property is registered land with a Land Court certificate.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth also runs a registry consumer notification service that emails you when a new document is recorded against your property. That is worth signing up for if you are selling an inherited home or one with a title question.

What should a Boston seller with tenants know?

Many Boston houses have more than one unit. If yours does, ask the city's Inspectional Services Department whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and ask your attorney how existing leases transfer to a buyer.

A direct sale lets you skip showings while tenants stay in place. We buy Boston houses as they are, and you can compare our number with a listing price before you decide.

Who are the biggest employers in Boston?

The 2023 top ten list is led by Brigham and Women's Hospital, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Massachusetts General Hospital and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.

How do I appeal my Boston property tax assessment?

File an abatement application with the Boston assessors on or before the due date of your first actual tax bill. If it is denied or ignored, you have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell a Boston house?

Where is Worcester, Massachusetts, and how big is it?

Worcester is the principal city of Central Massachusetts and the seat of Worcester County. It sits about 40 miles west of Boston, 50 miles east of Springfield and 38 miles northwest of Providence.

The city covers 38.4 square miles and borders Auburn, Grafton, Holden, Leicester, Millbury, Paxton, Shrewsbury and West Boylston. The Census Bureau counted 206,518 residents in 2020 and estimated 213,862 for 2025, which makes Worcester the second largest city in both Massachusetts and New England.

At that size, a Worcester house is compared with many others, and the local conditions below shape how buyers and cash investors look at it.

Why do people call Worcester the City of Seven Hills?

Worcester is built on hills, and the nickname lists seven of them: Airport Hill, Bancroft Hill, Belmont Hill, Grafton Hill, Green Hill, Pakachoag Hill and Vernon Hill. There are more than seven, including Indian Hill, Newton Hill and Wigwam Hill.

The Blackstone River begins in the center of the city where the Middle River and Mill Brook meet, then runs underground through downtown and reappears at the foot of College Hill. Lake Quinsigamond, also called Long Pond, stretches four miles along the Worcester and Shrewsbury border and is a rowing venue.

If your lot slopes or sits near a pond or brook, mention drainage or past water problems when you describe the property.

How did Worcester's industrial past shape its housing?

Worcester's housing stock comes straight from its factory years. The town was incorporated in 1722, and it became a city in 1848, the same year the Blackstone Canal closed. Canal and then railways carried raw materials in and finished machines, textiles and wire out.

The city as having many 19th century triple-decker houses, Victorian-era mills and lunch-car diners. Manufacturing faded after World War II and the population fell, then turned around from the 1990s as higher education, medicine and biotechnology grew. The population has risen 28% since 1980 and hit its highest count in 2020.

  • Triple-deckers are a common building type in the city.
  • A cash buyer prices the age and condition of an older house into the offer instead of asking you to fix things first.

What does Worcester weather mean for a house?

Worcester is known for snow, and the roof and gutters carry the cost. The city averages 64 inches of snowfall in a season and about 48 inches of total precipitation a year, Which also notes that Worcester sits higher than much of the surrounding terrain and is prone to nor'easters.

Extremes have been recorded. About 120 inches fell in the winter of 2005, and a blizzard in late January 2015 dropped almost 32 inches, the highest single-day snowfall in Massachusetts records dating to 1892. The city was also hit by the 1938 hurricane, and on June 9, 1953 an F4 tornado killed 94 people, the deadliest in New England history.

For a seller the lesson is simple. Roof, gutter and pipe damage after a hard winter is the kind of repair a buyer's inspector will look for. If you would rather not deal with repairs, an as-is sale skips that step.

Who are Worcester's biggest employers?

Healthcare and education lead Worcester's employment. The city's 2018 Comprehensive Annual Financial Report, as summarized on Wikipedia, lists these top employers:

Eight colleges and universities in the city, including Holy Cross, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Clark University, Assumption University and Worcester State University. Hanover Insurance was founded here in 1852 and keeps its headquarters in the city, and the Massachusetts Biotechnology Research Park hosts research companies.

If you own a multifamily house, tell us whether tenants stay or leave, since that affects how a buyer values the building.

What highways and rail connect Worcester?

Worcester is a highway crossroads. Route 146 and Interstates 90, 190, 290, 395 and 495 all serve the city and its suburbs, which have drawn Worcester closer to Boston's commuter zone since the 1970s.

Interstate 290 was cut through the center of the city in the 1960s, and Wikipedia says it permanently divided the city. Union Station reopened in 2000 after a $32 million renovation. Worcester Regional Airport reports its elevation as about 1,000 feet, well above the 479 feet listed for the city as a whole.

Access to the interstate and to Union Station is one of the details we ask about when you describe your house.

How are Worcester property taxes billed?

Worcester bills real estate tax four times a year, and each bill is due 30 days after its issue date. According to the city's Real Estate Tax page, bills are issued July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, on a fiscal year running July 1 through June 30.

The first two bills are preliminary, each based on the previous year's tax divided by four. The third and fourth are actual bills, calculated from the new assessment and rate, less what was already billed, divided by two. The city says any change from reassessment shows up only in the third and fourth quarters.

The page lists residential and commercial classes at separate rates, $13.28 and $29.06 per $1,000 of assessed value, without naming the fiscal year, so confirm the current rate with the city. Assessing is at City Hall, Room 209, 455 Main Street, phone 508-799-1098, email assessing@worcesterma.gov, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

  • An abatement is the route to dispute value or correct a billing error, and the city offers an online application.
  • Elderly, surviving spouse, blind and disabled veteran exemptions require an annual application.
  • Owners of apartment and mixed-use buildings are asked to file annual expense forms, which the city says are not public record.

For the statewide rules, see our Massachusetts property tax guide.

What steps come up when selling a Worcester house?

A Worcester sale follows Massachusetts law. Two state rules come up in nearly every closing, and local offices handle the rest.

  • Smoke detectors. M.G.L. c. 148, section 26F requires the seller to equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors on sale or transfer, enforced by the head of the fire department.
  • Deed excise. M.G.L. c. 64D, section 1 sets the excise at $2 for each $500 of consideration or fraction, and your closing attorney will work out the figure.
  • Taxes due. Ask the city for the status of every bill before closing so the attorney can settle them from proceeds.

If your Worcester house is a triple-decker with tenants, speak with an attorney early about notices and security deposits. We do not give legal advice, and rules for occupied properties can differ.

What does a cash sale look like in Worcester?

A cash sale in Worcester means a buyer purchases the house as is, with no lender to approve. We review the address, condition, tax status and whether tenants live there, then make an offer, and you decide whether to accept.

This route often suits owners who inherited a house they do not want to manage, who live out of state, or who face repair costs they cannot cover before listing. A title company or attorney handles the closing, and you pick the date within a reasonable range.

Call or text us and we will tell you plainly what we can and cannot do for your Worcester house.

How far is Worcester from Boston?

Worcester is about 40 miles west of Boston, 50 miles east of Springfield and 38 miles northwest of Providence, Rhode Island. Interstates 90 and 290 and Route 146 connect it to those cities.

When are Worcester property tax bills due?

Bills are issued July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each is due 30 days after it is issued. The first two are preliminary and the last two are actual, based on the new assessment.

How do I dispute my Worcester assessment?

File a real estate abatement application with the Assessing Division, which the city lets you do online or on paper. Call 508-799-1098 for the form and the current filing deadline.

Do I need a smoke detector inspection to sell in Worcester?

Yes. Massachusetts requires the seller to equip a residential building with approved smoke detectors when it is sold or transferred. The head of the fire department enforces the rule.

Can I sell a Worcester triple-decker with tenants?

Yes, a cash buyer can purchase a multifamily house with tenants in place. Talk with an attorney about notice and deposit rules first, and tell us the number of units and the rents when you ask for an offer.

Which Worcester employers are the largest?

According to the city's 2018 financial report, UMass Memorial Health Care is the largest with 13,745 employees, followed by the City of Worcester at 5,473 and UMass Medical School at 4,172.

Where is Springfield, MA, and what is the city like?

Springfield is the largest city in Western Massachusetts and the seat of Hampden County, on the east bank of the Connecticut River. The 2020 census counted 155,929 residents, and the surrounding metro area is about 699,000.

The city covers 33.1 square miles, of which 31.9 are land. The Westfield River meets the Connecticut opposite the South End Bridge, and the Chicopee River joins just north of the city. The Connecticut state line is about four miles south, next to Longmeadow.

The Metro Center district around Main Street is flat and follows the river. Moving east, the ground turns hilly. Springfield has also been nicknamed "The City of Homes" and "A City in the Forest," and more than 4 square miles of it, about 12% of the land, is urban parkland.

A short history of Springfield

William Pynchon founded Springfield on May 14, 1636, and it became a city on May 25, 1852. The town was named for Springfield in Essex, England.

It was once much larger. Chicopee split off in 1852, Longmeadow in 1783 and West Springfield in 1774. The city also owns the Springfield Country Club, which sits inside West Springfield.

Springfield is known as "The City of Firsts," and in December 2022 the National Park Service designated it an American World War II Heritage City, the first in Massachusetts. Landmarks include the Basketball Hall of Fame, Symphony Hall and the Springfield Armory.

What are the neighborhoods of Springfield, MA?

Springfield is divided into 17 neighborhoods, and the housing in each can look very different. The list includes Bay, Boston Road, Brightwood, East Forest Park, East Springfield, Forest Park, Indian Orchard, Liberty Heights, McKnight, Memorial Square, Metro Center, Old Hill, Pine Point, Six Corners, Sixteen Acres, South End and Upper Hill.

  • Forest Park and Forest Park Heights surround a 735-acre park and include more than 600 Victorian "Painted Lady" houses
  • McKnight is described as the first planned residential neighborhood in the United States, with over 900 Painted Ladies
  • Indian Orchard grew as a mill town on the Chicopee River and still has a Main Street and former mill buildings
  • Liberty Heights holds Baystate Health, Mercy Medical and Shriners Children's hospital
  • Sixteen Acres, Pine Point and East Forest Park are mostly residential
  • East Springfield is residential and working-class, close to the former Smith & Wesson campus and a food distributor

Brightwood is cut off from the rest of the city by the elevated Interstate 91, a detail worth mentioning to buyers who care about noise or access.

Who are the big employers in Springfield?

Health care, insurance and manufacturing anchor the Springfield economy. A list drawn from the state labor agency names Baystate Medical Center, Smith & Wesson, General Dynamics, MassMutual, Mercy Medical Center, the U.S. Postal Service and Big Y Foods among the top city employers.

Smith & Wesson moved its corporate headquarters from East Springfield to Tennessee in 2023, though it planned to keep many Massachusetts jobs. MassMutual is a Fortune 100 company with its headquarters in the Pine Point area. In 2018, CRRC began assembling Orange Line cars in Springfield, and the city has also invested in a casino and a redeveloped Union Station.

The region markets itself as the Knowledge Corridor, with dozens of colleges within a short drive, including Springfield College, American International College and Springfield Technical Community College.

How does the weather affect a Springfield house?

Springfield has a hot-summer humid continental climate with cold winters. January averages about 26 degrees Fahrenheit, July about 74, and several days a summer top 90.

Annual snowfall averages 40.5 inches, mostly between mid-December and early March, and temperatures below zero can occur in any year. That makes the roof, insulation, heating system and gutters standard inspection topics.

On June 1, 2011, a tornado with winds above 160 miles per hour struck Springfield directly. It killed three people, left more than 500 homeless in the city and cut a 39-mile path from Westfield to Charlton. If your house was repaired after storm damage, keep the records, since buyers and their lenders may ask.

How do roads and rail connect Springfield?

Springfield sits where north-south traffic along Interstate 91 meets east-west travel to Boston and New York. Union Station was redeveloped for roughly $95 million, and Peter Pan Bus Lines moved its Springfield terminal there in 2017.

The planned New Haven to Hartford to Springfield rail line was described as a $1 billion project. Anyone selling near Union Station or Metro Center may want to point out the walking distance to transit, while owners near the interstate should expect questions about traffic noise.

What steps apply when you sell a house in Massachusetts?

A Massachusetts home sale needs a fire department certificate showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules. The Department of Fire Services advises scheduling the inspection as soon as you have a closing date, and local departments charge a fee.

The alarm rules depend on the house's build date and the last building permit. Older battery smoke alarms must be swapped for ten-year sealed photoelectric units, and any alarm without a date stamp counts as expired.

The law library notes that most deeds are filed as recorded land at the county Registry of Deeds, and that attorneys are a regular part of closings. The same guide lists a state regulation on inspection waivers for certain residential sales, so ask your attorney whether it applies to your house.

What are your options to sell a house in Springfield?

Springfield owners can list, sell privately or accept a cash offer, and the right choice depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to close.

  • Listing helps if the house is in showing condition and you can wait for a financed buyer
  • A private sale saves agent fees but puts the paperwork on you
  • A cash offer as-is suits inherited, damaged, vacant or tenant-occupied houses

Houses in the neighborhoods above vary a great deal, so a buyer or cash investor will price each address on its own condition, lot and block. Photos, a repair list and any utility or tax paperwork help any buyer decide quickly.

Older Victorian houses in Forest Park or McKnight may carry deferred maintenance that a financed buyer's lender will flag. A cash buyer can purchase without repairs, but the offer will reflect those needs.

Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department when you sell. Call as soon as you set a closing date, and expect an inspection fee.

Yes. Buyers, including cash buyers, purchase houses with deferred repairs. Gather any repair records, since the price will reflect the condition.

They are rare, but a tornado struck Springfield directly on June 1, 2011, and caused significant damage across a 39-mile path.

Where is Cambridge, Massachusetts, and how is it organized?

Cambridge is a city in Middlesex County directly across the Charles River from Boston. It has 7.1 square miles of area, 6.4 of them land, and the 2020 census counted 118,403 residents, which made it the fourth-largest city in the state after Boston, Worcester and Springfield.

Somerville lies to the north, Arlington to the northwest, and Belmont and Watertown to the west. The city runs a council-manager government, and its ZIP codes run from 02138 to 02142.

Cambridge calls itself a city of squares, because most commercial districts sit at major street intersections that act as neighborhood centers. That shapes how people describe where a house is.

What are Cambridge's squares and neighborhoods?

Each square anchors a part of the city, and buyers often ask which one a house is closest to. These centers.

  • Kendall Square, at Broadway, Main Street and Third Street, is the biotech and technology center near MIT and the Kendall/MIT Red Line station.
  • Central Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue, has a Red Line stop and a mix of restaurants.
  • Harvard Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and JFK Street, has the Harvard Red Line station and Cambridge Common nearby.
  • Porter Square has both a Red Line stop and a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.
  • Inman Square sits at Cambridge and Hampshire Streets, and Lechmere Square is next to CambridgeSide.

Neighborhoods such as Cambridgeport, Baldwin (formerly Agassiz, renamed in 2021) and Mid-Cambridge round out the map. A listing that names the square it is closest to gives a buyer an instant sense of place.

What is the history behind Cambridge?

Cambridge was settled in 1630, was first called Newtowne, and was renamed Cambridge in May 1638 after the English university town. Harvard College was founded here in 1636, and the city was incorporated in 1846.

George Washington took command of the Continental Army on Cambridge Common in July 1775, so the Common is called the birthplace of the Army. Brattle Street was once nicknamed Tory Row because Loyalist families lived there in mansions.

Manufacturing was important in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and areas such as Kendall Square and East Cambridge were once centers of manufacturing before turning to biotech, labs and offices. Older buildings from each era remain across the city.

How do you get around Cambridge?

The MBTA Red Line is the spine of the city, with stops at Kendall/MIT, Central, Harvard and Porter squares. Porter Square also has a commuter rail stop on the Fitchburg Line.

Harvard Square is still a major bus terminal. Before the West Boston Bridge opened in 1792, crossing from Cambridge to Boston meant an eight-mile trip by road around the Boston Neck, and bridges over the Charles River now tie the two cities together.

If your house is a short walk from a Red Line stop, put that in the description.

How does Cambridge assess property and bill taxes?

The Assessing Department values property at what Massachusetts calls full and fair cash value, which is 100 percent of fair market value. It uses cost, income and market approaches and submits values to the state Department of Revenue for certification before bills are issued.

The office is at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, and the phone is 617-349-4343. For municipal lien certificates and online payments, the Finance Department is at 617-349-4220. Municipal lien certificates matter when you sell, since they show what is owed on the property.

The city's finances and its water system both show up in a sale. Cambridge held AAA ratings from Moody's, S&P and Fitch for 22 consecutive years as of 2021, and Wikipedia says its large commercial tax base has helped keep residential taxes fairly low. Its budget is the second largest in the state even though it is fourth in population.

Cambridge also runs its own municipal water system, including the Payson Park Reservoir in Belmont and the Hobbs Brook and Stony Brook watersheds in neighboring towns. The Assessing page warns that a first-half FY27 tax bill can carry a Water and Sewer Lien, so check your bill and call the Finance Department if one appears before you list or sign a contract.

The universities add another layer. MIT has a 168-acre campus here, and Harvard was founded in the city in 1636. Wikipedia also places Lesley University's University Hall and Porter campus at Porter Square,.

Cambridge houses often come with specific complications: older construction, multi-unit buildings, tenants and historic districts.

  • Estate sales take time because of probate.
  • Condominium sales require documents from the association.
  • Older houses can need work before a buyer's lender will move forward.

These are general sale issues, not Cambridge rules. If any apply to you, a direct cash sale is one way to avoid showings and repairs.

Book that inspection when you have a closing date, because the department charges a fee. Alarms older than ten years or past their expiration must be replaced with ten-year sealed photoelectric alarms with a hush feature.

Where is Lowell, Massachusetts, and how big is it?

Lowell is a city in Middlesex County at the meeting of the Merrimack and Concord rivers, and it shares the title of traditional county seat with Cambridge. The 2020 census counted 115,554 residents, which made it the fifth most populous city in the state and the third largest in the Boston metropolitan area.

The city covers 14.5 square miles, with about 0.8 square miles of that water. Lowell was settled in 1652, incorporated as a town in 1826 and became a city in 1836. It carries the name of Francis Cabot Lowell, a figure of the Industrial Revolution.

Lowell uses a city manager and city council form of government, and it has five ZIP codes, one of which (01853) is for post office boxes only.

How did mills and canals shape Lowell?

The Pawtucket Falls gave Lowell its power. Native people fished at the falls for centuries before the mills, and in the 1800s the falls drove the textile factories that made Lowell the cradle of the American Industrial Revolution.

Much of the old mill district is now preserved as Lowell National Historical Park, run by the National Park Service.

Lowell also took in refugees during the Cambodian genocide of 1975 to 1979. The city has a Cambodia Town and the second-largest Cambodian-American population in the country.

Which neighborhoods make up Lowell?

Lowell has eight distinct neighborhoods, and each has its own character and ZIP code grouping. Knowing which one you are in helps frame what buyers expect.

  • The Highlands (01851): the most populated area, with almost a quarter of residents. It lies in the southwest and includes Tyler Park, Drum Hill and the UMass Lowell South Campus.
  • Centralville (01850): the northeastern section north of the Merrimack River, including Christian Hill.
  • Downtown, Belvidere, Back Central and South Lowell (01852): the southeastern sections. Belvidere is mostly residential, and the Belvidere Hill Historic District runs along Fairmount Street.
  • The Acre and Pawtucketville: the remaining two of the eight neighborhoods. Ask which one a property sits in before comparing it with others.

Smaller names such as Ayers City, Bleachery, Chapel Hill, the Grove, Oaklands and Swede Village are still used, and Wikipedia notes that people are using them again.

What does the Lowell climate mean for a house?

Lowell has long cold winters and hot humid summers. The yearly average temperature is 49 degrees, and January highs average around 34 degrees in the 1991 to 2020 normals.

Snow is the main factor. Lowell averages about 56 inches a season, and the heaviest season on record brought 120 inches in the winter of 2014 and 2015. That kind of load tests older roofs, porches and gutters.

If you are selling a house with a patched roof, ice damage or an old boiler, a buyer's inspector will flag it. A cash buyer will usually price those items in directly instead of asking you to fix them first.

Who works in Lowell, and how do residents commute?

Higher education is a major presence. UMass Lowell has three campuses in the city, and Middlesex Community College has campuses in Lowell and Bedford, together serving more than 31,000 students. Lowell General Hospital and Saints Medical Center add health care jobs.

Roads include Interstate 495, U.S. Route 3, the Lowell Connector and Massachusetts Routes 3A, 38, 110, 113 and 133. The Lowell Regional Transit Authority runs local buses, and the MBTA Lowell Line has several daily trips to North Station.

Lowell Public Schools runs the public schools, and Lowell High School is the district high school. Greater Lowell Technical High School and several charter schools also serve students.

How do Lowell property taxes work, and what if I fall behind?

Lowell bills real estate tax in four installments, issued July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. Due dates are the first of August, November, February and May, or the first business day of the month.

If you do not pay by the due date, interest runs at 14 percent a year. A $30 demand fee and demand notice follow after May 1, and unpaid real estate tax can become a lien. If your mortgage company escrows your taxes, you are still responsible for making sure the bill is paid.

For questions about why a bill is high, the Treasurer points people to the Assessor's office. Online card payments carry a fee of at least 2.95 percent, with a $1 minimum, and e-check payments cost $0.40.

Can I challenge my Lowell assessment?

Yes, but you must follow a fixed schedule. Under the Appellate Tax Board's guide, an abatement application is due by the first installment due date of the actual tax bill, generally February 1 for a quarterly-billing city.

Assessors have three months to act. If they do not, the application is treated as denied and you have three months to file with the board. You must pay each installment on time for the board to hear your case, with narrow exceptions such as a tax of $5,000 or less.

The value is measured as of January 1 before the fiscal year, so recent sales of similar homes near that date are your best evidence.

What does a Lowell closing involve, and who buys as-is?

Attorneys handle Massachusetts closings, and your deed will be recorded at the Middlesex County registry. The fire department must issue a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate of compliance, and the state advises booking the inspection once you have a closing date.

The statute on deed excise lists $2 for each $500 of the price, so confirm the total at the registry. You also need payoff letters for any mortgage and a clear tax and water balance.

The state's law library explains that most Massachusetts land is recorded land, filed at the Registry of Deeds with a book and page number. A smaller share is registered land, described on a Certificate of Title issued by the Land Court. Your attorney will check which system applies to your lot, since registered land follows slightly different filing steps.

Late real estate tax in Lowell accrues interest at 14 percent a year. After the May 1 due date, a $30 demand fee is added, and a demand notice is mailed for any unpaid bill.

Is the postmark date accepted for a Lowell tax payment?

No. The city says a payment counts when the Treasurer's office receives it, so mail early or pay online. Rejected online payments can take up to three business days to become available again.

Lowell is in Middlesex County, so deeds are recorded through the county Registry of Deeds. You can search a deed copy at masslandrecords.com, which the state law library points to.

Where is Brockton, Massachusetts, and how big is it?

Brockton is a city in Plymouth County, about 22 miles south of Boston and 30 miles northeast of Providence. The 2020 census counted 105,643 residents, which makes it the sixth-largest city in Massachusetts and the most populous community in the county.

It covers 21.5 square miles of land. Avon, Holbrook, Abington, Whitman, East Bridgewater, West Bridgewater, Easton and Stoughton border it. Brockton and Plymouth share the role of county seat.

Most of the city is built up. The Salisbury Plain River once powered the shoe factories, and the largest green space is D.W. Field Park, an Olmsted-inspired park with ponds and a golf course. The city uses ZIP codes 02301 through 02305.

What is Brockton's history, and why does it matter for old houses?

Brockton was part of Bridgewater until June 15, 1821, when it was set off as North Bridgewater. Residents voted to rename it Brockton on May 5, 1874, and it became a city on April 9, 1881.

Shoes built the housing stock. Brockton was the country's largest shoe producer during the Civil War, and the shoe industry stayed large until late in the twentieth century. W.B. Mason, the office supply company, has been headquartered here since 1898.

On October 1, 1883, Thomas Edison switched on the first three-wire underground electrical system in the world in Brockton. In 1896 it became the first city in the country to abolish grade crossings.

What are Brockton's neighborhoods?

Brockton is often described through its villages and wards rather than one downtown. Montello and Campello are two villages with their own MBTA commuter rail stations and post offices. Campello is the smallest by area and the most populous.

  • West Brockton uses ZIP code 02301, East Brockton uses 02302.
  • Downtown runs along Main Street, and City Hall is at 45 School Street.
  • The South Street Historic District and D.W. Field Park are listed among the city's notable places.
  • The city council has seven ward councilors and four councilors at large.

If you are selling, tell a buyer which village or ward the house is in. Those three villages have rail stations.

What jobs and institutions anchor Brockton's economy?

The shoe economy has given way to health care, education and manufacturing. Brockton has three hospitals: Signature Healthcare Brockton Hospital on the east side, Boston Medical Center South in the northwest and the Brockton VA Hospital in the southwest.

Route 24 is a six-lane highway on the west side of the city with exits at Route 27 to the north and Route 123 to the south. Those two routes cross at the center of the city, and Route 28 runs north to south through the middle.

The MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line stops at Montello, Brockton and Campello. Brockton Area Transit buses also connect to Ashmont Station, Stoughton, the Bridgewater Industrial Park and Braintree Station via a stop in Montello.

Brockton gets about 50 inches of precipitation and about 34 inches of snow in a typical year, based on NOAA 1991 to 2020 normals reproduced on Wikipedia. January daily highs average near 39 degrees and July highs near 84 degrees.

The record high is 105 degrees and the record low is minus 19. Wikipedia also calls Brockton one of the windiest cities in the country, with wind speeds averaging 14.3 miles per hour. Wind and snow are the load a roof carries here.

Ice, wind and the freeze and thaw cycle test older roofs, chimneys, gutters and foundation walls. A buyer's inspector will check those items, so a roof quote or a chimney report can help you in a negotiation.

How do Brockton property tax bills and abatements work?

Brockton issues four bills a year. The first two, on July 1 and October 1, are preliminary and based on last year's taxes. The third, issued January 1, is the actual bill with the new rate. The fourth is issued April 1.

Each bill is due within 30 days of its issue date. The Board of Assessors says an abatement application must be filed by February 1, or postmarked by that date, and exemptions and deferrals are due within 90 days of the actual bill. The office is at City Hall, 45 School Street, and the phone is 508-580-7194.

The assessors also review deed recordings from the Plymouth County Registry of Deeds and building permits, then update the property's value. After you sell, expect the record to change. Details are on the city's assessors page.

The Massachusetts deed excise tax is $2.00 per $500 of price under MGL c. 64D, s. 1, and it is paid when the deed is recorded. Call the fire department as soon as you have a closing date, because it charges a fee for the inspection.

  • Gather the deed and your latest tax bill.

  • Collect permit records for work done in recent years.

Where is Lynn, Massachusetts, and how is the city laid out?

Lynn is a coastal city in Essex County, about 10 miles northeast of Boston. It sits on Massachusetts Bay and borders Nahant, Swampscott, Salem, Peabody, Lynnfield, Saugus and Revere.

The Census Bureau lists about 13.5 square miles, and nearly a fifth of that is water. Nahant splits the shoreline in two, with Lynn Harbor to the south and Nahant Bay to the north. The only land link to Revere is the General Edwards Bridge over the Pines River, which matters if you are weighing a commute or a showing schedule.

More than a quarter of the city is Lynn Woods Reservation, which fills much of the northwest. Two beaches, Lynn Beach and King's Beach, face Nahant Bay.

Which neighborhoods make up Lynn?

Lynn is divided into Central, West Lynn and East Lynn, and each of those breaks into smaller areas that buyers and sellers tend to name by square or park.

  • Central: the downtown business district and Central Square.
  • West Lynn: Pine Hill, McDonough Square and Barry Park, Tower Hill and Austin Square along the Saugus River, The Commons, The Brickyard, Walnut Street and Lynnhurst, and Veteran's Village.

A house near the water in the Diamond District sits in a different setting than a triple-decker near Central Square, and a cash buyer prices the two differently. When you describe your property, give the street and the nearest square.

What is the history behind Lynn's housing and economy?

Lynn was settled by Europeans in 1629 and made shoes from the 1600s until the last factory closed in 1981. At the start of the 20th century, 234 factories there produced more than a million pairs a day.

Electrical manufacturing followed. Thomson-Houston Electric, backed by Lynn shoe manufacturers, merged with Edison Electric in 1892 to form General Electric, and the jet engine plant has stayed in the city ever since.

Fire reshaped downtown twice. An 1889 blaze destroyed 296 buildings, including 142 homes. In 1981, a fire at former shoe factories on Broad and Washington Streets burned 17 downtown buildings. North Shore Community College's Lynn campus now occupies much of that burned area.

Mid-1800s estates and beach cottages lined the shoreline, and Lynn Shore Drive opened in 1910 and drew more building along the coast. Many of those structures sit in the National Register Diamond Historic District. Age is the thing to keep in mind: a Lynn house built over a century ago may carry old wiring, plaster and original systems, and that is when buyers who purchase as-is are most useful.

How do the weather and the coast affect a Lynn house?

Lynn has cold, snowy winters and warm, humid summers, much like Boston. Climate normals for 1991 to 2020 show a January average high of 36.7 degrees and an average low of 20.8, with about 47.8 inches of precipitation across the year.

Those numbers describe long freeze and thaw seasons next to salt air. Roofs, gutters, chimneys, exterior paint and basement walls work harder in a place like that, and deferred upkeep shows up fast. A cash buyer who accepts a house as-is takes on that repair list, so you do not have to pay for it before the sale.

How do you get around Lynn, and what does transit mean for a sale?

Lynn has no interstate highway. Route 1A, Route 107, Route 129 and Route 129A run through the city, and the nearest interstate is the combined I-95 and Route 128 in Lynnfield.

  • Lynn station on the MBTA Commuter Rail Newburyport/Rockport Line, with about 20 minute service to North Station.
  • MBTA ferry route F5 from Blossom Street Pier to downtown Boston.
  • Numerous MBTA bus routes to Boston and neighboring communities.
  • Boston Logan International Airport, about 5 miles south.

A Blue Line extension to downtown Lynn has been proposed but not funded. Newer apartment buildings are going up within a half mile of Lynn station, including a 259 unit building on Monroe Street and a 331 unit waterfront project on Carroll Parkway, so the blocks near the station are changing. Homes farther out, such as near Lynn Woods, rely more on cars.

What do you need to know before selling a house in Lynn, MA?

The first step is a smoke and carbon monoxide alarm certificate: the Massachusetts Department of Fire Services states that you need a certificate of compliance from the local fire department when you sell or transfer a home.

Call the Lynn fire department as soon as you have a closing date. The department charges a fee, so ask what it is. Battery-powered smoke alarms older than 10 years must be replaced with alarms that have 10 year sealed batteries, are photoelectric and have a hush feature.

The state also taxes the deed itself. Under Chapter 64D, Section 1, the excise is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of consideration, or fraction of it, outside Barnstable County. On a sale price of $500,000 that works out to $2,000.

Massachusetts has two title systems, recorded land and registered land, and about 80 to 90 percent of properties are recorded land. The Mass.gov law library notes that real estate attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling, both by law and practice. Ask the city of Lynn, and your attorney, about any local permits tied to your house.

How does a cash sale of a Lynn house work?

A cash sale in Lynn skips the buyer's mortgage, so there is no lender appraisal or loan approval to wait on. You still sign a purchase and sale agreement, clear title and close with a deed.

  1. You share the address, condition and your timeline.
  2. The buyer reviews the property and presents an offer.
  3. If you accept, an attorney handles the title work and the paperwork.
  4. The fire department certificate gets arranged according to what the contract says.
  5. You close at the registry date you agreed on and receive the proceeds.

Compare that with listing: showings, repairs a buyer's inspector requests, and financing that can fall through. Cash does not suit every seller, and an offer may land below a retail listing price. Weigh that against carrying costs and time.

Is Lynn a good place to sell a house quickly?

Lynn has a large, dense market, with 101,253 residents at the 2020 census and rail, ferry and bus service to Boston. How quickly a particular house sells depends on its condition, price and location. A cash offer can shorten the timeline because no mortgage approval is involved.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Lynn?

Yes. The Massachusetts Department of Fire Services says a certificate of compliance from the local fire department is required when you sell or transfer a home. Call the Lynn fire department for the fee and to schedule the inspection.

What is the Massachusetts deed excise tax?

It is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of consideration or fraction of it, set by Chapter 64D, Section 1, with a lower rate in Barnstable County. On a $400,000 sale, the tax is $1,600. Ask your attorney who pays it under your contract.

Can I sell a Lynn house that needs major repairs?

Yes. A buyer who purchases as-is accepts the house in its current condition, including repairs. You may still need the alarm certificate, and the contract should say who arranges it.

What if I inherited a house in Lynn?

You may need probate steps before you can sell, depending on how the property was held. Speak with a Massachusetts attorney or the probate court about authority to sell, then contact us about the house.

Where is Quincy and how is the city laid out?

Quincy is the largest city in Norfolk County, Massachusetts, sitting on Boston Harbor just south of the Neponset River. Wikipedia's Quincy entry lists Boston to the north, Milton to the west, Randolph and Braintree to the south, and Weymouth and Hull across the water to the east.

The city covers 26.9 square miles, but about 37.6 percent of that is water. A large piece of the land is not available for housing at all: the Blue Hills Reservation, a state park, takes up roughly 23 percent of the land area in the southwest corner and holds the city's high point, 517-foot Chickatawbut Hill.

So a Quincy house is usually either on the harbor side, where Quincy Bay and Wollaston Beach shape daily life, or inland on the hills around Quincy Center, South Quincy and West Quincy.

Quincy at a glance: what do the numbers say?

Which Quincy neighborhoods matter when you sell?

Quincy is a city of named neighborhoods, and buyers think in those terms. The main ones, as described on Wikipedia:

  • Wollaston: an early rail commuter area for Boston workers, now dense and mixed residential and commercial.
  • North Quincy: runs along Hancock Street and Quincy Shore Drive and is home to the city's largest high school.
  • Quincy Center: the historic commercial and government core, with City Hall and the Thomas Crane Public Library.
  • Quincy Point: densely settled, east of the center, and the site of the Fore River Shipyard.
  • Houghs Neck and Squantum: peninsulas that began as summer resort areas and are now year-round neighborhoods.
  • Marina Bay: built in the 1980s on the former Naval Air Station Squantum, with high-rise condominiums and a large marina.
  • West Quincy: close to Interstate 93, with the old granite quarries and the Granite Railway site.
  • Merrymount, Montclair, Adams Shore, Germantown and South Quincy: mostly residential, each with its own feel.

A condo at Marina Bay and a single-family house on Houghs Neck are different products with different buyer pools, so the way a sale gets priced and marketed can differ a lot inside one city.

How did Quincy's history shape its housing?

Quincy grew in stages, and its houses tend to show it. Granite quarrying dominated 19th century jobs, and the Granite Railway, built in 1826, is recognized as the first commercial railroad in the United States.

The Old Colony Railroad opened in 1845 and made Quincy about as reachable from Boston as Charlestown. The first suburban land company in the north of the city formed in 1870, and the population grew by more than 50 percent during the 1920s. Shipbuilding at the Fore River Shipyard then carried the 20th century economy.

A city built across that many decades usually has houses of many ages on the same street. That matters for a sale, because wiring, heating, roofs and smoke alarms can differ sharply from one house to the next.

What are the major employers, schools and commutes?

Quincy has moved from heavy industry to office and service work. Wikipedia names Stop & Shop, Arbella Insurance Group, Boston Financial Data Services and The Patriot Ledger as companies headquartered in the city, and lists State Street, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, Harvard Pilgrim Health Care and Boston Scientific among the larger employers with offices there.

The commute story is strong. The MBTA Red Line has four Quincy stops: North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams. Interstate 93 and U.S. 1 run together through the west side, and Route 3A, Route 28 and Route 53 cross the city.

Public schools are run by Quincy Public Schools, with two high schools (Quincy High School and North Quincy High School), five middle schools and a set of elementary schools. Quincy College, in Quincy Center, is unusual because the city itself operates it.

How does Quincy weather affect an older house?

Quincy gets a full New England winter, and that is what inspectors and buyers look at first. NOAA normals for the Blue Hill station put average snowfall at 69.7 inches a year, with about 29 snowy days, and January lows average 18.3 degrees Fahrenheit.

Rain is steady too, at 53.86 inches a year across about 140 days with measurable precipitation. In practice that points a buyer's attention to roofs, gutters, basements and heating systems, and to anything near the water on the Quincy Bay side.

If your house sits close to the shore, ask your insurance agent and the city building department about flood mapping before you list.

Quincy sellers face the same Massachusetts requirements as everyone else in the state, plus Norfolk County recording charges. The short list:

  • Smoke and CO certificate: The state Department of Fire Services says a seller needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the alarms meet the rules for a sale. Call the Quincy fire department as soon as you have a closing date, because there is an inspection fee.
  • Alarm age: Battery-powered smoke alarms over ten years old, or with no date stamp, must be replaced with sealed ten-year photoelectric units that have a hush feature.
  • Deed excise tax: Norfolk County's registry charges $2.28 for each $500 of the price on the deed. Its own example is a $155,000 deed costing $706.80.

Details are on the Mass.gov alarm inspection page and the Norfolk Registry fee schedule. The statute behind the rate is G.L. c. 64D, section 1.

How does Quincy bill property tax?

Quincy bills real estate tax quarterly. According to the Quincy Assessors page, the first two bills are preliminary, together about 50 percent of the prior year's tax, due August 1 and November 1.

The third and fourth bills use the new assessed value and the year's tax rate, with the payments already made subtracted. They are due February 1 and May 1.

Property record cards are posted online, and the assessors say a new valuation shows up on the third-quarter bill each January. The office is at 1305 Hancock Street and its listed phone is (617) 376-1170.

If you think your assessment is too high, state guidance from the Appellate Tax Board says the abatement application is due by the first installment due date, generally February 1 in quarterly cities. Assessors have three months to act, and an appeal to the board follows within three months of their decision. Taxes have to be paid on time for the appeal to stay alive. Ask your closing attorney how the current quarter will be handled at the table.

What do Quincy sellers usually run into?

Sellers in a city like Quincy tend to hit a handful of situations, and each has a practical first step:

  • A house that needs work: get a rough repair list before choosing between listing and a cash sale, so you compare real net numbers.
  • Alarm and certificate timing: book the fire department early so a missed inspection does not delay closing.
  • An inherited house: the estate may need court authority before it can sell, so talk to a probate attorney first.
  • Tight timelines: a job move or a payment problem favors a quick, certain closing over a long marketing period.

Every route, from a standard listing to a cash offer, ends at the same Norfolk County recording step. The difference is how many repairs, showings and weeks you need before you get there.

Norfolk County charges $2.28 for every $500 of the deed's stated price. On a $155,000 deed the registry's example comes to $706.80.

Where is New Bedford, Massachusetts, and what is it known for?

New Bedford is a port city in Bristol County on the Acushnet River, where the river meets Buzzards Bay. It is the ninth-largest city in Massachusetts, with 101,079 residents at the 2020 census, and it is known as the Whaling City.

The city borders Dartmouth to the west, Freetown to the north, Acushnet and Fairhaven to the east, and Buzzards Bay to the south. It stretches about 14 miles from the Freetown line to Clark's Point and only about 2 miles east to west, so it is long and narrow. New Bedford Harbor has the highest annual fishing catch value of any U.S. port as of 2019.

How did whaling and textile mills shape New Bedford?

Whaling made New Bedford one of the richest cities in North America, and the mills that followed left a large stock of older housing. English colonists bought the land in 1652 as part of Old Dartmouth, and the town was incorporated on February 23, 1787.

  • 1847: New Bedford becomes a city, and Abraham Hathaway Howland is its first mayor.
  • 1857: The harbor holds 329 vessels worth over $12 million at the whaling peak.
  • 1859: The discovery of petroleum in Pennsylvania starts the decline of whaling.
  • 1875: Wamsutta Mills processes 19,000 bales of cotton into 20 million yards of cloth.
  • 1928: A textile strike over a proposed 10 percent wage cut ends after months of work stoppage.

Irish immigrants arrived in the first half of the 1800s and Portuguese immigrants later in the century, and Wikipedia notes the city's large Portuguese and French populations today.

What does coastal weather mean for a New Bedford house?

That mix of damp air, freeze and thaw, and salt exposure near the harbor puts stress on roofs, siding, basements and wood framing. Buyers tend to check for moisture, so a seller can expect questions about gutters, foundations and older windows. The two-mile hurricane barrier, built in the 1960s south of Palmer's Island, protects the inner harbor where the fishing fleet anchors.

Which parts of New Bedford do people mention?

The city has a downtown historic core and several waterfront and park areas. Dozens of parks and playgrounds, and the main ones are below.

  • Acushnet Cedar Swamp State Reservation
  • Allen C. Haskell Public Gardens

The harbor is shared with Fairhaven, and the Roland J. Herbert Bridge links the two across Fish Island and Pope's Island. Clark's Point is the southernmost point of the city. The highest ground is an unnamed hill crossed by Interstate 195 and Hathaway Road west of downtown, over 180 feet above sea level.

Which schools and colleges are in New Bedford?

New Bedford Public Schools runs the city's schools, and New Bedford High School is the only public high school. Greater New Bedford Regional Vocational-Technical High School and two alternative junior-senior high schools also operate, along with the Global Learning Charter Public School and two campuses of Alma del Mar Charter School.

The University of Massachusetts Dartmouth has a marine campus at Fort Rodman and an arts campus downtown. Bristol Community College has a downtown campus, and Bridgewater State University runs an aviation program at New Bedford Regional Airport. Catholic schools include All Saints Catholic School and St. Teresa of Calcutta School.

How does New Bedford handle property taxes?

The New Bedford Assessor's Office values every property at full and fair cash value as of January 1, and the city uses its own full-time staff rather than an outside appraisal firm. Values go to the Department of Revenue for certification every five years, and the office reviews sales and the market each year.

The assessor is at 133 William Street, Room 109, and the phone is 508-979-1440. The treasurer-collector sits in rooms 101 to 104 of the same building at 508-979-1430, and bills can be paid at City Hall Room 101, at the Department of Public Infrastructure at 1105 Shawmut Avenue or at any BayCoast Bank with a payment stub.

See the Assessor's Office page for current rates.

What if there are unpaid taxes on a New Bedford house?

New Bedford's Tax Title Division handles delinquent accounts, and it can set up repayment agreements, process municipal lien certificates, foreclose and auction properties. The same division oversees the city's Side Yard Program.

A seller with back taxes should ask for a payoff figure before closing, since the balance has to be settled for clear title. The treasurer's page links a Tax Lien Foreclosure Process guide and Tax Title Taxpayer Resources. If a house has already moved into tax title, contact the office early, since foreclosure and auction are among the division's tools.

Sellers need a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate from the fire department, clear title and a closing attorney. Massachusetts splits title records into recorded land, which covers 80 to 90 percent of properties, and registered land held through the Land Court.

  • Call the fire department as soon as you have a closing date. The Department of Fire Services says the requirements depend on when the house was built and when the last permit was issued.
  • Replace expired battery smoke alarms with sealed 10-year photoelectric alarms that have a hush feature.
  • Request a municipal lien certificate from the treasurer-collector to show open taxes and charges.

Many New Bedford houses date from the whaling and mill eras, so sellers commonly deal with age-related repairs. Others are handling an inherited home, a property with a tax balance, or a rental with tenants in place.

Where is Fall River and what is the land like?

Fall River is a city in Bristol County on the eastern shore of Mount Hope Bay, at the mouth of the Taunton River, against the Rhode Island line. The 2020 census counted 94,000 residents, making it the tenth-largest city in Massachusetts.

The city has 40.2 square miles in total, with more than seven square miles of that water. Much of it is built on hillsides that rise sharply from the shore to more than 200 feet, and Copicut Hill, the highest point, tops 404 feet. A seller on the hill and a seller near the water face different driveways, different drainage and different foundations.

How did the mills shape Fall River housing?

Fall River was one of the leading textile centers in the country, and its houses came with the mills. By 1868 it had passed Lowell as the top textile city in America, and the city was second in the world only to Manchester, England, in output by 1876.

To house the workers, over 12,000 units of company housing were built. Thousands of wood-framed, multi-family tenements, often three-floor triple-deckers with up to six apartments. Many are still standing, and many are now owned by people who live in one unit and rent the others, or by heirs who never planned to be landlords.

Granite from local quarries built many of the mills and some homes. The population peaked at 120,485 in 1920 and the first wave of mill closures came in 1923.

How has Fall River's population changed?

Fall River grew from about 12,000 people when it became a city in 1854 to a peak of 120,485 in 1920. The 2020 census counted 94,000.

  • Bristol Community College, founded in 1965
  • Two University of Massachusetts Dartmouth sites in the city

Which roads and bridges serve Fall River?

Interstate 195 is the main east-west route, entering the city over the Charles M. Braga Jr. Memorial Bridge and continuing through the middle of the city to Westport. The bridge opened in 1966 as a six-lane cantilever truss span about 1.2 miles long.

Six other routes also serve the city: Route 6, MA 138, MA 79, MA 81, MA 177 and MA 24. The highway reaches New Bedford and Cape Cod to the east and Providence to the west, which makes Fall River workable for commuters into Rhode Island. The Route 79 viaduct was demolished in 2014 and replaced with a surface boulevard. Fall River's city hall is built over the interstate.

What water and weather issues affect a Fall River house?

Fall River has a long shoreline, a river and large ponds, so water is part of the city's geography. The Quequechan River falls 128 feet in its last half mile, and during the 1960s Interstate 195 was routed along it with a section carried underground in culverts.

The North Watuppa Pond is the city's main reservoir, and a large forested watershed lies east of it. Ask the city or your insurance agent for the flood zone of your parcel before you list, since buyers and lenders will.

Where is Newton, Massachusetts, and how is it laid out?

Newton is a city in Middlesex County about 8 miles west of downtown Boston, and it is a patchwork of thirteen villages instead of one center. It borders Boston's Brighton and West Roxbury neighborhoods, Brookline, Watertown, Waltham, Weston, Wellesley and Needham.

Newton was first part of Cambridge, which was settled as the "newe towne" in 1630. English settlement of the Newton area began in 1639, the town was incorporated as Cambridge Village on December 15, 1681, and it took the name Newton in 1766.

It became a city on January 5, 1874. The Boston and Worcester railroad reached West Newton in 1834, and wealthy Boston businessmen built houses on former farmland along the line and on Commonwealth Avenue. Streetcar lines and then automobiles brought later waves of building, and Oak Hill stayed farmland until the 1950s. Mills at Newton Upper Falls and Lower Falls made snuff, chocolate, glue and paper, and the Stanley Motor Carriage Company, maker of the Stanley Steamer, was based here from 1902.

Density works out to roughly 12,864 people per square mile. Lawrence is also one of Essex County's two county seats, alongside Salem, so the district and superior courts sit here.

How did Lawrence grow into a mill city?

A group of investors called the Essex Company incorporated in 1845 and began digging the Great Stone Dam that August to harness the river. Lawrence became a town in 1847 and a city in 1853, named for Abbott Lawrence.

Canals on both banks fed the mills, and workers arrived from Ireland, Germany, Sweden and French Canada, then later from Italy and Eastern Europe. Lawrence earned the nickname Immigrant City. Two events stand out. The Pemberton Mill collapsed on January 10, 1860, with an official toll of 88 dead, and the 1912 textile strike became known as Bread and Roses.

The city is dense, with historic rowhouses and mill-era buildings packed into a small footprint. Many Lawrence properties are older and may hold more than one unit, so a seller may be handling a multi-unit building as much as a single house.

What areas and landmarks define Lawrence?

  • South Lawrence: the Shawsheen Fields area, where the first settlement in the present city began in 1655.
  • Tower Hill: the high ground in the northwest, home to the 1895 High Service Water Tower.
  • Prospect Hill and Mount Vernon: hills on the northeastern and southern edges.
  • Den Rock Park: a wooded conservation area on the southern line shared with Andover.

The city has four ZIP codes: 01840, 01841, 01842 and 01843.

Where is Somerville, MA, and how big is it?

Somerville is a city directly northwest of Boston and north of Cambridge, in Middlesex County. It covers about 4.2 square miles, of which roughly 4.1 is land, and the 2020 census counted 81,045 residents.

That makes Somerville the most densely populated municipality in New England. Its neighbors are Cambridge, Medford, Everett, Arlington and the Charlestown section of Boston, and it sits on the west bank of the Mystic River. ZIP codes run from 02143 to 02145.

For a seller, the density shows up in the housing itself. Lots are small, houses sit close together, and a neighbor's fence line, driveway or shared wall often becomes part of the conversation with any buyer.

A short history of Somerville

English settlers first used the land in 1629 as part of Charlestown, and Somerville became its own town in 1842 and a city in 1872. For more than two centuries it was farmland and cow pasture, which is why early maps call it "beyond the Neck."

The Old Powder House on Broadway, where the colonial government kept the largest supply of gunpowder in Massachusetts, was emptied by British troops on September 1, 1774. Historians treat that raid as a rehearsal for Lexington and Concord. Railroads and slaughterhouses later filled in the Millers River marsh, and the city industrialized in the mid-1800s.

The city received the All-America City Award in 1972, 2009 and 2015. Whatever the age of your house, buyers will ask about wiring, heating and any past additions.

What are the Seven Hills and squares of Somerville?

Somerville is built on seven glacial ridges, and its commercial life gathers in squares instead of one downtown. The hills are Central, Clarendon, Cobble, Ploughed (Mount Benedict), Prospect, Spring and Winter Hill.

The squares and neighborhoods listed for the city include:

  • East Somerville, Winter Hill, Ten Hills and Brickbottom

The hills decide where roads and shops could go, according to the city history. If you sell on a slope, say so plainly, and note how far the nearest square or station is.

What kind of place is Framingham, Massachusetts?

Framingham is a city in Middlesex County and the MetroWest part of Greater Boston. It covers about 25 square miles of land and had 72,362 residents in the 2020 census, which made it the 14th most populous municipality in the state.

It was a town for more than 300 years. Framingham was incorporated in 1700, and before it changed status it was the largest town in Massachusetts by population. Voters approved a mayor and council charter in April 2017, and the city form of government began on January 1, 2018.

The area was home to the Nipmuc before English settlement, who lived along Farm Pond. The first European farm was started by John Stone in 1647, and Thomas Danforth later gathered more than 15,000 acres of grant land. The name comes from Danforth's hometown in England, with one letter dropped along the way.

How is Framingham laid out, and which areas do sellers hear about most?

Framingham is split into distinct business districts and villages, and a house in each one tends to attract a different kind of buyer. Local references describe three main commercial districts plus smaller village centers.

  • Golden Triangle: the retail and office district on the east side, bordered by Route 9, Route 30 and Speen Street. It grew from Shoppers World, opened in 1951, and TJX has its world headquarters at Route 30 and Speen Street.
  • Downtown and South Framingham: the commercial center that grew with the railroad in the 1880s. It held Dennison Manufacturing and the General Motors assembly plant until the late 1980s closures, then recovered partly through Brazilian and Hispanic immigration starting in the early 2000s.
  • West Framingham: centered on Route 9 with large office parks and the bulk of the city's apartment and condominium complexes.
  • Framingham Centre, Saxonville and Nobscot: older villages. The Framingham Centre Common Historic District is the physical and historic center, with Framingham State University beside it.

After World War II the town grew quickly, and much of the housing built in that period is split-level and ranch style. Sellers of those homes often deal with original kitchens, older baths and systems that have never been updated.

What drives the Framingham economy?

Framingham's economy comes mostly from retail and office complexes, with a scattering of small manufacturers and trade services. It is also known for the Framingham Heart Study and for the Dennison company, founded in 1844, which later merged into Avery Dennison.

Employers named in local references include TJX, Bose, Staples, Cumberland Farms, Genzyme and The MetroWest Daily News, spread between the Golden Triangle and the Route 9 industrial parks. Framingham State University and the Framingham campus of Massachusetts Bay Community College add education jobs and student housing demand.

For a seller, this mix means renters, commuters and employees of nearby office parks all show up as potential occupants. A house near Route 9 can carry both steady rental interest and heavy traffic noise.

How do roads and transit shape home values in Framingham?

Framingham sits roughly halfway between Boston and Worcester, and the road and rail links are a major reason people live here. The Massachusetts Turnpike (Interstate 90), Route 9, Route 30, Route 126 and Route 135 all cross the city.

Downtown is split by the rail tracks and Waverly Street (Route 135). Homes within walking range of the station and the downtown streets draw commuters, while houses near the Turnpike and Route 9 interchanges draw buyers who want quick highway access.

What are Framingham's schools?

Framingham Public Schools operates 14 public schools, including Framingham High School, three middle schools (Walsh, Fuller and Cameron) and nine elementary schools. The district's main offices are in the Fuller Administration Building on Flagg Drive.

The city also has a regional vocational high school, a regional charter school and several private schools. Buyers with children usually ask which elementary school serves a house, so have the school assignment answer ready from the district when you list or negotiate.

When are Framingham property tax installments due?

The City of Framingham bills property tax quarterly, and installments are due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Payments received after the due date accrue interest at 14 percent per year under G.L. c. 59, s. 57C, calculated from the day after the due date.

The city tries to mail bills at least 30 days before each due date. Not receiving a bill does not remove the obligation, so contact the Tax Collector if nothing arrives two or three weeks before a date. The Treasurer/Collector is at 150 Concord Street, Room 111, phone 508-532-5430.

If you sell in the middle of a billing quarter, the closing statement normally adjusts the current installment between seller and buyer. Ask the closing attorney to confirm which installments are paid and which are still open. You can read the city's explanation on its Important Tax Information page.

What does a Framingham smoke and carbon monoxide inspection involve?

Selling a one or two family home in Framingham requires a smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspection by the Fire Department before closing. The city asks you to apply and pay online, then call Fire Department Administration at 508-532-5930 to schedule the visit.

  • Allow at least three weeks between the inspection request and your closing date.
  • Inspections are generally held Monday to Friday, typically in the afternoon.
  • The house number must be on the structure itself, not on a door, at least 3 inches tall and visible from the nearest street.
  • Fire Headquarters is at 10 Loring Drive.

A failed inspection is a common reason a closing slips by a few days. Replacing old alarms before you apply is usually cheaper than a second visit. The city's inspection page links the requirements sheet.

What do Framingham sellers usually run into?

Most Framingham sellers face the same few problems, and several come from the housing stock and the city's mix of neighborhoods.

  • Mid-century houses with dated systems that need work before a conventional buyer's lender will approve them.
  • Inherited homes where the owner lives out of state and has not cleared the contents.
  • Tenant-occupied homes and multi-family properties, especially near downtown and along Route 9.
  • Open tax installments or a closing date that has to fit around the three-week fire inspection lead time.

A cash buyer who purchases as-is can sidestep repair lists and showings, which matters most on inherited and tenant-occupied properties. You still need a clear title, an inspection certificate and tax adjustments at closing, so line those up early.

How do you decide between listing and a cash sale in Framingham?

Listing in Framingham makes sense when the house is in good shape and you can wait out showings, an appraisal and a buyer's financing. A cash sale makes sense when time, condition or occupancy is the bigger problem.

Compare the net amounts, not only the headline prices. A listing involves agent commission, repairs a lender may require and weeks of carrying costs such as tax installments and utilities. A direct sale removes several of those lines but usually comes at a lower number. Ask any buyer for their offer in writing, and ask the closing attorney what you would actually receive after the mortgage payoff and tax adjustments.

Framingham is a city. Residents voted for a mayor and council charter in April 2017 and the city form took effect on January 1, 2018, after the municipality had been the largest town in Massachusetts.

Do I need a smoke and carbon monoxide inspection to sell in Framingham?

Yes. The Framingham Fire Department inspects residential smoke and carbon monoxide detectors for sales, and the city asks for at least three weeks of lead time before your closing date.

Installments are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Late payments carry 14 percent annual interest under the cited state statute.

The MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line runs to South Station and Back Bay in Boston. Travel time to Back Bay is about 42 to 45 minutes.

You can sell it, and some cash buyers purchase tenant-occupied homes as-is. The lease stays in force, so ask the buyer how they handle the existing tenancy before you sign.

Where is Haverhill, Massachusetts?

Haverhill is a city in Essex County on the Merrimack River, right at the New Hampshire border. It is about 35 miles north of Boston and 17 miles from the Atlantic Ocean, and the 2020 census counted 67,787 residents.

The city covers 35.7 square miles, of which 33 are land, and it is the largest city or town in Essex County. It borders Merrimac, West Newbury, Groveland, Boxford, North Andover and Methuen, plus Salem, Atkinson and Plaistow in New Hampshire. The Merrimack separates the Bradford section from the rest of the city.

What is Haverhill's history?

Haverhill was settled in 1640 as Pentucket, an Algonquian word for place of the winding river, and incorporated in 1641. It became a city in 1870.

Shoe manufacturing built the city. By the end of 1913, one tenth of the shoes made in the United States came from Haverhill, which earned it the nickname Queen Slipper City. A great fire on February 17, 1882, destroyed much of the mill district, with about 300 businesses lost.

Bradford was a separate town until January 1, 1897, when it joined Haverhill. Bradford remains the only Massachusetts town, apart from those joined to Boston, that was annexed by a neighboring city. In the 1950s and 1960s, urban renewal demolished much of downtown, but the Highlands district still has Victorian mansions from the shoe boom.

Which parts of Haverhill matter to a seller?

Haverhill is made of several districts with their own character, and a buyer will ask which one your house is in. The city has a downtown along the river, the Highlands next to it, Bradford across the Merrimack, Ward Hill and the historic district of Rocks Village.

  • Downtown: rezoned to encourage artist live-work lofts and educational uses, with a parking garage, boardwalk and boat docks added along the river.
  • The Highlands: a district beside downtown with Victorian mansions built in the shoe boom.
  • Bradford: the area on the far side of the Merrimack, home to the Bradford MBTA station.
  • Rocks Village: a historic district listed among the city's early architecture, alongside the 1691 Kimball Tavern.

Winnekenni Park, a conservation area with Winnekenni Castle and Lake Saltonstall, is one of the city's best known open spaces.

What does Haverhill's housing look like?

Haverhill's housing ranges from colonial-era houses to Victorian mansions and converted mill lofts. The 2020 census counted 26,696 households and 27,927 housing units, and 4.4 percent of units were vacant.
