A homeowner vacancy rate of 0.8 percent indicates that very few owned homes sat empty at the time of the census. Downtown rezoning has also converted old factories into loft apartments and condominiums, with about $150 million in public and private investment in the old factory district.

Who runs Haverhill, and who lives there?

Haverhill has a strong mayor and a nine-member city council. Melinda Barrett became mayor in 2024 and is the first woman to hold the office.

The 2020 census recorded a median age of 39.7, with 21 percent of residents under 18 and 15.6 percent age 65 or older. About 23.6 percent identified as Hispanic or Latino. The population grew 11.3 percent between 2010 and 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2024 estimate is 68,291. Steady growth usually means buyers keep looking, though it does not guarantee any price.

How is the Haverhill terrain and climate relevant to a house?

Glaciers shaped Haverhill, leaving drumlins, eskers, kettle ponds and gravel deposits across the city. The highest point is Ayers Hill, a drumlin of at least 335 feet. The city is drained by the Little and Merrimack rivers.

Haverhill's normals show about 49.6 inches of precipitation and 57.8 inches of snow a year. The record high is 105 degrees Fahrenheit and the record low is minus 21. Heavy snow on roofs, ice in gutters and basement dampness near the river are the normal concerns for homes here.

How do you get around Haverhill?

Interstate 495 runs through Haverhill with five exits, and Routes 97, 108, 110, 113 and 125 cross the city. Routes 108 and 125 end at the New Hampshire line and continue into that state.

  • MBTA Commuter Rail serves the Haverhill and Bradford stations on the Haverhill/Reading Line to North Station.
  • Amtrak also serves the Haverhill station, with service to Portland, Maine and Boston.
  • MeVa Transit provides local bus service in and beyond Haverhill.
  • Logan International Airport in Boston is the nearest international airport.

When you describe a house to a buyer, give the distance to the nearest I-495 exit or rail station.

Which schools and colleges are in Haverhill?

Haverhill Public Schools runs the city's public schools. Whittier Regional Vocational Technical High School takes students by lottery from Haverhill and nearby towns, and Hill View Montessori Charter Public School serves kindergarten through eighth grade. Northern Essex Community College has its main campus here, and Northpoint Bible College is also in the city.

The city has rebuilt Hunking Middle School in Bradford and is working on a new campus for the Dr. A.B. Consentino Middle School.

When are Haverhill property taxes due?

Haverhill's official page says real estate and personal property tax payments are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Interest accrues at 14 percent on bills not paid on the due dates.

Preliminary bills are estimates based on the previous fiscal year's actual net bill. The city's formula is last year's actual tax times 2.5 percent, added to the actual, divided by four. Unpaid balances after May 1 can lead to a tax lien, and new liens after November 2024 carry 8 percent interest. Liens are recorded with the Registry of Deeds.

When a property changes hands after the January 1 assessment, the bill stays in the January 1 owner's name. The new owner must contact the Assessors at 978-374-2316 for a duplicate bill. Abatement applications must reach the Assessors on or before February 1. See the tax payment page.

What does a Haverhill smoke and carbon monoxide inspection cost?

The Haverhill Fire Prevention Office inspects smoke and carbon monoxide detectors before each residential sale closes, under M.G.L. Chapter 148, Section 26F and 26F 1/2. Inspections are done on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and only a limited number can be done each day.

  • One residential unit: $50
  • Two units: $100
  • Three to six units: $150
  • Seven or more units: $500

The certificate is valid for 60 days, and the city will not schedule the inspection until payment is received. You will get an email with the date and a call with the appointment time. Applications and details are on the fire department's page, or call 978-373-8460.

What do Haverhill sellers commonly face?

Many Haverhill sellers own older houses that need updating or inherited property they cannot easily manage. Because the certificate is valid for only 60 days, you want to book the inspection close enough to closing that it will not lapse.

A cash sale as-is can fit when the house needs work or the owner cannot manage repairs. For other owners, a listing may bring more money if the home is in good condition. Weigh both before you decide.

It is valid for 60 days. Haverhill inspects on Tuesdays and Thursdays and does not schedule until payment is received.

How much is the smoke and carbon monoxide inspection for a single-family home in Haverhill?

The fee for one residential unit is $50, according to the Fire Department's page.

Who gets the tax bill after I sell my Haverhill house?

The bill stays in the name of the owner as of January 1. The new owner contacts the Assessors for a duplicate, and closing adjustments handle the split.

What is Malden, Massachusetts, like as a place to own a home?

Malden is a compact, dense city in Middlesex County, just north of Boston across the Mystic River. It covers about 5.1 square miles and had 66,263 residents at the 2020 census, which works out to roughly 13,000 people per square mile.

Malden borders Melrose to the north, Medford to the west, Everett to the south, Revere to the east and Saugus to the northeast. Its high ground is Boojum Rock in the Middlesex Fells Reservation, at about 275 feet, and the Malden River drains the city.

Malden 2020 census figuresCount
Population66,263
Households26,024
Housing units27,721, with 6.1% vacant
Owner occupied47.2% of units
Median age35.7 years

Fewer than half of Malden homes are owner occupied, so renting is common here. If you own a house with tenants, tell the buyer up front.

How is Malden organized into squares and neighborhoods?

Malden grew around squares at its crossroads, and many neighborhoods take the name of the square at their center.

  • Squares: Malden Square at Main and Pleasant Streets, Converse Square, Oak Grove Square at the Oak Grove station, Bellrock Square, Judson Square, Maplewood Square and Linden Square.
  • Neighborhoods: Faulkner, West End, Edgeworth, Linden, Ferryway, Forestdale, Maplewood, Bellrock and Belmont Hill.
  • Landmarks by area: Bell Rock Memorial Park and the New England Coffee headquarters in Bellrock, Macdonald Stadium in Edgeworth, and Pine Banks Park shared with Melrose.

Maplewood has a clear origin: in 1847 the president of the Saugus Branch Railroad bought 200 acres and planned wide streets with ornamental trees, and the maples he planted gave the area its name. Edgeworth was once the site of the Converse Rubber Factory, the original home of the Converse sneaker.

What is the history of Malden?

Puritans settled Malden in 1640, the town was incorporated in 1649, and it became a city in 1882.

The area was first called the Mistick Side and was part of Charlestown. It once included Melrose, which separated in 1850, and Everett, which separated in 1870. Malden's first mayor, Elisha S. Converse, funded the Converse Memorial Library, designed by Henry Hobson Richardson and built in 1885.

The Malden High and Medford High Thanksgiving football game dates to 1889 and is the second oldest continuous high school football rivalry in the country. The Saugus Branch railroad line now carries the Northern Strand Trail, a multi-use path that opened in December 2012 and passes through the middle of the city.

For a seller, this long history usually means older housing. A house built a century or more ago can come with original layouts, older heating systems and decades of deferred work.

How do you commute from Malden?

Malden is on the MBTA Orange Line, with stops at Malden Center and Oak Grove, and Malden Center is also a commuter rail stop.

  • U.S. Route 1 is the one limited access route through the city, linking Boston and the North Shore.
  • Routes 28, 60 and 99 run through Malden as arterial roads.
  • Route 16 and Interstate 93 are a short distance outside the city line.
  • MBTA buses reach every adjacent community.

The Northern Strand Trail, also called the Bike to the Sea trail, now gives a paved route from the Mystic River in Everett to Western Avenue in Lynn. Houses within walking distance of Malden Center or Oak Grove draw commuters, which is helpful for a listing, but a cash buyer will price a house on its condition and numbers either way.

Which schools serve Malden homes?

Malden Public Schools is the local district, with five elementary and middle schools, one public high school and one public preschool.

The elementary schools Beebe, Ferryway, Forestdale, Linden and Salemwood were replaced with new buildings in the late 1990s. The city's high schools are Malden High School, Malden Catholic High School and Mystic Valley Regional Charter High School. The Cheverus Catholic School serves pre-K through eighth grade.

A National Center for Education Statistics study in 2013 found Malden High to be the most diverse public high school in Massachusetts.

What parks and community services does Malden have?

Malden has about 30 park sites, and open space is a selling point for houses near them.

  • 56 acres of the Middlesex Fells Reservation lie inside the city.
  • Fellsmere Pond covers 25 acres, and the DCR runs a swimming pool.
  • MacDonald Stadium has a 400 meter synthetic running track.
  • The Malden YMCA finished construction in early 2007.
  • The ArtLine, a series of murals and sculptures, runs along the Northern Strand Trail.

Services reflect the city's makeup. Recent immigrants have come largely from Brazil, China, Haiti, India, Morocco and Pakistan, and groups such as the Immigrant Learning Center and the Tri-City Community Action Program serve residents. South Cove Community Health Center began building a Malden site in 2017. Sellers who need to relocate within Malden or nearby can use that network of services when planning a move.

What do sellers need to do before closing on a Malden house?

The Massachusetts Department of Fire Services requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the standard for a sale or transfer.

The state's steps are practical. Find out when your home was built and when the last building permit was issued, since the alarm requirements depend on those dates. List every alarm and check its manufacture date, because an alarm with no date has expired. Then call the fire department when you have a closing date. The department charges a fee for the inspection and certificate.

Other state costs apply as well. The deed excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1, is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of the sale price, or fraction of it, outside Barnstable County. Massachusetts also keeps deeds in county registries, and most properties are recorded land. Ask the City of Malden's building and assessing offices about permits and bills tied to your address.

How does a cash sale of a Malden house work?

In a cash sale the buyer does not need a mortgage, so the timeline depends on the title work and on when you want to close.

  1. Tell the buyer about the house, any tenants and your timeline.
  2. The buyer reviews the property and presents a written offer.
  3. Once you accept, a Massachusetts attorney handles title and the purchase and sale agreement.
  4. Smoke and CO certification and any payoffs are arranged.
  5. The deed is recorded and you receive the proceeds.

Yes, the Department of Fire Services says a certificate of compliance from the local fire department is needed when you sell or transfer a home. Call the Malden fire department for its fee and scheduling.

Can I sell a Malden two family with tenants?

Yes. Tell the buyer about the leases and rents at the start. Under the contract you can negotiate whether the house closes occupied or vacant, and a Massachusetts attorney can advise you on tenant notice rules.

What does the Massachusetts deed excise tax cost?

It is two dollars per five hundred dollars of the price or fraction of it. On a $600,000 sale that is $2,400. Your contract and attorney will confirm who pays it.

Where is Waltham, MA?

The center of Waltham is the Common on Main Street, where City Hall, the public library and the post office stand. The river runs through town with several dams that once powered the mills.

Why is Waltham called the Watch City?

The Waltham Watch Company opened its factory here in 1854 and was the first to make watches on an assembly line. It produced over 35 million watches, clocks and instruments before it closed in 1957.

Waltham also hosted the Boston Manufacturing Company, whose model of mill and worker housing became known as the Waltham-Lowell system. The English settled the area in 1634 as part of Watertown, and Waltham became a separate town in 1738 and a city in 1884.

The city also holds large historic estates, including Gore Place (built in 1806), the Robert Treat Paine Estate and the 400-acre Lyman Estate.

Waltham Public Schools run seven elementary schools, two middle schools and one high school. The elementary schools are Northeast, Fitzgerald, MacArthur, Plympton, Whittemore, Stanley and the Waltham Dual Language Elementary School.

The middle schools are McDevitt and Kennedy, and Waltham High School teams are the Hawks. Higher education includes Bentley and Brandeis, and private schools include Chapel Hill-Chauncy Hall and Gann Academy. The Waltham Times, a nonprofit online news outlet started in 2024, covers city news.

Where is Taunton, MA, and how large is it?

Taunton is the county seat of Bristol County in southeastern Massachusetts, on the Taunton River about 10 miles north of Mount Hope Bay. The city had 59,408 residents in the 2020 census, which places it third in Bristol County behind New Bedford and Fall River.

It covers 48.4 square miles, of which about 46.4 are land, making Taunton the third-largest city by area in the state after Boston and Barnstable. That size matters to sellers: a Taunton address can mean a downtown street near the Green, a lakeside lot, or a wooded parcel near the industrial park in the north.

The river has tributaries including the Mill River and the Three Mile River. The highest point is near the southwest corner, at 207 feet above sea level, and Prospect Hill above Lake Sabbatia reaches 197 feet.

What is Taunton's history?

Taunton was settled by English colonists in the late 1630s and incorporated as a town on September 3, 1639, which makes it one of the oldest towns in the country. It became a city in 1864 and was named for Taunton in Somerset, England.

The original boundaries took in land that is now Norton, Easton, Mansfield, Dighton, Raynham, Berkley and Lakeville. Elizabeth Poole, a financier of the first dam and ironworks, is described as the matriarch of the settlement, and the city motto, "Dux Femina Facti," means "A woman led the deed."

In the 1800s the city became known as the Silver City, because companies such as Reed & Barton, F. B. Rogers and Poole Silver made silverware here. Since December 1914 it has put on a large December light display on Taunton Green, which earned it the other nickname, the Christmas City.

What does Taunton's economy look like?

Taunton once ran on silversmithing and shipbuilding, and today leans toward manufacturing and industrial parks. Reed & Barton made the medals for the 1996 Summer Olympics, and the city produced the anchor for the USS Constitution.

Current descriptions emphasize semiconductor, silicon and electronics manufacturing, plus corporate headquarters, and the city has been courting biotechnology firms for its industrial parks. The Myles Standish Industrial Park in the north, next to Interstate 495, is the main one.

The Silver City Galleria mall closed on February 29, 2020 and was demolished on May 9, 2021, which reshaped retail in the area. Owners who sold or relocated for jobs in these industries sometimes need a fast, simple sale.

How do roads and transit work in Taunton?

Taunton is the highway hub of southeastern Massachusetts, and several major routes cross at the Green. U.S. 44, Route 138 and Route 140 meet there, Route 24 meets Route 140 near East Taunton, and Interstate 495 runs through the north.

The city has one MBTA Commuter Rail stop, East Taunton station. A proposed second phase of the South Coast Rail project would add a stop near downtown on Dean Street. The Greater Attleboro Taunton Regional Transit Authority (GATRA) runs local buses, and freight lines pass through the city.

Taunton has its own municipal airport for small aircraft. The nearest national airline service is T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island, and the nearest international service is Logan in Boston.

Taunton has a humid climate with hot summers and cold winters, and it gets about 48.8 inches of precipitation a year. January days average a high near 38 degrees Fahrenheit, and July highs average about 84.

Snow averages 25.7 inches a year, mostly from December through March, and measurable precipitation falls on about 115 days a year. The city is built around a river with two state parks, Massasoit State Park in East Taunton and Watson Pond State Park in the north.

Because the city has rivers, ponds and low ground, a buyer for a lot near water may ask about flood zones and drainage. FEMA maps and the local conservation office hold that information, so check them for your own parcel.

Downtown Taunton centers on Taunton Green, the city's central square, which was a militia training ground during the Revolution. A fountain sits at its center, and the Liberty and Union flag flies beside the U.S. flag.

Nearby are the Taunton Public Library, which opened in 1903 and has been expanded several times, and the Old Colony Historical Society, which archives the city's past. The Bristol County Superior Courthouse and a trial court complex finished in 2011 keep county business in the city.

Architecture ranges from the colonial era to modern buildings. If your house is old, buyers may ask for a history of updates, so a short list of dates for the roof, heating and wiring is useful.

Which public schools serve Taunton?

Taunton operates nine public elementary schools, three middle schools and Taunton High School. The middle schools are Benjamin A. Friedman, Joseph H. Martin and John F. Parker.

The city also has Taunton Alternative High School and Bristol-Plymouth Regional Technical School, and Our Lady of Lourdes School in Weir Village for pre-K to grade 8. Family buyers often start with the school list, so having it ready helps your listing or private sale.

What kind of city is Revere, Massachusetts?

Revere is a dense coastal city in Suffolk County, about five miles northeast of downtown Boston, and it is the end of the MBTA Blue Line. The 2020 census counted 62,186 people on 10.13 square miles, of which 4.43 square miles are water, so most of the city is marsh, beach and harbor edge.

Neighbors are Winthrop, Chelsea, East Boston, Everett, Malden, Saugus and Lynn, with Massachusetts Bay to the east. After the 2020 census Revere was reported as the fastest-growing city in the state, though the later population estimate on Wikipedia, 60,702 for 2024, is lower than the census count.

For a seller, the useful point is how packed the city is: roughly 10,900 people per square mile, so lots are tight, and several districts mix single-family and multi-family houses.

Revere in numbers

All figures are from the 2020 census and the 2019 American Community Survey, as summarized on Wikipedia. A homeowner vacancy rate of 0.6 percent means very few owner homes were vacant and for sale when the census was taken.

Which Revere neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Revere is organized around a handful of districts, each with a different housing mix:

  • Beachmont: the eastern edge near East Boston's Orient Heights, with single and multi-family homes and a Blue Line stop.
  • Revere Beach Boulevard: apartment complexes, restaurants and some single-family houses along the three-mile beach, with newer development adding luxury apartments.
  • Point of Pines and Oak Island: the north end of the beach, mostly single and multi-family homes beside the marsh and wetlands.
  • Shirley Avenue: the most ethnically diverse part of the city, with ethnic groceries, restaurants and community services.
  • Broadway and Revere Street: the central civic and commercial arteries that connect City Hall to the beach.
  • West Revere: single and multi-family homes plus the Squire Road business district with large shopping plazas and hotels.

Matching the right buyer to the right district helps a listing: a beachfront condo and a West Revere two-family attract different people.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Revere house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How did Revere's history shape what is for sale today?

Revere began as Rumney Marsh, was part of Boston from 1632 and then Chelsea, and split off as North Chelsea in 1846. In 1871 it took the name Revere after Paul Revere. Its beach became a public destination in 1896 when the Metropolitan Park Commission took over management.

Railroad lines, first the Eastern Railroad in 1838 and then the Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad in 1875, set off rapid growth, and the population rose from 5,668 in 1890 to 18,219 in 1910 and 28,823 in 1920.

That first boom is when most of Revere filled in. A later wave of growth pushed the city from 47,283 people in 2000 to 62,186 in 2020.

What does the Blue Line and the road system mean for Revere sellers?

The Blue Line ends in Revere, with three stations: Wonderland, Revere Beach and Beachmont. Houses within walking distance of a station can be easier to market to commuters who work in Boston.

U.S. Route 1 and state routes 1A, 16, 60, 107 and 145 run through the city.

When you list or sell, mention the station name and the walking time. Buyers searching for a Blue Line home compare those details first.

Who works in Revere and what is changing?

According to Revere's 2021 budget as quoted on Wikipedia, the leading employers are supermarkets and health or care operations: Market Basket (210 employees), Mass General Hospital (200), Price Rite (183), Lighthouse Nursing (182), Target (170) and Stop & Shop on Squire Road (150).

The city's 2018 master plan, "Next Stop, Revere," set goals for workforce, small business and science and technology industries over 10 to 20 years.

The biggest recent site change is Wonderland Greyhound Park. Greyhound racing ended there in 2009, the city took the land by eminent domain in 2022, and ground was broken on a new Revere High School at the site in August 2025.

What should Revere sellers know about weather and water?

Revere sits only about 20 feet above sea level and has marsh and ocean on several sides. Two events from its record show why buyers pay attention to storms: the Blizzard of 1978 destroyed many of the beach's remaining businesses, and an EF2 tornado came through Chelsea and into Revere on July 28, 2014, damaging many buildings including City Hall. It was the first tornado to hit Suffolk County since National Weather Service records began in 1950.

The year-round range as roughly 23 to 82 degrees Fahrenheit, with snow lasting about five months and the muggiest stretch running from mid-June to late September.

We did not find a city page on flood zones that we could open, so we make no flood claims here. If your house is near the beach or the marsh, ask your insurer and the city building office about flood zone status before listing, so you know the answer before a buyer asks.

What do you have to do before closing a Revere house sale?

Revere sellers follow state sale rules. The Department of Fire Services says you must obtain a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the requirements for a sale or transfer. Alarms that are more than ten years old, or have no date, must be replaced. The fire department charges for the inspection, so call as soon as a closing date is set. See the Mass.gov guidance.

Massachusetts also taxes deeds by statute. The base rate in G.L. c. 64D, section 1 is $2 per $500 of price.

On the tax side, Revere's Assessors Department is at 281 Broadway and answers at 781-286-8170, and the city lists senior, veteran, blind and hardship exemptions on its assessors page. Each requires ownership and occupancy, and if the property is in a trust the applicant must be both trustee and beneficiary or hold a life estate.

What can you do if your Revere assessment looks too high?

  • Pay every tax installment on time. The Appellate Tax Board treats timely payment as a condition for hearing an appeal.
  • File an abatement application with the assessors by the first installment due date printed on your bill.
  • Wait up to three months for a decision, then appeal to the board within three months of that decision or of the deemed denial.
  • Bring comparable sales and photographs of similar nearby houses.

Because the burden is on the owner, a short, evidence-based case does better than a general complaint. The board's guide explains each step.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What are your options if you want to sell a Revere house?

A traditional listing, a sale on your own and a cash sale are the three routes. Which fits depends on repairs, timing and how much effort you can give.

  • A listing exposes the house to the most buyers but brings showings, inspection negotiations and a timeline set by the buyer's lender.
  • A cash sale can close on a schedule you choose, and the buyer takes the house in its present condition.

If your house needs work, a cash buyer may make more sense than spending months on repairs, and you can compare both routes before deciding.

Frequently asked questions

What county is Revere in?

Revere is in Suffolk County, about five miles northeast of downtown Boston.

How many people live in Revere?

The 2020 census counted 62,186 residents. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate shown at the top of this page is 60,141.

Which MBTA line serves Revere?

The Blue Line ends in Revere with stations at Wonderland, Revere Beach and Beachmont.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Revere?

Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department for a sale or transfer of a home.

Who handles property assessments in Revere?

Where is Medford, Massachusetts, and how is it divided?

Medford is a city in Middlesex County, north of Boston, and the Mystic River runs from west to southeast through the middle of it. It covers 8.66 square miles and had 59,659 residents at the 2020 census.

Part of the 2,060 acre Middlesex Fells Reservation lies in the north, shared with Winchester, Stoneham, Melrose and Malden. Tufts University has its campus along the Medford and Somerville line.

What are Medford's neighborhoods?

People in Medford usually name their neighborhood first, and each has its own feel.

  • West Medford, described as the most affluent area, with a historic African American neighborhood dating to the Civil War.
  • South Medford, traditionally Italian.
  • Wellington, also called East Medford.
  • Fulton Heights, or The Heights, in North Medford.
  • Brooks Estates, Glenwood, Lawrence Estates and Medford Hillside, where Tufts is mostly situated.

Irish Americans live throughout the city. If you list or sell to a buyer, the neighborhood name tells them more about a house than the city name does, so use it.

What is the history of Medford?

English colonists settled Medford in 1630 as part of Charlestown, and it became a city in 1892.

The first toll bridge across the Mystic River went up in 1637 where the Cradock Bridge stands today, and it carried Main Street into Medford Square. For roughly 150 years it was the only bridge over the Mystic, which made Medford a crossing point into Boston from the north.

Medford was a center of industry. It made tiles, crackers, bricks, rum and clipper ships, such as the White Swallow and the Kingfisher. Tufts was chartered in 1852. The Boston and Maine Railroad reached Medford Center in 1847, and farmland was divided into lots for houses starting in the 1840s and 1850s.

Historic sites include the Peter Tufts House at 350 Riverside Avenue, thought to be the oldest all-brick building in New England, and the Royall House and Slave Quarters, a National Historic Landmark. Houses in the old Ship Street Historic District around Riverside Avenue are some of the oldest, and an old house can mean old systems.

How do you get around Medford?

Medford has both Orange Line and Green Line subway service, plus a commuter rail stop and many bus routes.

Interstate 93 runs north and south through the city, and state routes 16, 28, 38 and 60 cross it. Houses close to the new Green Line stops sit in a part of the city where transit changed recently, which can matter to buyers of all kinds.

Which schools serve Medford?

Medford Public Schools run two high schools, Medford High School and Medford Vocational Technical High School.

  • Middle schools: John J. McGlynn and Madeline Dugger Andrews.
  • Elementary schools: Missituk, Brooks, John J. McGlynn and Milton Fuller Roberts.
  • Private schools: St. Joseph's (K to 8) and St. Raphael's (pre-K to 8).
  • College: Tufts University.

The Medford and Malden high school Thanksgiving game dates from 1889.

How do Tufts and the local economy affect Medford sellers?

Tufts University is the best known institution in Medford, and the Tufts campus straddles the Medford and Somerville line, mostly on Medford Hillside. The university employs many local residents and runs community service projects with the city.

  • The median age in Medford is 35.6, and 14.1 percent of residents are under 18.
  • About 28.5 percent of households are one person.
  • Medford is governed by a mayor and a city council with a separate school committee.
  • The Meadow Glen Mall closed on February 1, 2016, and its site was being prepared for a retail plaza.

Owners of rental houses sometimes decide to sell after repeated turnover, damage or a change in family plans, and a cash buyer can take on a house with tenants or one left vacant. Tell the buyer which applies.

What should a Medford seller handle before closing?

A Massachusetts seller needs a certificate of compliance for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms from the local fire department, according to the Department of Fire Services.

The state tells owners to learn the year the house was built and the date of its last building permit, list each alarm and its manufacture date, and replace alarms that are expired or undated. Battery smoke alarms older than 10 years must be replaced with sealed 10 year photoelectric alarms that have a hush feature. After installing them, test them, then call the Medford fire department, which charges a fee for the inspection and certificate.

The deed excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1 is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of price or fraction of it, outside Barnstable County. Deeds are recorded at a county registry. Medford's county, Middlesex, has a South registry in Cambridge and a North registry in Lowell. Ask Medford's city offices about permits, open violations and any tax bills before you close.

How does a cash sale of a Medford house work?

With a cash sale the buyer does not wait on a mortgage lender, so the closing date follows your needs.

  1. You share the address, condition, tenants if any and your timing.
  2. The buyer reviews the house and sends a written offer.
  3. You accept, and a Massachusetts attorney handles title and the purchase and sale agreement.
  4. The alarm certificate and any payoffs get arranged.
  5. The deed is recorded and you receive the proceeds.

An offer should reflect the house itself, so ask any buyer how they arrive at their number. Compare the net result with listing, including repairs, showings and months of carrying costs.

Frequently asked questions

How many people live in Medford, MA?

The 2020 census counted 59,659 residents in Medford, living in 24,413 households. The Census Bureau ranked it among the nation's fastest growing populations between 2021 and 2022.

Is Medford close to the T?

Yes. Wellington is on the Orange Line, and Medford/Tufts and Ball Square are on the Green Line, which opened in 2022. West Medford has Lowell Line commuter rail.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Medford?

Yes. The Department of Fire Services says a certificate of compliance from the local fire department is required when you sell or transfer a home. Call the Medford fire department for the fee and scheduling.

What is the deed excise tax when I sell in Medford?

It is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of the sale price or fraction of it. A $700,000 sale produces $2,800. Your contract and attorney will confirm which party pays.

Where did Medford get its name and what shaped its early housing?

Settlers renamed the Mistick settlement Meadford in the 1630s, and the name may refer to a meadow by a ford on the Mystic River. Farmland was divided into house lots from the 1840s and 1850s, so many Medford homes likely date from the 1800s and early 1900s. Older houses can carry repair needs that a cash buyer will price in.

What river runs through Medford?

The Mystic River flows from west to southeast through the middle of Medford. The Cradock Bridge carries Main Street over it into Medford Square, and a toll bridge stood on that site as early as 1637.

Can I sell a Medford house that I inherited?

Often yes, once whoever holds authority to sell has it, which may require probate. Speak with a Massachusetts attorney about that, then share the address and condition with us.

Where is Weymouth, MA, and what are its four villages?

Weymouth is a Norfolk County city on the South Shore, bordered by Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor to the north. It covers 21.58 square miles, but 4.81 of that is water, and the 2020 Census counted 57,437 residents.

Residents describe four districts. North Weymouth sits north of the Church, North and Green Street junction and has the waterfront parks and beaches. South Weymouth lies mostly south of Route 3 and holds Weymouth High School and South Shore Hospital. East Weymouth has Whitman's Pond, Jackson Square and Town Hall, plus many Victorian houses. Weymouth Landing spans about a mile around Weston Park at the Braintree line.

Quincy, Braintree and Holbrook lie to the west, Abington and Rockland to the south, and Hingham to the east. Grape Island, Slate Island and Sheep Island in the Boston Harbor Islands National Recreation Area also belong to Weymouth.

What is Weymouth's history?

Weymouth began in 1622 as the Wessagusset colony, which makes it the second-oldest settlement in Massachusetts after Plymouth. The first attempt failed, but settlers who stayed formed the base of the permanent town, which took the Weymouth name in 1635.

Shoemaking was the main industry from the early 1700s until Stetson Shoe closed in 1973. The old Naval Air Station South Weymouth closed in the 1990s, and the land is being redeveloped as Union Point. Weymouth also voted in 1999 to replace town meeting with a mayor and council, ending 365 years of continuous town meeting. The first mayor took office in 2000.

How do Weymouth's waterfront and climate affect homes?

Water shapes much of Weymouth, from Hingham Bay to the Back River and Fore River. The city is especially vulnerable to sea level rise. It also describes North Weymouth waterfront cottages being bought and rebuilt, so condition and flood exposure vary a great deal from street to street.

Average precipitation runs about 44 inches a year, with January highs near 39 degrees. If you own near the shore:

  • Pull your flood insurance policy and any elevation certificate.
  • Document sea wall, bulkhead or drainage repairs with dates.
  • Tell buyers or the cash buyer about past water in the basement.

Put the history in writing for any buyer, since hiding it tends to surface at inspection.

What is the East Weymouth housing like, and what do older houses need?

East Weymouth has many Queen Anne, shingle and colonial revival houses, with restoration under way on streets such as Hillcrest Road. Whatever the village, it is worth having the roof, heating system, wiring and porches looked at before you decide how to sell.

The city's 2010 housing count showed 64 percent owner-occupied and 35 percent renter-occupied, so renters live in a large share of the housing. If you inherited one of these houses and live elsewhere, a repair list can be the biggest hurdle to a traditional listing.

Which schools and roads serve Weymouth?

Weymouth High School in South Weymouth is the city's only public high school and enrolls more than 1,800 students. The Maria Weston Chapman Middle School opened in September 2022, and eight primary schools and an early childhood center complete the system. Private options include South Shore Christian Academy and the Catholic Sacred Heart and St. Francis Xavier schools.

Routes 3, 3A, 18, 53, 58 and 139 pass through the city. The MBTA Greenbush Line stops at East Weymouth and Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, and the Kingston Line stops at South Weymouth. If your house is within reach of a station, say so in any listing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Weymouth houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What is Union Point, and what else is around Weymouth?

Union Point is the redevelopment of the former Naval Air Station South Weymouth. Plans for a parkway, residences, a sports facility and a movie studio, and notes the site has hosted several film shoots. The 25-acre Union Point Sports Complex is already open.

700 acres of parks and conservation land across 46 sites. North Weymouth has Great Esker Park, George Lane Beach and Webb Memorial State Park, and in spring hundreds of thousands of alewife herring run up the brook between the Back River and Whitman's Pond. Abigail Adams was born in Weymouth, and her birthplace is a local landmark.

How do Massachusetts property tax abatements work for Weymouth owners?

Weymouth assessors follow the state process explained by the Appellate Tax Board. You can seek an abatement if the assessed value is above the fair cash value as of the January 1 valuation date, or if an exemption or classification applies.

  • Bills in quarterly cities are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.
  • The abatement application is due by the first installment date, generally February 1 in those cities.
  • Assessors have three months, and no answer counts as a denial.
  • You then have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Weymouth's assessing office publishes its own schedule. Ask it which billing pattern applies and where to get the abatement form.

What does a Weymouth seller pay to record the deed?

Weymouth deeds are recorded with the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds. The registry charges $156 to record a deed and an excise tax of $2.28 for each $500 of the stated price. Its own example shows a $155,000 deed owing $706.80, and the excise must be paid with an attorney's check or bank check.

On a $600,000 sale the same rate gives $2,736. A municipal lien certificate costs $81 at the registry, and a mortgage discharge is $106 per marginal reference, so budget for these small items too.

Cash sale versus listing for a Weymouth house

A Weymouth listing can draw plenty of attention, particularly near the commuter rail, but showings and repairs take time. A cash sale suits owners who want to close on their own schedule, who inherited a house, or who face a repair bill they do not want to carry.

Ask any buyer for proof of funds, a written contract and a clear statement of who pays each closing cost. Then compare the net you would keep from each option.

Frequently asked questions

Is Weymouth, MA a city or a town?

Weymouth has a city form of government but keeps "Town of Weymouth" as its official name. Voters replaced town meeting with a mayor and council in 1999.

How many train stations are in Weymouth?

Three. The Greenbush Line stops at East Weymouth and Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, and the Kingston Line stops at South Weymouth.

How much is the deed excise tax in Norfolk County?

The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds charges $2.28 for each $500 of the stated price or fraction of $500, payable by attorney's check or bank check at recording.

Which parts of Weymouth are near the water?

North Weymouth faces Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor. The Back River and Fore River also run through the city, so check flood exposure street by street.

What happened to the Naval Air Station in South Weymouth?

It closed in the 1990s under the Base Realignment and Closure process, and the land is being redeveloped as Union Point, a mixed-use community with homes, a sports complex and film production space.

Can I sell my Weymouth house as is?

Yes. You can sell as is to an investor or cash buyer. Disclose known problems in writing, and expect the offer to reflect the repairs the house needs.

Where is Peabody, Massachusetts?

Peabody is a city in Essex County on the North Shore, about 15 miles northeast of Boston and 2 miles from the center of Salem. 16.81 square miles of area and an elevation of 16 feet.

The city is wedge-shaped, with the center in the wider northeastern end. South Peabody lies south of the center, and the more suburban West Peabody, where the high school sits, lies to the west beyond the highways and the Proctor neighborhood. Neighbors are Middleton, Danvers, Salem, Lynn and Lynnfield.

The Ipswich River forms the northwestern border and the Waters River drains the northeast. Low-lying lots near those waterways deserve a flood question before you sell.

What is Peabody's history?

Peabody was settled in 1626 as part of Salem and later belonged to Danvers. It split off in 1855 as South Danvers, took the Peabody name on April 30, 1868 in honor of the philanthropist George Peabody, and became a city in 1916.

Leather defined the economy for generations, and the city is still called the Leather City and the Tanner City. Tanneries drew immigrant workers, and by 1915 one third of residents had been born abroad. Tanneries have since closed or moved. Earlier, the Central Street corridor was a hub of redware pottery in the eighteenth century, and Walnut Street, known as Ottoman Street, filled with boarding houses for workers from the Ottoman Empire.

The early twentieth century brought cars as well: Corwin Manufacturing, a Brass Era automaker, was based here.

On October 28, 1915 a fire at St. Johns School killed 21 young children, and Peabody became the first city in the country to require public buildings to have push-open exits. The city's population doubled between 1950 and 1970, from 22,645 to 48,080, so a large share of its homes date from that postwar growth.

What does the Peabody economy look like?

Peabody replaced its tanneries with retail, health care and technology employers. The Northshore Mall opened in September 1958 as an outdoor shopping center, and Centennial Park, an industrial park in the middle of the city, has drawn medical and technology companies.

Employers named on the city's Wikipedia entry include:

  • Lahey Hospital and Medical Center and Boston Children's Hospital
  • Analogic, JEOL, Carl Zeiss and UTC Aerospace Systems
  • Saucony, Christian Book Distributors and Meridian Interstate Bancorp
  • The Northshore Mall

West Peabody was mostly farm land until the 1950s and has since developed into a middle-to-upper class residential area, in the entry's words.

How do highways and transit connect Peabody?

Highways include Interstate 95, Route 128, Route 129, U.S. Route 1 and Route 114. Several MBTA bus lines pass through town. The closest commuter rail stop is in Salem, on the Newburyport/Rockport Line to North Station, and the nearest airports are Beverly Municipal and Boston's Logan.

The Peabody Municipal Light Plant, owned by the city, provides electricity. National Grid supplies natural gas, and Comcast and RCN hold cable licenses. Transferring electric service to a new owner therefore runs through a city utility, which is a small difference from most Massachusetts towns.

Independence Greenway, a 5.25 mile rail trail, and Brooksby Farm, a 275-acre city-owned farm and conservation area, give the city green space that buyers often ask about.

A Peabody seller needs an alarm certificate from the fire department. The Department of Fire Services says to call for the inspection as soon as a closing date exists, and to expect a fee.

An attorney handles the closing and the recorded deed, since the Trial Court Law Libraries describe attorneys as part of Massachusetts sales by law and by practice. Deed excise is set by Chapter 64D, Section 1. Sellers of certain residential properties also cannot condition acceptance of an offer on a waiver of a home inspection under 760 CMR 74.

A direct purchase follows the same legal path, and you may still need to clear a mortgage payoff, estate paperwork or a lien before the deed records.

Who runs Peabody and which schools serve it?

Peabody has a mayor-council government, and Edward A. Bettencourt Jr. is listed as mayor on the city's Wikipedia entry. Peabody Public Schools run Brown, Burke, Carroll, Center, McCarthy, South, Welch and West elementary schools, Higgins Middle School and Veterans Memorial High School, whose teams are the Tanners.

Private options include Bishop Fenwick High School, Covenant Christian Academy and St. John the Baptist School. We list names only. The district confirms which school a given address feeds.

What neighborhoods and parks come up when sellers talk about Peabody?

Sellers and buyers tend to describe Peabody by section.

  • The center and Peabody Square in the northeast.
  • South Peabody, with Tillie's Farm, a city-owned farm.
  • West Peabody, home to the high school.
  • The Proctor neighborhood between the center and the west.

Other local landmarks include the Peabody Institute Library, established in 1852 after a bequest from George Peabody, the North Shore Children's Museum and Crystal Lake, a 21-acre conservation area. The Washington Street Historic District is a nineteenth-century residential area. If your house sits in a designated district, ask the city whether any local rules apply.

Where is Chicopee and how is the city laid out?

Chicopee sits on the Connecticut River in Hampden County and is the second-largest city in western Massachusetts after Springfield. The 2020 census counted 55,560 residents.

The city covers about 23.9 square miles, most of it land, and the Chicopee River runs through the southern part before it empties into the Connecticut. Chicopee began as a cluster of mill villages in the northern end of Springfield and broke away in 1848. That history still shapes how the city feels: each village kept its own center, its own church, and its own housing stock.

These communities inside the city limits:

  • Chicopee Center, also called Cabotville
  • Chicopee Falls
  • Willimansett
  • Fairview
  • Aldenville
  • Burnett Road, Smith Highlands and Westover

Newer pockets such as Chicomansett, Ferry Lane and Sandy Hill filled in later. A seller in Willimansett and a seller in Fairview are dealing with different streets, different lot sizes and often different ages of house, so a single citywide rule of thumb rarely fits.

What is the history behind Chicopee's older houses?

Many Chicopee houses were built for mill workers, which explains the dense streets of modest two-family and single-family homes near the old factories. The Boston Associates set up textile companies along the Chicopee River between 1823 and 1841, and by 1875 nearly one in four residents worked in cotton goods.

The city later became known for tools, swords, rubber tires, sporting goods and bicycles. Ames Manufacturing, Fisk Rubber and Spalding all had plants here, and the Duryea brothers built what Wikipedia describes as the first gasoline-powered automobile made in the United States in Chicopee.

Aldenville shows how the housing grew. In 1870 Edward Monroe Alden bought 600 acres east of Willimansett and later divided it into lots of 60 by 170 feet, first sold at a low price with a small down payment to French-Canadian factory workers. Houses on lots like these are often more than a century old, and buyers know to expect old wiring, older heating systems and possibly lead paint.

What does the Chicopee economy look like?

Chicopee has a service economy with a mix of small local businesses, national chains and specialty manufacturers. Westover Air Reserve Base is the largest Air Force Reserve base in the country, home to the 439th Airlift Wing, and it shares its runway with Westover Metropolitan Airport.

Wikipedia also names several private employers and landmarks of the local economy:

  • Callaway Golf, which makes golf balls at a plant in Willimansett
  • Chemex, headquartered in the city since 2013
  • Buxton, a leather goods maker founded in 1898 as L.A.W. Novelty Co.
  • Polish food producers such as Chicopee Provision Company and Millie's Pierogi
  • Chicopee Savings Bank, Alden Credit Union and the Polish National Credit Union

The Chicopee River Business Park and Westover Business Park are inside the city. A seller can point to these nearby employers when describing the location to buyers.

Which highways and roads serve Chicopee?

Four interstates cross the city: I-90, I-91, I-291 and I-391. State routes 33, 116 and 141 also run through it, which is why the city uses the nickname Crossroads of New England.

Hartford is about 29 miles away and Boston about 89 miles. Commuters can reach Springfield, Holyoke and Hartford quickly, which widens the buyer pool for a Chicopee house beyond people who work in the city itself. A house close to an interstate ramp can show well on commute time but may carry road noise, and buyers notice both.

What flood and weather issues should a Chicopee seller know about?

Chicopee sits between two rivers, so flooding is part of its story. The Willimansett Dike, an elevated levee in Willimansett, was built after the destructive flood caused by the Great New England Hurricane of 1938.

A house near the Chicopee or Connecticut River may need a flood zone check, and a buyer's lender can require flood insurance. Ask your insurance agent or the city for the flood zone of your parcel before you list. Basements in older mill-village homes can also see seasonal dampness, which inspectors tend to flag. If your house has had water in the basement, expect buyers to ask about it, and tell them plainly.

How does a Chicopee property tax abatement work?

Chicopee elects three assessors to three-year terms, and they handle abatement requests for homes in the city. The state's Appellate Tax Board guide explains the timeline that applies in every Massachusetts community.

  • You apply on the approved form with the local assessors by the due date of the first tax installment shown on your bill.
  • In towns and cities that bill quarterly, that date is generally February 1.
  • Assessors have three months to act, and silence counts as a denial.
  • An appeal to the Appellate Tax Board must follow within three months of the action or deemed denial.

You generally have to pay the tax by its due date for the Board to hear an appeal. If you are selling, an abatement can still matter because the buyer inherits the assessment going forward. Call the Chicopee assessors for the form and for your bill's actual due dates.

What does Massachusetts require before a Chicopee house closes?

You need a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the rules for a sale. The state Department of Fire Services recommends calling the department as soon as you have a closing date.

The department charges a fee for the inspection. Old battery smoke alarms past ten years, or ones with no manufacture date, have to be replaced with ten-year sealed photoelectric models that have a hush feature. This is a small cost that can delay a closing if left to the last week.

The deed itself carries a state excise tax under chapter 64D of the General Laws, calculated on the sale price and Your closing attorney will compute it and tell you who pays under your contract. Everything else, such as payoff of a mortgage or unpaid city bills, is handled at the same table.

What are the choices for selling a Chicopee house?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or sell to a cash buyer. Each fits a different situation.

Inherited houses, mill-era two-families with tenants and homes with deferred repairs are common in Chicopee. What common problems do Chicopee sellers face?

The houses are older, and the neighborhoods are tied to mill-era building patterns. Sellers tend to run into the same few issues:

  • Aging systems in houses that date from the mill years
  • Tenants in two-family homes who complicate showings
  • Estate sales where several relatives must agree
  • Smoke and CO inspection timing right before closing

Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department when you sell or transfer a home. Call the department once you have a closing date, because there is an inspection fee and older alarms may need to be replaced.

Can I sell a Chicopee house that has tenants?

Yes, but the tenants' rights stay in place and the sale can affect timing. Tell your buyer about leases and rent early, and talk to a Massachusetts attorney if you want a tenant to leave.

Does Chicopee have flood risk that affects a sale?

Parts of the city sit near the Chicopee and Connecticut Rivers, and a levee in Willimansett was built after the 1938 hurricane flood. Check the flood zone for your parcel, since a lender may require flood insurance.

How do I challenge my Chicopee property tax assessment?

File an abatement application with the Chicopee assessors by the due date of the first installment on your bill, generally February 1 where bills are quarterly. If the assessors deny it, you have three months to appeal to the state Appellate Tax Board.

It borders Haverhill, North Andover, Lawrence, Andover and Dracut in Massachusetts, and Pelham and Salem in New Hampshire. The 2020 census counted 53,059 residents, and Wikipedia's estimate for 2024 is 54,272. Methuen is part of the Merrimack Valley, and its ZIP code is 01844.

Methuen was settled in 1642 as part of Haverhill and became its own town after the General Court approved a petition on December 8, 1725. The first town meeting followed on March 9, 1726, and it was named for Sir Paul Methuen.

Industry arrived in the 1800s. The Methuen Cotton Mills went up at the Spicket River falls in the 1820s, and hat and shoe makers set up small factories along the river. Housing, schools and churches clustered around Osgood, Broadway, Hampshire and Pleasant streets. The city was hit by the 1922 New England Textile Strike, and it adopted city status in 1917.

Three families shaped the center of town: the Nevins, the Tenneys and the Searles. Their buildings include the Nevins Memorial Library, the Searles building, Tenney Gatehouse and the Methuen Memorial Music Hall, which houses the Great Organ.

What is the Searles Tenney Nevins Historic District, and does it affect a sale?

The Spicket Falls Historic District and the Pleasant-High Historic District sit inside the larger area, and both are on the National Register of Historic Places. How do you get around Methuen?

Methuen sits at the northern end of Interstate 93 in Massachusetts, and three exits serve the city. Interstate 495 crosses the eastern side, and Route 213, called the Loop Connector, links the two highways. Routes 28, 110 and 113 also pass through, and Routes 110 and 113 meet at I-93 Exit 43.

  • The closest MBTA commuter rail stations are Lawrence, Bradford and Haverhill on the Haverhill/Reading Line.

The Methuen Rail Trail uses a former railroad corridor and connects to the Spicket River Greenway in Lawrence.

Which rivers, lakes and parks shape Methuen?

Methuen lies along the northern bank of the Merrimack River, and the Spicket River splits the city in two. There are also many brooks, several ponds, a town forest, a bird sanctuary and Tenney State Park.

Forest Lake is a great pond of more than 55 acres bordered by the town forest, with access managed by the Forest Lake Association. Pine Island sits in the Merrimack near the southern edge of town and belongs to Methuen. Saint Monica's is a Catholic school for pre-K through grade 8, and St. Ann's Home and School serves children with special learning and emotional needs.

Presentation of Mary Academy, a private Catholic high school on the former Searles Estate, closed in 2020.

Methuen assesses property at full value and sets separate residential and commercial rates each fiscal year. The FY2026 rates are $10.40 per $1,000 for residential and $20.08 for commercial, according to the city's assessing page.

State law requires a revaluation every five years, and the Department of Revenue must certify values before the tax rate is set. The department also handles abatement applications, exemptions for seniors, disabled veterans, surviving spouses and blind persons, and reassessment after building permits are issued.

Buyers will ask for the current bill, so keep it handy. The Methuen assessing page has the forms and contacts.

What steps come before a Methuen closing?

A Methuen seller needs a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate from the local fire department, a title search and, in practice, a real estate attorney.

  • Older battery-powered smoke alarms must be replaced with sealed 10-year photoelectric units with a hush feature.
  • Deeds are recorded at a county registry of deeds. About 80 to 90 percent of Massachusetts properties are recorded land, while the rest are registered land in the Land Court system.
  • The state levies a deeds excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1. Ask your attorney for the current amount.

Methuen sellers often deal with old mill-era housing, inherited properties and houses that need work. A house built in the early 1900s may need alarm upgrades, repairs flagged by an inspector or permit records pulled before a buyer will close.

What is the history of Everett?

Everett was part of Charlestown and later Malden, and it separated from Malden in 1870. It was named for Edward Everett, a former governor and Harvard president, and it became a city in 1892.

Landfill has pushed the shoreline outward over the centuries, and at some point between 1905 and 1912 fill connected the mainland to what had been White Island in the Mystic River. A refinery opened by Beacon Oil in 1920 and closed in 1965, and the tank farm remained. Everett was also the last American city with a two-chamber legislature, until voters approved a new charter in November 2011 that created an eleven-member City Council.

Where is Barnstable and how is the town laid out?

Barnstable is a town on Cape Cod and the county seat of Barnstable County. It is the largest community on the Cape by both land area and population, and it sits roughly 70 miles southeast of Boston.

The town covers about 76 square miles, and a little over a fifth of that is water. Cape Cod Bay forms the northern edge and Nantucket Sound the southern edge. Sandwich and Mashpee border Barnstable on the west, and Yarmouth borders it on the east.

Barnstable is a group of villages that have no legal boundaries of their own, and these seven are the ones most often listed:

  • Barnstable village, which includes Cummaquid
  • Centerville
  • Cotuit
  • Hyannis, which includes Hyannis Port and West Hyannisport
  • Marstons Mills
  • Osterville
  • West Barnstable

The Sandy Neck dunes run along Barnstable Harbor in the north. Pines and oaks surround Wequaquet Lake in the middle of town. Most residents live in the south, and many of them live near the beaches of Centerville and Hyannis Harbors. Hyannis is the biggest village.

What is the short history of Barnstable?

English settlers founded Barnstable in 1638, and it was incorporated in 1639 as one of the early towns of Plymouth Colony. It was named after Barnstaple in Devon, England.

Farming, fishing and salt works came first. By the end of the 1800s the town harbored hundreds of ships, and the railroad arrived in 1854. Summer visitors followed, and the Kennedy family compound in Hyannis Port is the best known result of that history.

In 1989 the town rewrote its charter and moved from selectmen and town meeting to a council and town manager system. Barnstable is one of thirteen Massachusetts municipalities that hold a city form of government but keep "the town of" in their official name. For a seller, the practical point is that you deal with Town Hall in Hyannis, not a city hall, even though the government is council based.

What does the Barnstable economy run on?

Hyannis acts as the commercial center of Cape Cod, and that gives Barnstable a mix of tourism, health care, transportation and education jobs.

  • Cape Cod Hospital is in Hyannis and serves the central Cape.
  • Barnstable Municipal Airport is the regional hub for flights between the Cape and the islands, and Cape Air is headquartered in town.
  • The main ferry lines to Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard leave from Hyannis.
  • Cape Cod Community College is based in Barnstable.
  • The county courthouse and the offices of the Cape and Islands District Attorney are here because Barnstable is the county seat.

Barnstable also has the largest public school enrollment on the Cape, with more than 5,000 students.

How does Cape Cod weather affect a Barnstable house?

Barnstable has a humid continental climate, with an average seasonal snowfall of about 30 inches from November through April. February is typically the snowiest month, and it lines up with the peak of nor'easter activity.

The USDA places the town in plant hardiness zone 7a. With snow and nor'easters in the picture, the roof and the heating system are the items a buyer's inspector is likely to look at first.

A cash buyer does not need those repairs finished. If a nor'easter has already damaged a roof or a deck, the house can still be sold as it stands.

How do roads, rail and ferries shape buyer demand in Barnstable?

Route 6 is a four lane freeway across Barnstable, and Route 28 runs east and west through town as well. Routes 6A, 132 and 149 are the other main roads, and Routes 132 and 149 lie entirely inside the town.

Rail is limited. The CapeFlyer runs on weekends between Memorial Day and Labor Day. The nearest MBTA commuter rail stations with year round service are Middleborough and Kingston, so a commute to Boston is mostly a drive. Logan Airport is the nearest national and international airport, while Barnstable Municipal Airport handles regional flights.

When are Barnstable property tax bills due?

Barnstable bills real estate tax in four quarterly payments each fiscal year. For fiscal 2027, the Treasurer/Collector lists these dates:

BillDue date
First quarter (preliminary bill)August 3, 2026
Second quarter (preliminary bill)November 2, 2026
Third quarter (actual bill)February 1, 2027
Fourth quarter (actual bill)May 3, 2027

Preliminary bills were mailed by July 1, 2026, and actual bills are to be mailed by December 31, 2026. The Collector also bills motor vehicle and boat excise, sewer usage, and betterments for roads, water, sewer and septic. A betterment is a charge tied to the property, so mention any you know of to your closing attorney.

The Collector's page carries a municipal lien certificate request form. Ask your closing attorney whether one is needed for your sale. The Tax Collections line is 508-862-4054, and Town Hall is at 367 Main Street in Hyannis.

If you think your assessment is too high, an abatement application goes to the assessors. In towns that bill quarterly, that application is generally due February 1, and the Appellate Tax Board hears appeals after that.

Does a Barnstable house on septic need a Title 5 inspection before a sale?

Yes, in most cases. Under the state's Title 5 rules, a septic system generally has to be inspected within two years before a sale, or within six months after it if weather prevents an inspection beforehand. The Collector's page shows that Barnstable bills for sewer and for septic betterments, so some addresses are on sewer and some are not. Check which applies to yours.

  • Only MassDEP approved inspectors can do the inspection, and the report goes on the state form within 30 days.
  • The buyer must receive a copy of the report.
  • A passing inspection is generally good for two years. It is good for three years if the system is pumped every year and the records are in the report.
  • A conditional pass covers items like a cracked tank or a broken pipe, but cesspools and soil absorption systems cannot be repaired under a conditional pass.
  • A failed system must be upgraded within two years unless the Board of Health agrees to another schedule.

Transfers between spouses, parents and children, or full siblings are exempt, as are some trust and estate planning transfers. Buyers can also sign a binding agreement with the Board of Health to upgrade or connect to sewer within two years.

What does it cost to record a deed in Barnstable County?

Massachusetts charges a deed excise tax when a deed is recorded, and the statute sets a lower rate for Barnstable County than for the rest of the state. The statutory text gives $1.50 for each $500 of consideration or fraction of it in Barnstable County.

Sale priceDeed excise at $1.50 per $500
$400,000$1,200
$600,000$1,800
$900,000$2,700

Recording fees are set separately by the registry, so ask your closing attorney for the current figure.

What must be done before closing a Barnstable sale?

Three items come up in nearly every Massachusetts sale of a one or two family home.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. You need a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your alarms meet the rules for a sale. Call the department as soon as you have a closing date, and expect a fee. Battery alarms older than ten years must be replaced with sealed ten year photoelectric alarms.
  • An attorney. Massachusetts treats real estate closings as legal work. A Massachusetts court decision describes closings as requiring an attorney's substantive participation on behalf of the lender.
  • Title system. Most properties are recorded land filed at the Registry of Deeds. A smaller share is registered land with a Land Court certificate of title.

State rules also stop sellers of certain residential properties from conditioning an offer on a buyer waiving a home inspection.

What do sellers in Barnstable usually run into?

The town spans seven villages with different surroundings, from harbor streets in Hyannis to the wooded interior near Wequaquet Lake. A house in Cotuit and a house in West Barnstable can have very different sewer, water and tax situations, so confirm the details with the Treasurer/Collector and the Board of Health rather than assuming.

If the house needs septic work, has a betterment on it, or has been vacant through a Cape winter, a direct sale can save you the repair bills and the wait for an inspector. We buy Barnstable houses as they are.

Frequently asked questions

Is Barnstable a town or a city?

Both. Barnstable keeps the name Town of Barnstable but has run under a council and town manager charter since 1989, and it is one of thirteen Massachusetts municipalities with a city form of government that kept the town name.

How many villages are in Barnstable?

Seven are commonly listed: Barnstable, Centerville, Cotuit, Hyannis, Marstons Mills, Osterville and West Barnstable. They have no legal boundaries, and some lists count as many as eleven.

When is the next Barnstable property tax payment due?

For fiscal 2027 the remaining dates are February 1, 2027 for the third quarter and May 3, 2027 for the fourth. Check your actual bill, since the Treasurer/Collector sets the schedule each year.

Do I need a septic inspection to sell my Barnstable house?

Usually yes if the home has a septic system. Title 5 calls for an inspection within two years before the sale, or within six months after if weather blocks it, unless an exemption such as a family transfer applies.

What is the deed excise tax in Barnstable County?

The statute sets $1.50 for each $500 of the sale price or fraction of it in Barnstable County. On a $600,000 sale that comes to $1,800.

Where is Attleboro and how big is it?

Attleboro is a city in Bristol County on the Rhode Island line, with 46,461 residents at the 2020 census, its highest count ever.

It covers 27.77 square miles and is shaped like a truncated triangle pointing west. It borders North Attleborough, Mansfield, Norton, Rehoboth, Seekonk, Pawtucket, Cumberland and a short stretch of Central Falls. The Ten Mile River runs through the city, and the high point is Oak Hill, at 249 feet, in the south. Attleboro is part of the Providence metropolitan area and is also linked to Boston.

The data is from Wikipedia's Attleboro page, which cites the Census Bureau.

What areas make up Attleboro?

Attleboro is a patchwork of older mill villages and crossroads, and a listing there usually names the village.

  • City Center, the downtown business district beside the L.G. Balfour Riverwalk
  • South Attleboro, near the Rhode Island border
  • West Attleboro and East Attleboro
  • Hebronville, Dodgeville and Maple Square
  • Briggs Corner, North Corner, Oak Hill, Park Square, East Junction and Camp Hebron

The city also sits on a dialect boundary: the eastern part speaks like Boston and the western part like Providence.

Why is Attleboro called the Jewelry City?

Attleboro was once known as the jewelry capital of the world because of its many manufacturers.

The industry took off in 1913, especially through the L.G. Balfour Company, whose plant site is now a riverfront park. Firms such as Guyot Brothers, which dates to 1904, General Findings, Garlan Chain and Leach & Garner remain in operation. In 2011 the city won $5.4 million in state and federal funding to turn underused industrial and commercial parcels in the historic downtown into mixed-use space and to improve MBTA rail, GATRA bus service and roads.

Check the age of any house before you set expectations. Homes in a city that has been settled since 1634 range widely in age, so heating systems, wiring and roofs deserve a careful look.

How do you get around Attleboro?

Attleboro sits beside Interstate 95, with commuter rail stations and a regional bus system.

  • Highways: Interstate 95 enters the state between Attleboro and Pawtucket, Interstate 295 ends nearby, and US Route 1 and Routes 1A, 118, 123 and 152 cross the city. Routes 118, 123 and 152 meet at the city center.
  • Rail: two MBTA commuter rail stations, one downtown and one in South Attleboro near the Rhode Island line.
  • Bus: the Greater Attleboro Taunton Regional Transit Authority, GATRA, links Attleboro, Taunton and surrounding towns.
  • Air: T.F. Green International Airport in Warwick, Rhode Island, and Boston Logan International Airport.

A house near a rail station or an I-95 ramp appeals to commuters going toward Providence or Boston.

Which schools serve Attleboro?

Attleboro Public Schools runs the city's district, with five elementary schools, three middle schools and two high school programs.

The elementary schools are Hill-Roberts, Hyman Fine, A. Irvin Studley, Peter Thacher and Thomas Willett. The middle schools are Brennan, Coelho and Wamsutta. Attleboro High School opened a new building in 2022, following a $260 million project, and Attleboro Community Academy is an evening program for students aged 16 to 25. Bishop Feehan High School is a Catholic school, and Bristol Community College and Bridgewater State University both have satellite sites in the city.

When are Attleboro real estate taxes due?

Attleboro's tax bills have four due dates a year: August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.

If a date lands on a weekend or holiday, the payment is due the following Monday. The city collector's real estate tax page adds some details that surprise people.

  • Unpaid amounts accrue daily interest at 14 percent per year.
  • The city does not accept postmarks as proof of timely payment.
  • Not receiving a bill does not excuse the tax or the interest.
  • Payment can be made online, by phone, by mail, in person at City Hall at 77 Park Street, or at the drop box at the Pine Street entrance.

The collector's page also lists separate pages for municipal lien certificates and tax title, which sellers should consult when a balance is owed.

Who gets the bill when a house sells?

The collector must send the bill to the owner of record as of January 1 of the year the property was assessed.

That means a new owner may not see a bill in their own name for some time after a purchase. The city suggests that new owners contact the Assessor's Office to confirm the right owner details are on file. For a seller, the lesson is to settle taxes through the closing statement rather than assuming a later bill will go to the buyer.

Which dates matter at the Attleboro Assessor's Office?

The Assessor's Office, at 77 Park Street, publishes a short calendar of deadlines.

DateWhat happens
July 1First day of the fiscal year, and the qualification date for personal exemptions
December 1Deadline to apply for farm, recreational or forest classification
January 1Assessment date for the following fiscal year
February 1Deadline to apply for a property tax abatement
April 1Deadline to apply for personal exemptions
June 30End of the fiscal year

See the city's key dates page. For the steps after an abatement is denied, the Appellate Tax Board's appeals guide gives a three-month window to appeal.

What if an Attleboro tax bill goes unpaid?

The city gets a lien on the property automatically, and a tax taking can follow.

The Land Court's overview says a demand can go out after 30 days of nonpayment, and a taking can be recorded 14 days after that. An owner can still redeem by paying what is owed before the court enters a foreclosure judgment. Selling during that period is one way to pay the balance from proceeds.

What do you need to close a sale in Attleboro?

One state requirement applies to every one or two family home sale: a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate of compliance.

The Department of Fire Services guide says to call the local fire department as soon as you have a closing date. Battery-powered smoke alarms older than 10 years, or expired, must be replaced, and the department charges for the inspection. Deeds for an Attleboro property are recorded at the Bristol County Registry of Deeds, which the Assessor's page links for deed searches.

How do Attleboro owners compare listing, selling alone and cash offers?

Each route trades price against speed and effort.

A listing can bring a higher price for a house in good shape. Selling alone saves a commission but puts marketing and negotiation on the owner. A direct cash offer fits a house that needs work, an estate, or an owner who wants a firm closing date. Compare each offer by what you walk away with after taxes, payoffs and repairs.

Frequently asked questions

How many people live in Attleboro, Massachusetts?

The 2020 census counted 46,461 residents, the highest count in the city's history. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 47,447.

When are Attleboro property taxes due?

August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. If a date falls on a weekend or holiday, payment is due the following Monday.

Does Attleboro accept postmarks for tax payments?

No. The city collector says it does not accept postmarks, so payment has to be received by the due date. Interest accrues daily at 14 percent per year on late amounts.

What is the deadline for an Attleboro abatement application?

February 1. The Assessor's Office lists it as the deadline to apply for a property tax abatement.

Which Attleboro train stations serve commuters?

Attleboro has two MBTA commuter rail stations, one downtown and one in South Attleboro near the Rhode Island line.

Can I sell my Attleboro house with taxes owed?

Yes. Taxes and liens are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so request a written payoff figure from the collector before your closing date.

Where is Salem, Massachusetts, and how is it arranged?

Salem is a historic harbor city in Essex County on the North Shore, about 15 miles northeast of downtown Boston. Its 2020 population as 44,480 and its total area as 18.3 square miles, of which more than half is water.

Water cuts the city into small pieces. Salem Harbor separates it from Marblehead, Beverly Harbor and the Danvers River separate it from Beverly, and the North and South rivers divide the neighborhoods. Beverly, Danvers, Peabody, Lynn, Swampscott and Marblehead all touch its borders.

Salem was one of the two county seats of Essex County until county government was dissolved in 1999.

Source for all rows: Wikipedia's Salem entry.

How does Salem's history affect houses and sales?

Few Massachusetts cities carry as much preservation weight. Salem was a leading seaport in early American trade, and the 1692 witch trials still define its public image. Two of its historic residential areas, the Federal Street District and the Charter Street Historic District, are named on Wikipedia, and Chestnut Street is known for its Federal architecture.

The Great Salem Fire of 1914 destroyed more than 400 homes and left 3,500 families homeless, yet it spared the Chestnut Street block of Federal houses. That is part of why Salem has older neighborhoods beside areas rebuilt in the early 1900s.

If your house is in an historic district, ask the city's planning office before you plan exterior changes or a teardown.
