Which Salem neighborhoods should sellers know?

Salem as divided by its natural features into small neighborhoods:

  • Downtown: the historic core of the city, 15 miles northeast of Boston.
  • Salem Neck and Winter Island: a peninsula northeast of downtown, with a 30-acre Winter Island Park.
  • North Salem: west of the Neck, across the North River.
  • South Salem: south of the South River and mostly along the banks of Salem Harbor.

Water separates these areas, so a house a few blocks away across a river can feel like a different neighborhood to buyers.

What do Salem's economy, university and schools look like?

Wikipedia calls Salem today a residential and tourist area. Salem State University, the largest of the nine campuses in the state university system, enrolls more than 10,000 undergraduate and graduate students and houses about 2,000 of them in campus residence halls.

Tourism around the witch trials is large, though Wikipedia notes residents have debated how much the city should rely on it. For a house owner, the tourism question is also a rules question, covered in the next section.

Public elementary schools include Bates, Carlton, Horace Mann, Saltonstall and Witchcraft Heights, with Collins Middle School and Salem High School. Two charter schools, Salem Academy and Bentley Academy, are also public.

What else shapes Salem's identity and its land?

Salem's story is bigger than 1692. The National Guard first mustered on Salem Common in 1636, and during the Revolutionary War the port became a center of privateering, with about 1,700 Letters of Marque granted. Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote about the area in the 19th century.

Winter Island, on Salem Neck, once held a Coast Guard air station that moved to Cape Cod in 1970. The island is now a 30-acre city park. Gallows Hill is a city park too, and Proctor's Ledge, identified in 2016 as the site of the executions, is a memorial.

These public lands, plus the harbor frontage, limit how much of the city can ever be built on. A smaller land base is part of what you are selling into.

How do you get in and out of Salem?

Salem has its own station on the MBTA Commuter Rail's Newburyport/Rockport Line. Routes 1A, 114 and 107 pass through the city, and Route 1A uses the Veterans Memorial Bridge to Beverly.

There is no highway inside the city. The closest access to Route 128 is along Route 114 in Peabody, which is worth stating up front in a listing, since some buyers assume a highway exit is close.

A former rail line toward Marblehead has been turned into a bike path, and the city has discussed a possible South Salem rail station on Ocean Avenue West.

What are Salem's short-term rental rules?

Salem regulates short-term rentals more tightly than most Massachusetts cities, and that matters if you own a house that has been listed on Airbnb or a similar site. According to the City of Salem short-term rental page, the City Council adopted ordinances in 2018 that require:

  • Annual registration of the rental with the city.
  • A Certificate of Fitness.
  • For a property that is not the owner's primary residence, a special permit from the Zoning Board of Appeals and registration for the non-owner-occupied trash fee.
  • Collection of the state and local room occupancy excise tax.

The page states that new non-owner-occupied short-term rentals are not permitted, and that the special permit path applies only to properties that were operating as short-term rentals before July 16, 2018. Zoning also limits the use to certain neighborhoods.

For a seller, that rule can decide what a buyer may do with the house. If you bought a house as a short-term rental, confirm its registration and permit status with the city before you list it.

What does a Salem seller have to do before closing?

Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department, showing smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the rules for a sale or transfer. The state says to call the fire department as soon as you have a closing date, that alarms with no date stamp count as expired, and that a fee applies. Details are on the Mass.gov alarm page.

The deed excise tax is set by G.L. c. 64D, section 1, which names a base rate of $2 for each $500 of consideration.

We also could not open a Salem page on tax due dates, so check the dates printed on your bill or call the assessor's office.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How can you contest a Salem assessment?

A tax abatement is a reduction granted when your house's fair cash value is lower than its assessed value. State law sets a short path:

  1. Pay your tax installments on time.
  2. File the approved abatement application with the assessors by the first installment due date on your bill.
  3. Assessors have three months to act, and silence counts as a denial.
  4. Appeal to the Appellate Tax Board within three months of the decision.

Valuation is as of January 1 before the fiscal year. The Appellate Tax Board's guide describes each step.

What are your choices if you want to sell a Salem house quickly?

The three routes are listing, selling on your own, or accepting a cash offer. A listing suits a house in good shape in a sought-after area. A cash sale suits a house that needs repairs, an inherited property or a landlord who wants out.

In Salem, extra items can add time: a historic district review for exterior work, a short-term rental permit transfer question, or a certificate delay at the fire department. Spotting them early lets you pick the route that avoids the slowest steps.

Frequently asked questions

What county is Salem, MA in?

Salem is in Essex County, on the North Shore of Greater Boston.

Why is Salem called the Witch City?

The nickname comes from the 1692 Salem witch trials, which still shape the city's identity, tourism and even its school team names.

Is there a highway in Salem?

No. The nearest Route 128 access is along Route 114 in neighboring Peabody.

Can I run a short-term rental in Salem?

Only with city registration, a Certificate of Fitness and, for a non-owner-occupied unit, a special permit. The city says new non-owner-occupied short-term rentals are not permitted.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Salem?

Yes. Massachusetts requires a local fire department certificate of compliance for the sale or transfer of a home.

Where is Leominster, Massachusetts, and what is it like?

Leominster is a city in Worcester County, north of Worcester and northwest of Boston, and it is the second most populous city in the county. The 2020 census counted 43,782 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2024 estimate is 44,209.

At 29.7 square miles it is much larger than nearby mill cities such as Lawrence. The city sits mostly on a plateau above the Nashua River. Fitchburg and Lunenburg border it to the north, Lancaster to the east, Sterling and Princeton to the south, and Westminster to the west.

Route 2 and Route 12 both pass through the city, and Interstate 190, Route 13 and Route 117 begin or end here. That road network is a big reason Leominster draws shoppers and commuters from a wide area.

How did plastics make Leominster?

Leominster became known as the Pioneer Plastics City after combs, celluloid and injection molding put its factories ahead of the country. It was incorporated as a town in 1740 and chartered as a city on November 2, 1915.

The comb industry grew first, and by 1853 there were 146 workers in 24 comb factories. Celluloid arrived in 1868. Samuel Foster launched Foster Grant and used injection molding machines in 1931, and the company sold 20 million pairs of plastic sunglasses in 1937. Tupperware began here in 1938, and the plastic pink flamingo was invented in Leominster in 1956.

The city's population jumped from 2,069 in 1840 to 19,744 by 1920 as Irish, French Canadian and Italian workers arrived. Many plastics firms still operate in the city, though the large-scale decline came late in the 20th century.

Which parts of Leominster are distinct areas?

Leominster as divided into several small villages, and their names still appear in local history.

  • French Hill: a hill of planned triple-decker blocks between 1st and 12th Streets, named for its French immigrant population.
  • Lincoln Terrace: where Italian families settled in the early 1900s.
  • North Leominster: home to the MBTA station on the Fitchburg Line.
  • Morse Hollow, Rice Hill, the Flats, the Bowery, the West Side and the Car Barn area: other named areas, with the last one along the Fitchburg line.
  • North and South Monoosnoc Hills: the high ground in the west, with the South hill at 1,020 feet.

French Hill shows how housing type varies by area within the city, so ask which area a property sits in before comparing it with others.

The Leominster Public School District has four neighborhood elementary schools, two middle schools (Samoset and Skyview) and Leominster High School, which includes the Center for Technical Education. Mount Wachusett Community College has a Leominster campus, and Fitchburg State University is next door.

The MBTA Fitchburg Line stops at North Leominster, and the Montachusett Regional Transit Authority runs local buses in Leominster, Fitchburg and Gardner. Outdoor space includes the 4,300 acre Leominster State Forest and the 167 acre Doyle Community Park.

The Collector and Treasurer's office bills real estate, personal property, water and sewer, and excise. It also issues municipal lien certificates and administers tax titles, liens and foreclosed land sales.

The office is at City Hall, Room 1, 25 West Street, open Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday from 8:30 am to 4 pm and Thursday from 8:30 am to 5:30 pm. The phone is 978-534-7500, extension 1172.

Municipal lien certificates are listed among the office's services, so ask the office how to request one for your closing. The state's appeals guide says quarterly-billing communities generally bill on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.

Abatement applications go to the local Board of Assessors, and the timeline comes from state law. The Appellate Tax Board states that the application is due on or before the first installment due date of the actual bill, generally February 1 where bills are quarterly.

The assessors then have three months to respond. If they deny or do not act, you have three months from the decision, or from the deemed denial, to file with the board in Boston. Taxes must be paid on time during the process.

Use recent sales of similar houses close to the valuation date, since the board values property as of January 1 before the fiscal year.

Woburn is a city in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, about 9 miles north of Boston. It covers roughly 12.9 square miles and shares borders with Wilmington, Reading, Stoneham, Winchester, Lexington and Burlington.

The 2020 census counted 40,876 residents living in 16,590 households, with 17,540 housing units, about 5.4% of them vacant at the time. The median age was 40.8. Woburn runs on a mayor and city council, and it was the last Massachusetts municipality to stop calling council members aldermen.

Woburn sits at about 98 feet of elevation, and Horn Pond, where the town was first settled, is a primary source of the Mystic River. For a seller, the practical point is that a buyer can compare your house with others in a city of roughly 44,000 people, which the Census Bureau estimated at 43,962 in July 2025.

How much of Woburn's history is still visible in its houses?

A good deal of it is. Woburn was first settled in 1640 near Horn Pond and became a town in 1642. Its territory once included what are now Winchester, Burlington and parts of Stoneham and Wilmington, which split off over the next two centuries.

The city grew around tanning and transport. A tannery was built in 1668, the Middlesex Canal opened in 1803, and the Boston and Lowell Railroad began running through town in 1835. Route 128 opened in 1951 and Route 93 came through in 1963, which pulled the city toward Boston commuters and offices.

  • Several 18th and 19th century houses survive, including the 1790 House and the Baldwin House beside a stretch of the old canal.
  • The population jumped from about 20,500 in 1950 to 31,200 in 1960 and 37,400 in 1970, so a large share of the housing dates from those postwar decades.

If your house is one of the older ones, a cash buyer prices the age and condition into the offer directly instead of asking you to fix things first.

Who employs people in Woburn?

Woburn has a mixed economy of retail, healthcare, manufacturing and office parks. Companies headquartered here include Boston Acoustics, Monotype and Skyworks Solutions. Cummings Properties, a large commercial landlord in the region, was founded in Woburn in 1970.

What should a seller know about Woburn's water and groundwater history?

Woburn is one of the few communities near Boston that supplies its own drinking water. The supply comes mostly from five wells in the Horn Pond aquifer, treated at the Horn Pond Treatment Plant, with about a third supplemented by the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority.

The city also carries a well-known environmental history. In 1979, high levels of chemical contamination were found in city Wells G and H, and families in the Pine Street area of east Woburn raised concerns about childhood leukemia. A lawsuit followed in 1982, and the story became the book and film titled A Civil Action.

That history is decades old, and we are not saying any particular street is affected today. It does explain why buyers and their lenders in Woburn sometimes ask about environmental questions on older industrial or neighboring parcels. If your house sits near former industrial land, ask the city's Water Department and the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection what records exist, and tell any buyer what you learn.

The older Mishawum commuter rail stop stopped service on December 14, 2020. Location near the station or highway ramps is one of the first things a buyer will weigh, and it is worth mentioning when you describe your house to us.

Which schools serve Woburn?

Woburn Public Schools runs seven elementary schools: Goodyear, Altavesta, Shamrock, Malcolm White, Reeves, Linscott-Rumford and Hurld-Wyman. Students then move to the John F. Kennedy or Daniel L. Joyce middle school and on to Woburn Memorial High School. Northeast Metro Tech serves as the vocational school, and St. Charles is a private Catholic school for kindergarten through eighth grade.

Several former school buildings, including Clapp, Plympton and Wyman, have been closed or repurposed.

The city also announced cyclical property inspections running from May to November 2026, so a visit from an assessor is possible.

A Woburn sale follows Massachusetts law, plus a few local contacts. Three items come up most often.

  • Smoke detectors. Under M.G.L. c. 148, section 26F, a residential building must be equipped by the seller with approved smoke detectors when it is sold or transferred, and the head of the fire department enforces it. Call the Woburn Fire Department to schedule the inspection.

  • Tax proration. Unpaid or current tax is settled at closing, typically from the seller's proceeds.

These are the same steps whether you list, sell by owner or take a cash offer. What changes is how long they take and how many contingencies surround them.

Selling for cash in Woburn means a buyer purchases the house as it stands, without a mortgage contingency. We look at the address, the condition and any liens or taxes, then present an offer. Where is Beverly and what is it like?

Beverly is a city on the Massachusetts North Shore in Essex County, about 17 miles northeast of Boston. It covers 22.6 square miles, and roughly a third of that is water.

Manchester-by-the-Sea borders Beverly on the east, Wenham on the north, Danvers on the west and Salem on the south. The Danvers River and Beverly Harbor separate Beverly from Salem, and three bridges connect the two cities. The city also includes two small islands, Great Misery and Little Misery, plus a large part of Wenham Lake and a city forest.

The western half of Beverly is more built up. The eastern half, roughly from Woodbury Point eastward, is more rural. The areas residents name most often are:

  • Ryal Side
  • North Beverly
  • Centerville
  • Cove
  • Montserrat
  • Beverly Farms and Prides Crossing

The 2020 census counted 42,670 residents and 17,887 housing units, of which 4.9 percent were vacant. About 31.7 percent of households were one person living alone.

How did Beverly become the city it is today?

English colonists under Roger Conant settled the area in 1626, and Beverly was set off from Salem and incorporated as a town in 1668. It became a city in 1894.

Beverly had the first cotton mill in America in 1787. In 1902 the United Shoe Machinery Corporation began building a quarter mile of reinforced concrete factory buildings, which went into production in 1906 and closed in 1987. Cummings Properties bought the complex in 1996 and turned it into a campus of offices, medical practices, shops and restaurants. Parker Brothers, the game maker, was once headquartered in Beverly too.

President William Howard Taft rented a summer White House in Beverly in 1909 and 1910 and a different house in 1911 and 1912. The city's Beverly Farms section is the reason Beverly Hills, California, has its name.

Who employs people in Beverly?

Beverly's major employers include Axcelis Technologies, Beverly Hospital (part of Lahey), Endicott College and the YMCA of the North Shore. The city is also home to Montserrat College of Art.

Beverly has five public elementary schools for kindergarten through grade 4: Ayers Ryal Side, Centerville, Cove, Hannah and North Beverly. Beverly Middle School serves grades 5 through 8 and opened in 2018, and Beverly High School serves grades 9 through 12. The high school was founded in 1858.

Those employers and campuses sit in different parts of the city, so the address of your house relative to them matters more than the city name alone.

What places draw people to Beverly?

Lynch Park and its beaches in the Cove section are the city's main public park and a popular summer spot for swimming and kayaking. Beverly has five beaches in all, and two yacht clubs, Jubilee Yacht Club in Beverly Harbor and Bass Haven Yacht Club on the Bass River.

Downtown has two historic theaters. The Cabot opened in the 1920s era of movie palaces and reopened as a nonprofit performing arts center in 2014. The Larcom Theatre dates to 1912 and seats 560. The Beverly Cotton Manufactory site in North Beverly marks the first cotton mill in America.

Beverly also calls itself the birthplace of America's Navy because the schooner USS Hannah sailed from Beverly Harbor on September 5, 1775, though Marblehead disputes the claim.

What does North Shore weather mean for a Beverly house?

Beverly has an oceanic climate that borders on humid continental. NOAA normals for the city show about 48 inches of precipitation a year and about 51 inches of snow.

Thunderstorms, tropical rainstorms in summer, and nor'easters in the cooler months are all part of the pattern. Houses near the harbor, the Bass River or the coves are more exposed to that weather than houses inland.

How do roads, rail and bridges affect Beverly sellers?

Route 128 crosses Beverly from east to west and connects to Interstate 95 and Route 1 in Peabody. Route 1A runs north and south through downtown. Routes 22, 62, 97 and 127 end in the city.

Beverly sits where the Newburyport and Rockport lines of the MBTA Commuter Rail split, and it has more commuter rail stations than any municipality in the state except Boston. Stations include:

  • Beverly Depot, near downtown, served by both lines
  • North Beverly, on the Newburyport line
  • Montserrat and Beverly Farms, on the Rockport line

Service to Prides Crossing station is suspended indefinitely. Beverly Municipal Airport sits partly inside Danvers.

One local item stands out. The Hall-Whitaker Bridge over the Bass River on Bridge Street was closed to vehicles by MassDOT in June 2023, with a permanent replacement expected in 2027. Buyers who drive past it daily may ask about it, and a house near that stretch is a fair thing to mention honestly.

The Beverly Assessors set values for 13,037 real estate parcels and 1,551 personal property accounts as of January 1 each year. For fiscal 2026 the city's residential tax rate is $10.81 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the commercial rate is $20.98.

On a house assessed at $700,000, that rate works out to about $7,567 for the year before any exemption. That is arithmetic on the posted rate, not a quote for your bill, so use your actual bill.

The assessing office also reviews building permits to see how they change a property's value, which means a renovation can raise the next assessment. City Hall is at 191 Cabot Street, and the assessor's line is 978-605-2307. The office posts a fiscal 2026 abatement application, exemption guides for veterans, seniors and others, and a deferral application.

If you want to contest an assessment, the state's Appellate Tax Board guide says the abatement application must reach the assessors by the due date of the first actual tax bill. In quarterly billing towns that is generally February 1. Ask the Beverly collector which schedule applies to you.

What does the closing process look like for a Beverly sale?

Beverly is served by the Southern Essex District Registry of Deeds, and a deed is recorded there at closing. Ask the registry or your closing attorney for the current excise tax and recording fees, because the registry sets its own fee schedule.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department for a sale. Call as soon as you have a closing date, and expect an inspection fee.
  • Septic, if any. The eastern part of Beverly is more rural. If your house has a septic system, Title 5 calls for an inspection within two years before the sale, or within six months after if weather prevents it.
  • Attorney. A court decision cited by the Trial Court Law Libraries holds that lender side closings need an attorney's substantive participation.

Most Massachusetts property is recorded land, filed at the Registry of Deeds. A minority is registered land, which has a Land Court certificate of title.

Beverly is a coastal city with a large share of its land in the water and a long list of named areas, so two houses a few miles apart can sell very differently.

What is Pittsfield's history, and where does General Electric fit?

The land was bought in 1738 by Colonel Jacob Wendell as a speculative investment, and Pittsfield was incorporated as a town in 1761 and as a city in 1891. Merino sheep arrived in 1807, and woolen manufacturing dominated the economy for almost a century.

William Stanley Jr. produced the first electric transformer here after relocating his company in 1891, and General Electric acquired the firm in 1903. By 1930 the population had passed 50,000. GE later cut its workforce from over 13,000 to a small number, and General Dynamics now occupies many of the old GE buildings.

The 2020 census counted 43,927 residents, so the city is smaller than at its peak, and the population has declined in recent decades.

What is the environmental history sellers hear about in Pittsfield?

The Housatonic River and its floodplain were contaminated with PCBs from the former General Electric plant, and the area is a federal Superfund site. EPA added it to the Superfund list in September 1997, and a settlement valued at over $250 million was reached in 1999 and entered as a consent decree the next year.

Between 2005 and 2018, GE finished remediation and restoration of the ten plant areas within the city, and it continues monitoring and maintenance. Downstream cleanup was not complete as of 2025.

Pittsfield has a humid continental climate with harsh winters because of its elevation. Average annual snowfall is about 73 inches, temperatures reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit or colder 13 times a year, and measurable precipitation falls on 173 days.

Heating cost, roof condition and pipe protection matter more here than in a milder climate. A house that sat empty for a winter may carry freeze damage, which lenders and buyers' inspectors both check.

Pittsfield is at the crossroads of U.S. Route 7 and U.S. Route 20. Route 8 passes through the northeast corner, combined in part with Route 9, and Route 41 starts in the southwest. The nearest interstate is I-90, the Massachusetts Turnpike, about 10 miles south in Lee.

The Joseph Scelsi Intermodal Transportation Center serves Amtrak trains and Peter Pan buses and is the hub of the Berkshire Regional Transit Authority. Pittsfield Municipal Airport serves private and charter flights, and Albany International is the nearest airport with national service.

Long-distance travel runs through the intermodal center, where the regional bus system also has its hub.

What do Pittsfield sellers need to know about schools, jobs and government?

Pittsfield's public schools enroll more than 6,000 students and include eight elementary schools, two middle schools and two high schools, Pittsfield High and Taconic. Berkshire Community College's main campus is in the city.

Berkshire Medical Center is the only hospital in the northern part of the county, and the Berkshire Athenaeum is among the largest libraries in western Massachusetts. Pittsfield uses a mayor-council form of government, with Peter Marchetti elected to a four-year term in January 2024.

In 2017 the National Center for Arts Research ranked Pittsfield and Berkshire County as the top medium-sized community in the nation for the arts. Tax rates and bill dates are set by the city.

The west branch of the Housatonic is fed by Onota Lake and Pontoosuc Lake, the latter lying partly in Lanesborough. Houses near those shores and near the river sit in different conditions from hillside homes, and a seller should know whether the property is near water.

  • Wahconah Park, built in 1919, has hosted professional and summer baseball since 1894.
  • The Berkshire Museum and Berkshire Athenaeum are downtown landmarks.
  • Pittsfield State Forest has hiking, camping and swimming.

A 1791 town bylaw barred playing baseball near the meeting house, which Wikipedia calls potentially the earliest known reference to baseball in America. A 1902 trolley collision on the road to the Pittsfield Country Club threw President Theodore Roosevelt into the street.

What state steps apply when you sell in Pittsfield?

Massachusetts requires a fire department certificate for the sale of a home. Mass.gov says to call the local fire department once you have a closing date and that the department charges a fee. Alarms with no manufacture date count as expired.

The Trial Court Law Libraries describe attorneys as part of Massachusetts sales by law and by practice, and note that most deeds are filed as recorded land at the registry of deeds. Deed excise appears in Chapter 64D, Section 1 and counts the sale price without liens that stay on the property.

Under 760 CMR 74, sellers of certain residential properties may not condition an offer on a waiver of the home inspection.

No. The Superfund site covers the plant area, the river, its banks and floodplains, and other named areas. Ask your attorney what is on record for your address.

How did Marlborough grow from a trail crossing to a tech corridor?

Families from Sudbury petitioned in 1656 for a town at the crossing of two Native American trails, and Marlborough was incorporated as a town in 1660 and as a city in 1890.

It became a stop on the Boston Post Road, and George Washington visited Williams Tavern in 1789. In 1836 Samuel Boyd and his brother Joseph opened the first shoe factory, and by 1890 the city had about 14,000 residents and was a major shoe center. The Rockport Company was founded there in 1971.

Interstates 495 and 290 and the Massachusetts Turnpike then brought high technology and electronics. In November 2016 the state announced a $3 million grant for infrastructure along U.S. Route 20 to support commercial development.

That mix of old industrial streets near downtown and newer suburban neighborhoods means Marlborough houses vary widely in age and condition, and so do the repairs a buyer must price in.

Much of the work is in office parks. The southwestern corner, locally called the Southwest Quadrant, holds office and corporate buildings along Forest Street, Cedar Hill Street, Simarano Drive, Ames Street, D'Angelo Drive and Campus Drive, close to Interstate 495.

Europeans settled the area in 1730 as part of Lunenburg, and Fitchburg was incorporated in 1764 and became a city in 1872. It was named for John Fitch.

The Fitchburg Railroad ran through the Hoosac Tunnel to link Boston and Albany, and the rock drill used to build the tunnel was made in Fitchburg. Water-powered mills made machines, tools, clothing, paper and firearms. Paper mills lined the Nashua River, and the 1922 New England textile strike shut the mills over an attempted wage cut.

Fitchburg is also a shire town, so it hosts the Northern Worcester County Registry of Deeds, established in 1903. Deeds for Fitchburg property are recorded there.

What are Amherst's rental permit and inspection rules?

Registration of residential rental property is required in Amherst, and permits must be renewed every year by June 15.

The town's rental property page says the Inspection Services Department has launched a Residential Rental Property Inspection Program, and that inspections are now a condition of keeping a permit. With over 5,000 rental units in town, the program is expected to run for several years, with up to 500 randomly selected units scheduled each year. Owners receive a postcard when their unit is picked. The rental bylaw was adopted on April 8, 2024.

  • Permitting is done online through the town's portal.
  • Inspection Services can be reached at 413-259-3030 or inspections@amherstma.gov.

Voters approved a charter in March 2018 by a 58 percent majority, and a 13-member council took office on December 2, 2018. A seller with an aging furnace, an older roof or an uninsulated attic should expect the buyer to raise it.

How do people get around Amherst?

Amherst is served by local buses and intercity coaches, with rail and air a drive away.

  • The Pioneer Valley Transit Authority runs local service, operated by UMass Transportation Services.
  • Peter Pan Bus Lines connects Amherst with Springfield, Boston and other New England cities, and Megabus runs to New York City and Burlington, Vermont.
  • Amtrak's Vermonter stops in nearby Northampton, and Springfield's Union Station has more frequent trains to New York and Washington.
  • Bradley International Airport in Windsor Locks, Connecticut is about an hour by car.

Which schools serve Amherst?

Amherst belongs to the Amherst Regional School District along with Leverett, Pelham and Shutesbury.

Three elementary schools serve kindergarten through grade 6: Crocker Farm, Fort River and Wildwood. Amherst Regional Middle School covers grades 7 and 8, and Amherst Regional High School serves the older students. The town also has a five-member School Committee elected to two-year terms.

What draws visitors and residents to central Amherst?

The center of town holds a cluster of cultural sites, and the Amherst Center Cultural District was formed in 2016.

Among them are the Emily Dickinson Museum, the poet's birthplace and lifelong home, the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art, the Mead Art Museum at Amherst College and the Beneski Museum of Natural History. The W. E. B. Du Bois Library at UMass is the tallest academic library in the United States. Sellers near the center can point to this cluster when describing the location.

What about property tax in Amherst?

The rules below apply across Massachusetts. They come from the Appellate Tax Board's appeals guide.

  • In towns that bill quarterly, bills are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.
  • An abatement application is due by the first installment date of the actual bill, generally February 1 in quarterly towns.
  • Assessors have three months to act, and an appeal to the board follows within three months of their action.

Ask the Amherst Assessors for the current rate and bill dates. If a bill goes unpaid, the lien process in the Land Court's foreclosure overview applies: a demand after 30 days, a possible tax taking 14 days later, and redemption until a court judgment.

What does an Amherst sale require?

Sellers of one and two family homes need a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate, and any rental use needs its permit in order.

The state's alarm inspection guide explains that you must call the local fire department once you have a closing date, and that the department charges a fee for the inspection and certificate. Alarms with no manufacture date are treated as expired.

The certificate is a requirement of the transfer whoever the buyer is, so settle in writing which side handles the inspection and the fee.

How do Amherst sellers choose between a listing and a cash offer?

The tradeoff is time and effort against price.

A listing exposes the house to many buyers, which is helpful for a well-kept home near campus. It can also bring weeks of showings and repair requests. A direct cash purchase suits owners with a worn-out rental, an inherited house or a deadline, because there are no showings and the buyer takes the house as is. Expect the price to reflect the repairs the buyer will take on.

Do I need a rental permit in Amherst?

Yes. Amherst requires registration of residential rental property, renewed each year by June 15, and rental units are subject to inspection.

How often will Amherst inspect a rental property?

The town expects to inspect up to 500 randomly selected units each year across more than 5,000 rentals, so some owners may wait years to be selected.

Is Amherst a town or a city?

Both in a legal sense. Massachusetts treats it as a city because of its council-manager charter, but it keeps the name Town of Amherst.

When are Massachusetts quarterly property tax bills due?

In towns that bill quarterly, bills are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Ask the Amherst Assessors for the exact dates.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Amherst?

For a one or two family home, yes. The local fire department inspects and issues a certificate of compliance, and it charges a fee.

Where is Westfield, MA, and how big is it?

Westfield is a Hampden County city in the Pioneer Valley of western Massachusetts, about 10 miles west of Springfield and 95 miles west of Boston. It is large by land, at 47.31 square miles, with 40,834 residents in the 2020 Census, so it has far more open ground per person than a city like Watertown.

The Westfield River splits it into the North Side and the South Side, and the northwest corner is known as Wyben. Neighbors include Southampton, Holyoke, West Springfield, Agawam, Southwick, Granville, Russell and Montgomery.

The 2020 Census found 15,887 households and 16,869 housing units, with 5.8% of units vacant. The median resident was 40.6 years old, and 19.1% of residents were 65 or older.

Why is Westfield called the Whip City?

Westfield earned the nickname from the buggy whip trade that made it a manufacturing center in the nineteenth century. Early settlers farmed the river's alluvial soil for about 150 years, and in the 1800s the city added bricks, whips, cigars, bicycles, paper products, pipe organs, boilers, radiators and precision tools.

Westfield was first settled in 1660, became a town in 1669 and a city on November 2, 1920. It was the westernmost settlement in the Massachusetts colony until 1725. In 1939 it elected Alice Burke, the first woman mayor in Massachusetts and in New England. Manufacturing eroded in the second half of the twentieth century, and the north side turned to warehousing, with C&S Wholesale, Home Depot and Lowes listed among the operators.

Is Westfield prone to flooding, and what does the climate mean for a house?

Westfield sits in a floodplain zone and Wikipedia describes the city as flood-prone. The Westfield River drops out of the Berkshire Hills with a large, steep, rocky watershed, so it has a history of severe floods in the adjoining neighborhoods. Pumps, dikes, waterways and upstream dams help, but they do not remove the risk.

Winters are cold. At Westfield-Barnes Regional Airport the January mean high is about 33 degrees and the mean low about 13, and the record low is 20 below zero. Annual precipitation averages 48.39 inches.

What schools, hospitals and college are in Westfield?

Westfield Public Schools run one preschool, five elementary schools, an intermediate school, a middle school and two high schools, Westfield High School and Westfield Technical Academy. The 2024-25 enrollment was 4,772. Westfield River Elementary School opened on January 6, 2025, replacing Franklin Avenue and Abner Gibbs.

Westfield State University anchors the south side, and students make up roughly 15 percent of the population. Baystate Noble Hospital and the state-run Western Massachusetts Hospital are the two main hospitals.

How do roads, buses and airports serve Westfield?

The Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90) crosses just north of Westfield Center and meets I-91 about three miles east. U.S. 20 is the main east-west street, and U.S. 202 and Route 10 run north and south. The Great River Bridge over the Westfield River, called the Green Bridge, was doubled in the 2000s so each span carries one direction.

Pioneer Valley Transit Authority routes R10 and B23 connect to Springfield, West Springfield and Holyoke. Passenger trains no longer stop in the city. The nearest Amtrak and CTrail Hartford Line service is in Springfield, 9.6 miles east, and Bradley International Airport in Windsor Locks is 18 miles south. What should Westfield owners know about property tax abatements?

Westfield follows the same state procedure as every Massachusetts city. An abatement lowers a bill when the assessed value exceeds fair cash value, when an exemption applies, or when the classification is wrong. The burden of proof sits with the taxpayer, and the strongest evidence is recent sales of similar nearby houses.

  • File the abatement application with the assessors by the first installment due date.
  • The assessors have three months to decide.
  • The Appellate Tax Board hears appeals filed within three months of the decision.
  • Most single-family appeals use the informal procedure, which has no formal discovery.

Westfield's assessor posts local forms and deadlines. Check them with that office, because the state guide gives only general timing.

What parks, trails and public spaces sit near Westfield homes?

Westfield has a lot of green space for a city its size, and a buyer will notice it. Stanley Park, Amelia Park Ice Rink and Memorial Garden, the Columbia Greenway Rail Trail, East Mountain and the 114-mile Metacomet-Monadnock Trail, which crosses the city. The Westfield Athenaeum, a free public library, has served the city since 1868.

The City Council meets on the first and third Thursday of each month at 7:30 p.m. in City Hall, which is where zoning and ordinance questions end up. Wikipedia also notes a mitigation action over PFAS in the city's water. If your house has a private well, ask the local health office about testing before you list.

What are the closing costs for a Westfield seller?

Westfield deeds are recorded at the Hampden County Registry of Deeds, which charges $155 to record a deed and applies an excise tax of $4.56 per $1,000 of taxable value. The registry accepts cash and checks only.

At that rate a $250,000 sale carries $1,140 in deed excise. A recorded municipal lien certificate costs $80 there. Your lender payoff, title work and any agent fee come on top, so ask the closing attorney for an itemized estimate before you accept an offer.

Selling a Westfield house fast: your realistic options

Westfield owners usually weigh three paths. A listing can bring the strongest price when the house shows well. A private sale saves the commission but needs paperwork help. A cash sale closes quickly and skips the repair list.

For an inherited house, a flood-damaged basement or a home with tenants, speed and certainty often matter more than squeezing out the last dollar. Parts of the city lie in the Westfield River floodplain, and the city is considered flood-prone despite dikes and dams. Confirm your own address on the FEMA flood map and with your insurer.

Meetings on the first and third Thursday of each month at 7:30 p.m. in City Hall. Confirm the current schedule with the city clerk.

Where is Chelsea, Massachusetts, and why is it so dense?

Water borders it on three sides. The Island End River separates Chelsea from Everett to the west, the Mystic River and Chelsea Creek form the boundary with Boston to the south and east, and Mill Creek marks part of the border with Revere. The elevation at 9.8 feet, with a few small hills rising above the flat ground.

The hills are Admirals Hill, Mount Bellingham, Powderhorn Hill, Mount Washington and Mill Hill. They help divide the city into distinct neighborhoods.

What are Chelsea's neighborhoods?

Chelsea has several named areas, each with its own housing mix. These come from Wikipedia's description.

  • Admirals Hill holds the Naval Hospital Historic District and Mary O'Malley Park, the city's largest park.
  • Addison-Orange is flat, residential and densely populated.
  • Bellingham Square became the center of commerce and government after the 1908 fire and includes City Hall and the public library.
  • The Box District, named for early box factories, was rezoned for residential use in the 2000s.
  • Carter Park and Wyndham are a small enclave of mostly single-family Queen Anne homes.
  • Mill Hill has mostly two- and three-story wood-frame detached buildings.
  • Prattville is the northwestern section, and Soldiers Home covers Powderhorn Hill.

If your house is in one of these areas, say so when you talk to a buyer. A single-family house in Carter Park sells to a different buyer than a three-decker in Mill Hill.

What happened in the Great Chelsea Fires?

Chelsea has burned twice on a large scale, and both fires shaped the housing. On April 12, 1908, nearly half the city was destroyed and 18,000 people, 56 percent of the population, lost their homes. The city took about two and a half years to rebuild and was redesigned with wider streets and better emergency access.

In 1973 a second fire destroyed 18 city blocks and affected nearly one-fifth of the city. It started in the rag shop district, where many small businesses handled scrap materials, and spread through wood-frame, closely spaced multifamily buildings.

Chelsea's housing as dense, with many wood-frame multifamily buildings. The Department of Fire Services requires a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate for the sale of a home, so fire safety is part of the paperwork whatever the building type.

Samuel Maverick built a palisaded trading post at Winnisimmet in 1624, which is considered the first permanent settlement in Boston Harbor. Chelsea was incorporated as a town in 1739 and became a city in 1857. The Battle of Chelsea Creek in 1775 was the second battle of the American Revolution.

In 1991 Massachusetts placed Chelsea under receivership after a budget deficit of about $9.5 million against a $40 million budget. Voters approved a new charter on June 21, 1994, which replaced the mayor and aldermen with a council-manager system, and local control returned in 1995 when the deficit was gone and the bond rating reached triple-A.

Today an 11-member city council, with three at-large and eight district councilors, works with a city manager. Public schools include four elementary schools, three middle schools and Chelsea High School, plus Excel Academy and Phoenix Charter Academy as public charters. Bunker Hill Community College has a satellite location in the city.

Where is Braintree and how big is it?

Braintree is a community of 39,143 residents (2020 census) in Norfolk County, south of Boston on the South Shore. It covers about 14.6 square miles, and only 0.8 of those are water.

Quincy borders Braintree on the north, Weymouth on the east and Holbrook on the south. Randolph lies to the west, separated from Braintree by the Cochato River. Parks and open space include Pond Meadow Park, Sunset Lake and part of the Blue Hills Reservation, and South Shore Plaza is the best known retail destination in town.

Braintree has two historic village centers, Braintree and South Braintree, which were separate communities in 1888. The ZIP codes are 02184 and 02185.

Is Braintree a town or a city?

Braintree is officially the Town of Braintree, yet it has been a city under Massachusetts law since 2007, with a mayor and a town council. The first mayor was Joe Sullivan, who served until January 2020. Erin Joyce was elected mayor in 2023.

That naming matters when you look for paperwork. Departments such as the Assessors, the Collector and the Treasurer sit under Municipal Finance on the official website, braintreema.gov.

What is the history of Braintree?

Settlers arrived in 1625 on land first called Mount Wollaston, and the town was incorporated in 1640. Its original territory later split into Quincy in 1792 and Randolph in 1793, and Holbrook broke off Randolph in 1872. Braintree was part of Suffolk County until Norfolk County was formed in 1793.

John Adams and John Hancock are both on the list of notable people from Braintree. In 1920 it was the site of the murders that led to the Sacco and Vanzetti trial. Its population grew by more than half that same decade, and after World War II some Irish American and Italian American families moved to Braintree from lower income parts of Boston.

The 2020 census counted 39,143 residents, and Wikipedia's 2024 estimate is 39,134, so the population has been flat since then.

Braintree has several rail options. Braintree station is served by the MBTA Red Line, two commuter rail lines (the Fall River/New Bedford Line and the Kingston Line) and the seasonal CapeFLYER. The Weymouth Landing/East Braintree station on the Weymouth border is served by the Greenbush Line.

It helps owners with exemption forms, abatement forms and abutter lists, and it runs a property record website. Town Hall is open Monday, Wednesday and Thursday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Tuesday until 7 p.m., and Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m.

What happens if a Braintree owner appeals an assessment?

An owner who disagrees with the Braintree Assessors files an abatement application first, and assessors then have three months to act on it. If they deny it or do nothing, the owner has three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Where is Holyoke, Massachusetts, and how is the city laid out?

Holyoke is a city in Hampden County, about 8 miles north of Springfield, on the west bank of the Connecticut River. It covers 22.8 square miles, and the Mount Tom Range rises behind the built-up area at 1,202 feet.

Most homes sit on the terraces between the mountain and the river. Small wooded ravines called dingles cut through those terraces and drain toward the water, which gives many Holyoke streets a stepped, hilly feel. The city is also one of a few in New England built on a street grid, because it was planned alongside its dam rather than growing out of a village green.

The 2020 census counted 38,238 residents. A seller here is usually dealing with housing that was built for mill workers more than a century ago, so age and condition come up in nearly every sale conversation.

How did the canals and paper mills shape Holyoke's houses?

The dam and canal system finished in 1849 pulled factories to the river, and the housing followed them. Holyoke grew from just under 5,000 people in 1860 to over 60,000 by 1920, and the city incorporated in 1873.

Early on, mill companies built housing themselves. The Hadley Falls Company housing district dates to 1847 and 1848, and later the Holyoke Water Power Company sold lots to working families. The result is a mix of Italianate, Gothic Revival, Queen Anne and Second Empire buildings, plus Philadelphia-style rowhouses along downtown streets.

That history matters when you sell. Brick tenements, rowhouses and older two- and three-family buildings can carry old wiring, aging heat systems and deferred repairs. Buyers who want a finished house tend to shy away from these, while a cash buyer who plans to renovate can price the work directly.

Which neighborhoods are in Holyoke?

Holyoke has 15 neighborhoods, and each one has a different housing mix. Some began as streetcar suburbs for mill workers, while others were villages that existed before the city did.

  • Downtown and the Flats: City Hall, the Volleyball Hall of Fame, the canal system and the Holyoke Innovation District.
  • South Holyoke: older rowhouse and tenement streets near the canals.
  • Springdale and Oakdale: streetcar suburbs from the 1800s. Springdale Park was designed by the Olmsted Brothers, and Holyoke Medical Center is in Oakdale.
  • Elmwood and Rock Valley: villages that predate the city. Elmwood is the oldest neighborhood and was once called Baptist Village.
  • Ingleside and Homestead Avenue: the Holyoke Mall area and Holyoke Community College.
  • Smith's Ferry: the northern edge, annexed from Northampton in 1909.
  • Churchill, Highlands, Highland Park, Jarvis Avenue and Whiting Farms: the remaining residential areas.

What does the Holyoke economy look like today?

Holyoke is still called the Paper City, though writing-paper production has largely left. Specialty paper makers and converters remain, along with plants making medical devices, industrial vacuums, plastics and rubber goods, and archival supplies.

The city holds one of three foreign-trade zones in Massachusetts. It also hosts the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center, which opened in 2012 and draws power from the canal system. Because the canals are municipally owned, Wikipedia reports that Holyoke has among the lowest electricity costs in the state.

Holyoke Community College was the first community college in Massachusetts, and Holyoke Public Schools serves the city's students. For a seller, a stable base of manufacturing, college and hospital jobs means demand for housing in the area does not depend on a single employer.

When are Holyoke property taxes due?

Holyoke bills real estate tax in four quarters, and the fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. The tax collector's page lists the fiscal 2027 due dates as follows.

  • First quarter: August 3, 2026
  • Second quarter: November 1, 2026
  • Third quarter: February 1, 2027

The first two bills are preliminary and run about half of the prior year's total tax. The last two are actual bills based on assessed value once the rate is set in December. Anything still owed 14 days after the fourth-quarter due date picks up interest and a $15 demand fee.

If a bill goes unpaid, the collector records an Instrument of Taking at the Registry of Deeds, which puts a lien on the house and starts a tax title account. After six months without payment, a petition to foreclose can be filed in Land Court. Sellers with unpaid bills should ask the collector for a payoff figure before choosing how to sell.

Can you appeal a Holyoke assessment?

Yes. The Board of Assessors handles abatement requests, and its office is at City Hall, open weekdays from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm.

The state Appellate Tax Board explains the order of steps. You must pay the tax on time, file the abatement application with the assessors by the first installment due date on the actual bill (generally February 1 in a city that bills quarterly), and then file with the board within three months of the assessors' decision. The assessors have three months to act, and silence counts as a denial.

The law presumes the assessment is right, so you carry the burden of showing the fair cash value is lower. Recent sales of similar homes nearby are the usual proof. An appeal rarely helps a seller who wants to close in a few weeks, but it matters for owners keeping the house another year.

What does a Holyoke seller need from the fire department?

Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the standard for a sale. The Department of Fire Services advises scheduling the inspection as soon as you have a closing date.

The inspection depends on when the house was built and when the last building permit was issued. Battery alarms older than 10 years, or with no date stamp, must be replaced with 10-year sealed photoelectric units that have a hush feature. The fire department charges a fee for the inspection, so ask Holyoke's department what it is.

Hard-wired alarms may need an electrician. In an older multi-family house with several floors, this small repair can hold up a closing if nobody starts it early.

How does a Holyoke closing work, and what does recording cost?

Massachusetts closings run through attorneys. The state's law library notes that the closing of a typical transaction involves an attorney acting for the lender, and that sellers in practice use real estate attorneys as well.

Deeds for most Massachusetts properties are recorded at the county Registry of Deeds, and a small share of land is registered through the Land Court instead. The deed excise tax statute lists $2 for each $500 of consideration or fraction of it, and the seller normally pays it at recording. Registries publish fee schedules, so confirm the total with the Hampden County registry before closing.

Anyone selling to a buyer who plans to renovate should still expect a lien search, payoff letters for any mortgage, and a final tax and water balance. Holyoke's collector issues the tax figures.

Many Holyoke sellers inherited an older multi-family house, own a rental with long-term tenants, or are carrying a house that needs work they cannot fund. Others fell behind on taxes and want to avoid tax title.

  • Tenants in place in two- and three-family buildings.
  • Delinquent tax bills that need a payoff before closing.
  • An estate with several heirs and no one living in the house.

A cash buyer can look at the house in its current condition and work around these problems. You can compare that route with listing by asking for an offer and reading it against what repairs, fire department items and carrying costs would cost you on the open market.

The collector can record an Instrument of Taking at the Registry of Deeds, which places a lien on the property. If the tax stays unpaid for six months, a petition to foreclose can be filed in Land Court, and advertising fees are added to the balance.

Can I sell a Holyoke house with tenants in it?

Yes. Tenants do not prevent a sale, though they affect timing and who can buy. Ask the buyer how they handle leases, and check Massachusetts landlord and tenant rules with the Attorney General's office or an attorney.

Who do I call about my Holyoke assessment?

Call the Holyoke Board of Assessors at (413) 322-5550. The office is at City Hall and is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. Ask about abatement forms and deadlines for your bill.

Two chapters shaped the modern city. The Watertown Arsenal made military armaments from 1816 until 1995, when the Army sold the site. It has since turned into offices, shops, restaurants and the Mosesian Center for the Arts. Along Arsenal Street you now find Arsenal Yards and the Watertown Mall facing each other.

Where a city bills quarterly, installments are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A city that bills twice a year usually sets the due date thirty days after mailing. Where is Randolph, Massachusetts, and what kind of place is it?

Randolph is a suburban city of about 35,000 people in Norfolk County, south of Boston, and it borders Quincy to the north. Its 2020 census count was 34,984, and the land area is 10.1 square miles with very little water.

The Cochato River and the Blue Hill River drain the town into the Neponset River. Elevation is about 184 feet, well above Quincy's 30 feet, and Randolph has almost no harbor frontage, with water making up only about 4 percent of its area.

One quirk: Randolph runs under a city form of government but kept "Town of Randolph" as its official name, one of thirteen Massachusetts municipalities that did so. You will see both forms on documents.

What is the history behind Randolph's houses?

Randolph was set off from Braintree in 1793 as a separate town and named for Peyton Randolph, first president of the Continental Congress. Shoe and boot making became its main industry, and by 1850 it ranked among the nation's leading boot producers.

When the shoe trade faded in the early 1900s, the town turned into a residential community, with light manufacturing and services replacing the factories. Population jumped from 9,982 in 1950 to 18,900 in 1960 and 27,035 in 1970, according to the census counts on Wikipedia.

The town's population nearly tripled in two decades. That surge suggests a large share of Randolph's housing went up in a short window, so houses of similar age may need roofs, boilers and windows replaced around the same time. A seller can check each house's age on the assessor's property card.

How does a tax abatement work if you own a house in Randolph?

An abatement is a reduction in your property tax, granted when you can show your home's fair cash value is below its assessed value. The process is set by state law, and the Appellate Tax Board's guide spells out the steps.

  • Pay each installment on time. Late payment can cost you the right to appeal.

Randolph shares the Blue Hill climate record with neighboring Quincy. Averages there are 53.86 inches of precipitation and 69.7 inches of snow a year, and January lows average 18.3 degrees Fahrenheit.

The record low on that station is minus 21 degrees, and the record high is 101. Houses here carry real heating load in winter and real humidity in summer, so buyers check insulation, the furnace and the roof.

Two rivers drain the town, so ask the town and your insurer whether your lot has any flood exposure.

What local landmarks and institutions come with Randolph?

Randolph's National Register of Historic Places listings include the Jonathan Belcher House, built in 1806, Stetson Hall, built in 1842, the Appalachian Mountain Club's Ponkapoag Camp and the Gills Farm Archaeological District. The Turner Free Library, opened in 1875, serves as the public library and belongs to the Old Colony Library Network.

The town also has an unusual bit of public-health history. The national Great American Smokeout grew out of a 1969 conversation with a Randolph High School guidance counselor, and the Randolph High class of 1970 organized a local quit-for-a-day event that went national in 1977.

For a seller these are small selling points, but a listing that mentions the library, the schools and the rail station gives a buyer from outside the area a picture of daily life.

  • Selling on your own: you save a commission but handle marketing, paperwork and buyer screening.
  • Cash sale: a faster, simpler close, with a price that can come in below a fully prepared listing.

Is Randolph a town or a city?

What is Randolph's population?

Who do I call about my Randolph property assessment?

Contact the Board of Assessors at Town Hall, 41 South Main Street. The board meets the first Thursday of each month at 5:15 p.m.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Randolph?

Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your alarms meet the standards for a sale.

It is $2.28 for each $500 of the price stated on the deed, according to the Norfolk Registry of Deeds.

Where is Franklin, Massachusetts, and is it a town or a city?

Franklin sits in Norfolk County, southwest of Boston, along the Interstate 495 belt. It is officially the "Town of Franklin" but runs under a city form of government, one of thirteen Massachusetts municipalities that adopted a city structure and kept "Town of" in the name.

The 2020 census counted 33,261 people. The area totals about 27 square miles, almost all of it land. The elevation is around 299 feet, and the ZIP code is 02038. The town uses a council-manager structure, so a Town Administrator runs day-to-day operations rather than an elected mayor.

What is Franklin's history?

Franklin was first settled by Europeans in 1660 and was formed from the western part of Wrentham. It was incorporated on March 2, 1778, and it became the first municipality in the country named for Benjamin Franklin.

The town had hoped for a church bell from Franklin. He sent 116 books instead, and in 1790 the town decided to lend them to residents for free. That collection became the Franklin Public Library, which is described as the oldest running public library in the nation. The Ray Memorial Library building was dedicated in 1904.

Franklin is also the birthplace of Horace Mann, often called the father of American public education. The Red Brick School, built in 1833, kept operating until 2008. St. Mary's Catholic Church, with about 15,000 members, is the largest parish in the Boston Archdiocese.

What does the land look like, and why does it matter for a house?

Most of Franklin lies in the Charles River watershed, with a small southwestern corner draining to the Blackstone River. Principal streams include Mine, Shepard's, Miller, Uncas, Dix and Miscoe Brooks.

Much of the marshland along Mine Brook is protected by the Army Corps of Engineers Natural Valley Storage Project. The town also has the Franklin Reservoir, a chain of lakes that is not used for public drinking water, plus the Franklin State Forest, the Franklin Town Forests and the Ernest DelCarte Recreation and Conservation Area.

For a seller, wetlands and protected open space mean some lots carry limits on what can be built or cleared. If your house backs onto marsh, a brook or conservation land, ask the town before promising a buyer an addition or a new shed.

What is the weather like in Franklin?

How do people get around Franklin?

Franklin has two exits on Interstate 495, at Route 140 and King Street. The MBTA Franklin/Foxboro Line stops at Franklin and at Forge Park/495, and the town is in the GATRA service region, which offers demand-responsive transit.

  • Households that drive to jobs along I-495 value quick on-ramp access.

When you describe your property to a buyer, give the distance to a station or an I-495 exit. It answers a question almost every out-of-area buyer asks.

Franklin Public Schools serves the town, and Franklin High School built a new building and demolished the old one in 2014. Tri-County Regional Vocational Technical High School accepts students from numerous nearby towns, and the Benjamin Franklin Classical Charter Public School serves kindergarten through eighth grade.

Dean College, founded in 1865, is a private residential college with over 1,100 students. It sits across the street from the library. Confirm school assignments with the district rather than relying on listing descriptions.

The Treasurer/Collector is at 355 East Central Street and can be reached at 508-520-4950. Payments by mail go to a lockbox in Boston, so check the town's page for the current address before mailing. You can pay online, at the drive-through window or in the office. The town also lets you request a municipal lien certificate online, and a buyer's attorney will normally order one before closing.

See the town's Treasurer/Collector page for payment options and the lien certificate form.

What does it cost to record a deed in Norfolk County?

Franklin deeds are recorded at the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds, which charges an excise tax of $2.28 for each $500 of consideration, or fraction of that amount. The registry's own example shows that a $155,000 deed requires $706.80 in excise tax.

The recording fee for a deed is $156 for recorded land. The excise tax must be paid with an attorney's check or a bank check, separate from the recording fee check. Your closing attorney normally handles this, but it is worth knowing the figure so you can read your settlement statement. The registry publishes the schedule on its fee schedule page.

What does Franklin require for a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate?

Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 148, Section 26F and 26F 1/2 require the Fire Department to inspect a property for smoke and carbon monoxide alarm compliance when it is sold. In Franklin, inspections are held Monday through Friday from 9 am to 11 am, and you schedule through the town's online link or by calling 508-528-2323.

  • All smoke alarms must be photoelectric, or combination carbon monoxide and photoelectric. Ionization alarms are not allowed.
  • If a central station company such as ADT monitors the home, someone who can reset the system must be present.
  • Battery-operated Nest alarms are allowed only in homes built before 1975 that have not been substantially renovated.
  • Nest systems are not allowed in homes built or substantially renovated since 2008, which need heat detectors in garages.

The on-duty Battalion Chief does the inspection, so emergency calls can delay arrival. The town's scheduling page lists the details.

What are your options for selling a Franklin house quickly?

You can list with an agent, sell privately or accept a cash purchase. Listing works best when the house is clean and updated. A cash purchase suits owners who are dealing with an inherited house, a move that cannot wait or repairs they cannot afford.

Franklin has a city form of government but keeps "Town of Franklin" as its official name. It is one of thirteen Massachusetts municipalities that did this.

No. Franklin's Fire Department requires photoelectric alarms, or combination carbon monoxide and photoelectric alarms, for home sale inspections.

The city touches Plainville to the north, Mansfield to the east, Attleboro to the south and Cumberland, Rhode Island to the west. A seller in the Falls and a seller downtown may use different post offices, since downtown uses ZIP 02760 and Attleborough Falls uses 02763.

Water shapes the ground. The Ten Mile River and the Seven Mile River run through the city, along with Greenwood Lake and Falls Pond. World War I Memorial Park in the north holds Sunrise Hill, listed at 390 feet, the highest point in Bristol County.

The area was settled in 1669 and became part of Attleborough, which was incorporated in 1694. In 1887 the East Attleborough village voted to separate and took the Attleborough name, and what remained became North Attleborough.

Industry came early. A brass forge opened around 1780, button making followed, and by 1834 Attleborough produced more buttons than anywhere else in the country. Jewelry became the staple trade. Jostens and the Balfour Company both operated here in the twentieth century.

That history is visible in the housing stock. Older mill-era streets near the center sit beside later subdivisions, and an older house often means older wiring, an older heating system and a deed that has changed hands many times. Buyers who finance may balk at those items, which is one reason owners of dated homes look at as-is offers.

Where is Northampton, Massachusetts?

Northampton is the county seat of Hampshire County, on the west side of the Connecticut River in the Pioneer Valley. It about 19 miles north of Springfield, 7 miles west of Amherst and 104 miles by highway west of Boston.

The city covers 35.75 square miles, including 1.51 square miles of water, and about 21% of the city is permanently protected open space. Florence and Leeds are villages inside the city limits. Hatfield and Williamsburg border it on the north, Westhampton on the west, Easthampton on the south and Hadley across the river on the east.

The Connecticut River's Oxbow lies within the city at the northern base of Mount Nonotuck. Land near the river and its old channels is where a seller should ask about flood history.

What is Northampton's history, and why does it matter for older houses?

Settlers from Springfield received a township charter on May 18, 1653 and arrived in the spring of 1654. Northampton became a city on September 5, 1883.

A few events left marks on the housing map. The Mill River flood of May 16, 1874 destroyed most of the Leeds neighborhood and killed 139 people in Leeds and nearby areas. Smith College opened in 1871 and the Clarke School for the deaf in 1867. The city then went through decades of economic decline before a cultural revival from the late twentieth century.

Houses here range from nineteenth-century homes close to downtown to later builds in Florence and Leeds. The older the house, the more likely it has an old foundation, an older furnace or a layout that a lender's appraiser will question.

What is the Northampton economy like?

Northampton is known as an academic, artistic and music hub, and Smith College is the largest of the Seven Sisters colleges. Wikipedia also lists Northampton High School, Smith Vocational and Agricultural High School and the Clarke Schools for Hearing and Speech among local institutions.

Downtown has had retail strain. The entry reports that nearly one in five storefronts was vacant as of September 2022. Events such as the Paradise City Arts Festival, held twice a year at the Three County Fairgrounds, and a Pride parade each May bring visitors.

How does Northampton's climate affect a house?

Northampton has a humid continental climate with cold, snowy winters and warm, humid summers. Precipitation is spread evenly through the year, averaging 46.14 inches, and the January mean daily low is 13 degrees Fahrenheit.

Cold winters stress heating systems, roofs and pipes, and wet months stress basements. The listed record low is minus 30 degrees, set in the winter months, so a house with an aging boiler or poor insulation can carry real repair costs.

How do roads and trains work for Northampton sellers?

Four exits of Interstate 91 serve the city, east of downtown along the river. U.S. Route 5 and Massachusetts routes 9 and 10 meet downtown, and Route 66 passes partly through.

Amtrak's Vermonter and Valley Flyer trains make three daily round trips between Springfield, Northampton and Greenfield. The Pioneer Valley Transit Authority runs local buses to Amherst, Hadley, South Hadley, Holyoke and nearby colleges.

One bridge crosses the river toward Amherst, which causes downtown congestion. For sellers, that means showing times and buyer visits can be slow on busy days. A direct sale avoids a run of open houses.

Massachusetts requires a fire department certificate for a sale. Battery smoke alarms over 10 years old must be replaced with sealed 10-year photoelectric units.

The Trial Court Law Libraries say real estate attorneys take part in sales by law and by practice, and most deeds are filed as recorded land at the registry of deeds. Deed excise comes from Chapter 64D. Smith's Ferry once belonged to Northampton and was ceded to Holyoke in 1909, so check that your parcel is in the right city.

How is Northampton governed, and who do sellers deal with?

Northampton has a mayor-council government. Gina-Louise Sciarra is the mayor, and the city council has nine members: seven ward representatives and two at-large members, elected to two-year terms. Calvin Coolidge served as mayor in 1910 and 1911, before he became president.

Three other bodies are elected citywide: the School Committee, the Trustees of Smith Vocational and Agricultural High School and the Trustees of Forbes Library. For a sale, the departments that matter are the Assessors' Office, the Treasurer/Collector and the fire department that issues the alarm certificate.

The city's name goes back to the Native name Norwottuck, or Nonotuck, meaning the midst of the river, and the 1786 Shays' Rebellion stopped the civil court from sitting here. Long local history means long title chains, and your attorney will review the deed history at the registry.

What schools serve Northampton?

Northampton's public schools include four elementary schools for kindergarten through grade 5, one middle school for grades 6 to 8, one high school and one vocational-agricultural high school. Private schools operate in the city, and charter schools are in neighboring towns.

The schools are listed here by type only. Attendance zones come from the district, so ask the school office to confirm which school serves your address if you want to discuss it with a buyer.

Where is Gloucester, Massachusetts, and how is it laid out?

Gloucester is a coastal city in Essex County that occupies most of the eastern end of Cape Ann, on the North Shore. It lies about 31 miles northeast of Boston, and it is far more water than most cities: of its 41.5 square miles, 15.3 are water.

The Annisquam River splits the city in half. At its southern end the river connects to Gloucester Harbor through the Blynman Canal. Only three links join the two halves: the canal bridge, the A. Piatt Andrew Memorial Bridge that carries Route 128, and the Boston and Maine railroad bridge just north of the canal.

The urban core sits on the north side of the harbor, and the rest of the city is made up of separate neighborhoods, so houses in different parts of Gloucester can feel like they belong to different towns.

  • East Gloucester, including Eastern Point and Rocky Neck
  • Downtown and the Harbor area
  • Annisquam, Bay View, Lanesville, Folly Cove and Riverdale
  • West Gloucester, including the Wingaersheek area and Magnolia

How old is Gloucester, and what is its history?

Gloucester was first settled in 1623 when men from the Dorchester Company set up a fishing outpost. That first settlement was abandoned around 1626, and the town was formally incorporated in 1642. It became a city in 1873.

Gloucester is known as America's oldest seaport. Samuel de Champlain mapped the harbor in 1606, and the Agawam people lived in the area before English settlement. The city later grew around fishing, shipbuilding and granite quarrying. Portuguese and Italian immigrants arrived in the late nineteenth century to work in the fishing industry, and their influence still shows in local festivals such as St. Peter's Fiesta, held the last weekend in June.

What does Gloucester's economy depend on?

Gloucester's economy still centers on the harbor, along with arts, tourism and marine research. In 2013 the port ranked 21st in the nation for fish landings, with 62 million pounds caught and an estimated value of $42 million.

Gorton's of Gloucester, founded in 1849, is a major seafood business based in the city, and Ocean Alliance, a marine conservation organization, is headquartered here. The Rocky Neck Art Colony is described as the oldest working art colony in the country, and the Cape Ann Museum and Gloucester Stage Company add year-round activity.

Gloucester is described as a popular summer destination, and that brings the city's short-term rental rules into play for sellers whose houses have been rented out, covered below.

There are roughly 1,800 more housing units than households, a gap that can include vacant, seasonal or second homes. Owners who inherit a Gloucester house from an older relative often live elsewhere and need a sale that does not require them to come back repeatedly.

How does the weather affect Gloucester houses?

Gloucester sits between Ipswich Bay and Massachusetts Bay, and the exposure shapes both the climate and the housing. Normals show about 47 inches of precipitation and 42 inches of snow per year, with record temperatures from minus 15 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit.

Salt air, wind and coastal storms wear on roofs, siding, decks and windows. Buyers' inspectors tend to look closely at those items and at basement moisture. The city's Inspectional Services pages list a floodplain development permit application, so if your property is near the water, ask the city whether it sits in a flood zone before you describe it to a buyer.

How do you get to and around Gloucester?

Gloucester is at the northern end of Route 128, and Routes 127, 127A and 133 also run through the city. The MBTA Newburyport/Rockport Line stops in West Gloucester and Downtown Gloucester, and the Cape Ann Transportation Authority serves the city and nearby towns.

The nearest national and international flights are at Boston's Logan International Airport. The nearest local airport is Beverly Municipal Airport. Buyers who commute to Boston often pay close attention to how far a house is from either rail stop.

Which schools serve Gloucester?

Gloucester Public Schools includes Gloucester High School, O'Maley Innovation Middle School, and several elementary schools: East Veterans, Plum Cove, Beeman and West Parish. The district also runs a preschool. Check with the district for the school that serves a specific address.

How and when does Gloucester bill property tax?

Gloucester bills quarterly. Bills are scheduled to be issued on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each is due 30 days after issuance. The first two are preliminary bills based on 25 percent of last year's tax. The third and fourth bills carry the actual amounts, once the assessed values and tax rate are set.

  • Abatement applications must be filed in a window that runs from the third quarter bill, typically January 1, to its due date, typically February 1. The deadline is firm.
  • A 1 percent Community Preservation Act surcharge, approved by city voters in 2008, appears on the bill.
  • Personal exemptions use a July 1 qualification date and an April 1 application deadline.

Details are on the city's assessor FAQ. Ask your closing attorney to split the quarter in progress between you and the buyer.

What does Gloucester require before a house sale closes?

The Fire Prevention Bureau handles real estate transfer inspections, and appointments are scheduled through the city's ViewPoint Cloud online permitting system. Fees are collected at the time of inspection online, or by check to the inspector.

One easy-to-miss rule is house numbering. Gloucester's ordinance, Section 21-4, requires numbers at least three inches tall in a contrasting color, visible from the street. A building without the right number cannot be approved for transfer, and a revisit costs $50. The bureau also points sellers to the state's smoke and carbon monoxide requirements, which vary with the age of the home. See the city's guidance for realtors.
