What are Gloucester's short-term rental rules?

Gloucester adopted a short-term rental ordinance that took effect April 1, 2025, under Section 5-63 of the city code. A short-term rental is a property rented for 30 days or less, and operators must register for a permit through the online permitting system.

Requirements include an information binder in the unit, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors with a battery log, two egress doors, and a safe and sanitary condition throughout. If you are selling a house that has been used as a summer rental, the permit and compliance status should be part of the conversation with any buyer. The full list is on the city's short-term rental guidelines.

What are the practical choices for a Gloucester seller?

Sellers in Gloucester tend to face an older house, a coastal exposure issue, or a property that is hard to maintain from a distance. A cash buyer who purchases as-is can take on those conditions. A traditional listing may bring more attention in summer and slow down in winter.

Before you decide, get the transfer inspection scheduled, confirm the tax installment status, and decide whether the buyer will take over any rental permit. Those three items are the ones most likely to hold up a closing.

Gloucester is a city. It was settled in 1623, incorporated as a town in 1642 and reincorporated as a city in 1873, with a mayor and council form of government.

When are Gloucester property tax bills issued?

Bills are scheduled to be issued July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each is due 30 days after it is issued.

The window runs from the third quarter bill, typically January 1, to its due date, typically February 1. The deadline is firm and the Assessors cannot grant an abatement after it.

Does Gloucester require an inspection when a house is sold?

Yes. The Fire Prevention Bureau handles real estate transfer inspections, scheduled through the city's online permitting system, and the building must display a house number.

Can I rent my Gloucester house short term?

Only with a short-term rental permit. The city's ordinance has applied since April 1, 2025, and covers rentals of 30 days or less.

Where is Melrose, Massachusetts, and what kind of city is it?

Melrose is a small city in Middlesex County, about seven miles north of Boston. It as sitting in the middle of the triangle formed by Interstate 93, Interstate 95 and U.S. Route 1, and it borders Malden, Saugus, Stoneham and Wakefield.

The city covers only 4.77 square miles, so almost every house sits close to a pond, a park or a train stop. The 2020 census counted 29,817 residents and 12,614 housing units, with 3.7% of those units vacant. Melrose peaked at 33,180 people in 1970, slipped for four decades, then grew 10.5% between 2010 and 2020.

For a seller, that history shows up in the housing stock. The first lots were carved out of farmland in the second half of the 1800s, so plenty of Melrose houses are old, and old houses bring their own checklists at sale time.

How did Melrose get its name and its shape?

Melrose began as North Malden, a lightly settled farming area that became its own town in 1850 and took its name from Melrose, Scotland. The Boston and Maine Railroad had added three stops by 1845, and Boston workers who wanted a country setting started commuting from here.

  • 1850: North Malden splits from Malden and becomes the Town of Melrose.
  • 1853: The town annexes the highlands from Stoneham, which set today's borders.
  • 1873: The town hall is built.
  • 1899 to 1900: Melrose becomes the 33rd city in Massachusetts, and Levi S. Gould takes office as first mayor on January 1, 1900.
  • 1982: Downtown Melrose is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Those three railroad stops are still the commuter rail stations on the Haverhill Line and all three remain in service today.

Which Melrose neighborhoods come up most often?

Ell Pond sits near the center of the city. Swains Pond and Towners Pond are on the east side near Mount Hood Golf Club, and the eastern reaches of the Middlesex Fells Reservation also fall inside the city line. A house near water or park land can show different grading, drainage and basement conditions than one on a hilltop, so a seller should expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at the lower floors.

How do people get around Melrose and into Boston?

Melrose has no major highway of its own, only a short stretch of Route 99, and relies on nearby roads and the MBTA instead. Residents reach Route 1 in Saugus, Interstate 93 in Stoneham, Route 16 in Everett and Route 128 or Interstate 95 in Wakefield.

Three Haverhill Line commuter rail stations serve the city: Melrose Highlands, Melrose/Cedar Park and Wyoming Hill. MBTA bus routes 131, 132 and 137 also run through, and the Orange Line terminal at Oak Grove sits just across the line in Malden. Access to Boston by rail is part of why Melrose has long been a commuter suburb.

What local institutions anchor Melrose?

MelroseWakefield Hospital, a 234-bed non-profit, is the best-known institution in the city, and Wikipedia notes it was home to the world's first cochlear implant. The Milano Senior Center runs programs for older residents.

The Melrose school district operates the Franklin Early Childhood Center, five elementary schools (Roosevelt, Lincoln, Winthrop, Hoover and Horace Mann), Melrose Veterans Memorial Middle School and Melrose High School. St. Mary of the Annunciation runs a private elementary school. The city has also appeared on screen, with scenes from The Town, Spirited and Beetlejuice Beetlejuice filmed locally.

Call as soon as you have a closing date, because the requirements depend on when the house was built and when the last building permit was issued.

  • Attorney and title: The Trial Court Law Libraries say real estate attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling in Massachusetts, by law and practice.

The state also bars sellers from conditioning an offer on a buyer's waiver of a home inspection for certain residential sales, under 760 CMR 74. Your attorney can tell you whether your sale falls under that rule.

Three Haverhill Line stations serve Melrose: Melrose Highlands, Melrose/Cedar Park and Wyoming Hill. The Orange Line stop at Oak Grove is in neighboring Malden.

Yes, you can sell a Melrose house as it is, with repairs undone or tenants in place. The smoke and CO certificate, title work and tax settlement still have to be handled, so ask your attorney about the order of steps.

Where is Bridgewater, Massachusetts, and how is it laid out?

Bridgewater sits in Plymouth County about 25 miles south of Boston and roughly 35 miles east of Providence. It covers 28.2 square miles, which makes it one of the larger municipalities in the county by land area.

The town borders West Bridgewater, East Bridgewater, Halifax, Middleborough and Raynham, and Brockton is about five miles to the north. The Taunton River runs through it, and Lake Nippenicket lies along the western edge. A large part of the Hockomock Swamp Wildlife Management Area is in the western part of town, so some house lots back onto wetland or conservation land.

These named neighborhoods and villages:

  • Stanley
  • Scotland Park
  • Pratt Town
  • Paper Mill Village
  • South Bridgewater

Two ZIP codes serve the town, 02324 and 02325. If you are selling a house here, the neighborhood name matters less to a buyer than the street, the lot and how close it is to Route 24, Route 18 or the train.

How does Bridgewater work as a town and a city at once?

Bridgewater is officially the Town of Bridgewater, but it runs under a city form of government. Voters approved the change in an April 24, 2010 town election, which replaced the Board of Selectmen and open Town Meeting with a nine-member Town Council.

The council has three district councilors and six councilors at large, and the Town Manager, Assessor and Tax Collector are appointed. For a seller, the practical point is that permits, tax questions and municipal records go through town offices at the center of town, and the assessor's page on bridgewaterma.gov is the place to confirm anything about your bill.

What is the history behind Bridgewater's housing and economy?

Bridgewater was set up as a township from Duxbury on June 3, 1656, and it was placed in Plymouth County when counties were formed in 1685. Over the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries its economy leaned on factories, including iron works, paper mills, sawmills and a boot and shoe factory.

The Bridgewater Iron Works is a registered historic site, and most of the factory was torn down in 1994 and turned into Ironworks Park. The old boot and shoe factory building stood off Broad Street next to the commuter rail tracks.

By the late 1960s the local economy depended heavily on state institutions: the Old Colony Correctional Center and other Massachusetts correctional facilities, Bridgewater State Hospital and the teachers' college that is now Bridgewater State University. The Department of Correction still operates several facilities in the Bridgewater Correctional Complex.

Public school students attend the Bridgewater-Raynham Regional School District. George H. Mitchell Elementary serves kindergarten through grade two, M.G. Williams Intermediate serves grades three to five, Bridgewater Middle School serves grades six to eight, and Bridgewater-Raynham Regional High School is west of the town center.

High school students may also choose West Bridgewater Middle-Senior High, Bristol-Plymouth Regional Technical School, Coyle-Cassidy High School, Cardinal Spellman High School, Norfolk County Agricultural High School or Bristol County Agricultural High School.

What does New England weather mean for a Bridgewater house?

Snow load is the weather risk with a documented local example. In February 2015 the roof of Mitchell Elementary collapsed under heavy snow, and students were moved to other school buildings.

A private owner can face a smaller version of the same problem, so a buyer's inspector may look closely at the roof. Brockton, five miles away, records about 34 inches of snow in an average year according to NOAA normals reproduced on Wikipedia, so Bridgewater owners should expect similar winters.

The Taunton River and the Hockomock Swamp also mean wet ground in parts of town. If your lot is near water, expect a buyer to ask about basement moisture, sump pumps and flood history. You can answer those questions from your own records, and your insurer can tell you about coverage.

How do Bridgewater property tax bills work when you sell?

Bridgewater bills real estate tax four times a year. The town has used quarterly billing since July 1, 2010.

  • Preliminary bills go out at the end of June and are estimates without a tax rate or assessed value. They are due the first business day of August and November.
  • Actual bills are mailed at the end of December and show the rate, the assessment, abatements, exemptions and previous payments. They are due the first business day of February and May.

The state approves the tax rate, usually in December. If you sell in the middle of a fiscal year, ask your closing attorney how the current quarter is handled and whether the bill is paid at the table. The assessor's online database shows the property record card for your address.

What rules apply when you sell a house in Bridgewater?

Two statewide rules come up on almost every sale. First, the deed excise tax is $2.00 for each $500 of price or fraction of $500, under Massachusetts General Laws chapter 64D, section 1, and the statute exempts instruments where the state, a town or the United States is a party. The registry of deeds collects it when the deed is recorded.

Second, the Department of Fire Services says you need a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale requirements. Call the Bridgewater fire department as soon as you have a closing date, because the department charges a fee and schedules the inspection. Battery alarms older than ten years or expired must be replaced with ten-year sealed photoelectric alarms that have a hush feature.

Before you choose, gather the deed, your latest tax bill, any permit records, and a list of known repairs. If the house is inherited, bring the probate paperwork. Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department for the sale or transfer of a home. Call the fire department once you have a closing date, since it charges a fee.

It is $2.00 for each $500 of consideration or fraction of $500, per MGL c. 64D, s. 1. Barnstable County has a lower rate of $1.50, which does not apply to Bridgewater.

Both in practice. Its official name is the Town of Bridgewater, but it has had a city form of government with a Town Council since the 2010 vote.

Where is West Springfield, MA, and why is it called the West Side?

West Springfield sits in Hampden County on the west bank of the Connecticut River, directly across from Springfield. Locals call it the West Side for that reason, and the city bills itself as the Crossroads of New England.

It covers 17.54 square miles, of which 16.73 are land, and had 28,835 residents in the 2020 Census. The Westfield River runs along its southern side, and a ridge of volcanic trap rock called East Mountain, part of the Metacomet Ridge, forms the western boundary. Hartford is about 27 miles away and Boston about 90.

What is West Springfield's history?

West Springfield was incorporated as a town in 1774 after more than a century of friction over crossing the river to reach Springfield's meetinghouse, and it became a city in 2000. The first settlers farmed good land on the west bank, and market gardening grew around Riverdale Road from the 1830s.

Rail changed the town next. The Western Railroad arrived in 1841, and for decades the railroad was one of the largest employers, with rail yards in Mittineague and near Memorial Avenue. Paper mills clustered along the Westfield River, including Southworth Paper, Agawam Paper and Strathmore. Holyoke split off in 1850 and Agawam in 1855, which is why the city's map looks smaller than its colonial territory.

Does flooding or storm history affect a West Springfield house?

Yes, water and weather are a documented part of the city's past, so buyers and insurers ask about them. The Westfield River flooded the town in 1936, when 8,000 people were displaced out of about 17,000. The 1938 hurricane flooded crops along Riverdale Road, and the floods of 1955 came with Hurricanes Connie and Diane five days apart.

More recent events were just as serious:

  • On June 1, 2011, a tornado touched down in West Springfield before crossing the river into Springfield, and two people died in the city.
  • On October 29, 2011, a wet snowstorm brought down limbs and wires, and some homes waited more than a week for power.
  • Dikes now protect low neighborhoods, and the 1950s highway work reinforced them.

If your house is near the river or the dikes, gather any flood insurance records and repair receipts. Those papers answer the first questions a buyer will ask.

Which West Springfield neighborhoods do listings mention?

West Springfield is a city of named districts rather than one downtown. Amostown, Ashleyville, Cayenne, Downtown (also called Center), Memorial, Merrick, Mittineague and Tatham. Memorial surrounds Memorial Avenue and the Big E fairgrounds, Ashleyville sits near I-91 and Riverdale Street, and Mittineague lies on the north bank of the Westfield River.

The Eastern States Exposition, known as the Big E, started in 1917 and is the city's biggest tourist draw. The former Eastern States Farmers' Exchange headquarters now serves as West Springfield Town Hall.

How do roads and buses connect West Springfield?

Interstate 91 crosses the northeast part of town, the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90) passes through, and U.S. 5 (Riverdale Street), U.S. 20 (Westfield Street) and Route 147 (Memorial Avenue) run through it. Pioneer Valley Transit Authority buses link the city to Springfield and to Westfield State University, and Amtrak serves Springfield.

There is no airport in the city. Bradley International in Windsor Locks, Connecticut, is the nearest with commercial flights, while Westover Metropolitan Airport and Westfield-Barnes Regional Airport handle general aviation. Highway access is a real selling point for a commuter, and highway noise is something to mention honestly if your street is close to the ramps.

How should winter weather and storms shape repairs before a sale?

Snow and ice are part of West Springfield's record, and roofs and trees take the brunt. The Great Blizzard of 1888 dropped over 5 feet of snow with 20-foot drifts, and blizzards followed in 1978 and 1996. The October 2011 storm snapped limbs because trees still held their leaves.

Before listing, walk the property with these in mind:

  • Look for ice-dam stains on ceilings and along exterior walls.
  • Check large limbs that hang over the roof or service lines.
  • Test the sump pump if the basement is below the neighborhood grade.

A buyer paying cash may skip these fixes and adjust the price, which can be simpler than repairing a house you plan to leave.

How are property tax abatements handled in West Springfield?

West Springfield assessors follow the state process that the Appellate Tax Board describes. Taxpayers can seek an abatement when the assessed value is higher than fair cash value, the price a willing buyer and seller would agree on without pressure, or when an exemption or classification is wrong.

  • The valuation date is January 1 before the fiscal year starts on July 1.
  • Apply to the assessors by the first payment due date shown on your bill.
  • The assessors have three months to answer, and silence counts as denial.
  • Appeal to the Appellate Tax Board within three months after that.

The city's assessors and collector post their own dates and forms, so ask them which installment schedule applies to your bill.

What does a West Springfield seller pay at closing?

The seller usually pays the deed excise tax. The Hampden County Registry of Deeds states the effective rate as $4.56 per $1,000 of taxable value or fraction of $1,000, with no tax when the stated price is under $100. Its fee for recording a deed is $155, and it takes cash or checks.

On a $300,000 sale, $4.56 times 300 comes to $1,368 in excise tax. Other closing items, such as a payoff, title work and a municipal lien certificate, depend on the property. The Hampden registry lists a municipal lien certificate at $80, which gives you a sense of scale for small charges.

Ways to sell a West Springfield house quickly

A West Springfield owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or take a cash offer from an investor. Listing works well when the house is in good shape and you can wait out showings and a buyer's financing. A cash offer fits when the house has deferred repairs, flood or storm damage, tenants or probate issues.

Whichever route you pick, ask for the contract in writing, check who pays closing costs, and confirm that the buyer can show proof of funds before you commit.

Frequently asked questions

Why is West Springfield called the West Side?

It lies on the west bank of the Connecticut River, across from Springfield, so people shortened it to the West Side. Early residents had to cross the river by boat to reach Springfield's meetinghouse.

How much is the deed excise tax in Hampden County?

The Hampden registry lists the rate as $4.56 per $1,000 of taxable value or fraction of $1,000. A $200,000 sale would carry $912 in excise tax.

Is West Springfield in a flood zone?

Parts of it have flooded repeatedly, including in 1936 and 1955, and dikes now protect low areas. Check the FEMA flood map and your insurance records for your exact address.

What is the Big E and where is it?

The Big E is the Eastern States Exposition, a fall fair that began in 1917 on grounds near Memorial Avenue in West Springfield. It is the city's largest tourist attraction, and the fairgrounds host events through the year.

Which highways run through West Springfield?

Interstate 91, the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90), U.S. 5, U.S. 20 and Route 147 all pass through the city.

Can I sell a West Springfield house with tenants in it?

Yes. Many buyers, including cash buyers, purchase occupied homes. Read the lease and the Massachusetts tenant guidance first, and ask the buyer in writing how they will handle the tenancy.

Where is Agawam and what is it like?

Agawam sits in Hampden County on the west bank of the Connecticut River, directly across from Springfield, and about 28,700 people lived there at the 2020 census.

The city covers 24.34 square miles. It touches West Springfield to the north, Southwick and Westfield to the west, Longmeadow and Springfield to the east, and Suffield, Connecticut to the south. Provin Mountain, at 640 feet, is the high point and anchors a trap rock ridge that forms the western edge of town. Feeding Hills, the western section along the Southwick and Westfield lines, carries its own ZIP code, 01030. The main Agawam ZIP, 01001, is the lowest standard ZIP code in the continental United States.

The figures come from Wikipedia's Agawam entry, which draws on Census Bureau data.

How is Agawam governed?

Agawam is a mayor-council city that still uses "Town of Agawam" in its official name.

It adopted a city charter effective January 1, 1973, and has elected a mayor since May 1989. Eleven council members, all elected at large, make up the legislative branch. For a seller, the council matters on one point in particular: according to the town's own FAQ, the decision to split the tax burden among property classes is made each year by the Town Council with the Mayor's approval.

How does Agawam's history show up in the housing stock?

Agawam was a small mill and distillery town for much of its history, then added residents quickly after the Second World War.

Population was under 8,000 in 1940 and passed 15,000 by 1960 and 21,000 by 1970. It has hovered between roughly 28,000 and 28,700 since 2000. Most of that growth came in the decades after 1940, so many homes date from the postwar boom, with older buildings in the village centers.

Some of the land has changed use. The Bowles Agawam Airport and the racetrack beside it were demolished in the late 1980s, and the area is an industrial park now. Six Flags New England stands on the river site where a cotton mill was built in 1810.

Which schools and parks serve Agawam homes?

Agawam runs its own school district, and buyers often start there when they compare towns.

  • Four elementary schools for kindergarten through grade 4: Benjamin J. Phelps, Clifford M. Granger, James Clark and William P. Sapelli
  • Roberta G. Doering Middle School for grades 5 and 6
  • Agawam Junior High for grades 7 and 8
  • Agawam High School for grades 9 through 12

For outdoor space, the city has Robinson State Park, a narrow 852-acre park entered from North Street, and a stretch of the 110-mile Metacomet-Monadnock Trail along Provin Mountain. The Massachusetts Veterans Memorial Cemetery is off Main Street.

Who handles property tax in Agawam?

The Assessor's Office at 36 Main Street handles values, abatements and mailing address changes, and you can reach it at 413-786-0400, extension 8700.

The town's real estate tax FAQ says the assessor values every parcel as of each January 1, using market, income and cost approaches. Ownership changes follow the recorded deed: the office receives deeds recorded at the Hampden County Registry of Deeds, and a new owner's name usually appears on the next billing cycle. If it does not, call the office.

Ask the Assessor or the Collector for the exact schedule and payoff amount before you set a closing date.

How do you contest an Agawam assessment?

You file an application for abatement, and for fiscal year 2026 the town set the deadline at 4:30 pm on February 1, 2026.

The application becomes available right after the first actual bill, which is the third quarter bill. A mailed application must carry a postmark dated no later than the deadline, and the assessors say they cannot waive it. The grounds listed by the town are overvaluation, disproportionate assessment, misclassification and a statutory exemption.

  • Pay each installment on time while the request is pending.
  • Gather recent sales of similar homes nearby and note the condition of each.
  • If the assessors deny the request or do not act, the state's Appellate Tax Board guide sets a three-month window to appeal.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Agawam houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What can go wrong if you fall behind on Agawam taxes?

An unpaid tax bill turns into a lien, and the city can eventually record a tax taking.

The Land Court's tax lien foreclosure overview explains the sequence. After a bill sits unpaid for 30 days, a demand can go out. If it stays unpaid 14 days after that, a taking can be recorded at the Registry of Deeds. An owner can still redeem by paying everything owed until the court enters a judgment of foreclosure. For an owner who cannot catch up, a sale before the taking or before judgment keeps equity in play.

What paperwork does an Agawam sale need?

Two items come up on nearly every Agawam closing: a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate, and clean ownership records.

  • The Department of Fire Services says a one or two family home needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the alarms meet requirements for a sale. Its guide tells owners to schedule the inspection once there is a closing date, and the department charges a fee.
  • Battery-powered smoke alarms over 10 years old, or expired, must be replaced with sealed 10-year photoelectric models that have a hush feature.
  • The deed is recorded at the Hampden County Registry of Deeds, and the assessor's records follow it.

Deed excise tax is set by state law and collected by the registry. Ask the registry or your closing attorney for the current figure on your sale price.

What do Agawam sellers usually weigh?

Most owners compare a traditional listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale and a direct cash offer.

A listing can reach the widest pool of buyers, but it can bring repair requests, showings and a wait for a buyer's financing. A direct cash purchase usually trims that timeline and lets the owner sell the house in its current condition, which suits inherited homes, rentals with problem tenants and houses that need roof or system work. The price is usually lower than a fully prepared listing would bring, so compare the net, not just the headline number.

Whichever route you choose, confirm what you owe in taxes, ask for the offer in writing, and give yourself time to read the contract.

Frequently asked questions

Is Agawam a town or a city?

Both. Agawam has had a city form of government since January 1, 1973, with a mayor and council, but it keeps "Town of Agawam" as its official name.

Where do I file an Agawam property tax abatement?

With the Assessor's Office at 36 Main Street. For fiscal year 2026 the application was due by 4:30 pm on February 1, 2026, and mailed forms needed a postmark by that date.

Who do I call about a change of owner on my Agawam tax bill?

Call the Assessor's Office at 413-786-0400, extension 8700. The office updates ownership from deeds recorded at the Hampden County Registry of Deeds, usually by the next billing cycle.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell my Agawam house?

For a one or two family home, yes. The local fire department issues a certificate of compliance for sale, and you should schedule it when you have a closing date.

Can I sell an Agawam house that needs repairs?

Yes. A direct buyer can purchase a house as it stands, though the price reflects the work needed. A listing may bring a higher price but often expects repairs first.

What happens to an Agawam tax lien when I sell?

The amount owed is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so ask the city for a written payoff before the closing date.
